News.title: Storm Boelo live: Train station flooded and roads closed as UK battered by 80mph winds
News.content:
There are 17 flood warnings in place across Scotland, according to the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (SEPA).

This means flooding is expected and people should act now in the affected areas.

One of the warnings, for Stonehaven, reads: "A combination of high tides and prevailing weather conditions means that flooding from the sea is expected to affect low lying land, roads and properties along the coast in Stonehaven.

"Flooding in and around low lying parts of Cowie is possible. Wave overtopping is expected to affect low lying parts of Boatie Row and The Links.

"Flooding impacts are expected around the time of high tide at 01:00 GMT Monday 26th October.

"Remain vigilant and remember, it is your responsibility to take actions which help protect yourself and your property."

Eleven flood warnings are also in place across Scotland, with SEPA saying this means flooding is possible and people should "be prepared".

One of the alerts, for Aberdeenshire and Aberdeen City, reads: "Hide tides together with a storm surge, spray and wave overtopping associated with Storm Boelo are likely to cause localised coastal flooding impacts around the times of high water.

"The time of greatest risk is the high water overnight Sunday into Monday. Impacts could include flooding of roads, properties and disruption to transport and infrastructure.

"Persistent heavy rain will continue across Aberdeenshire due to Storm Boelo. Small watercourses and rivers in western Aberdeenshire are responding to the rainfall meaning river flooding impacts are possible through Sunday.

"Surface water impacts are also possible. Impacts could include flooding of roads, properties and disruption to transport and infrastructure.

"Remain vigilant and remember, it is your responsibility to take actions which help protect yourself and your property."

News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle left 'quite surprised' as public make feelings clear
News.content:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle left 'quite surprised' as public make feelings clear

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle were reportedly left surprised and emotional by the reception they received from crowds during their recent visit to Nottingham

View 3 Images Harry and Meghan moved to the US after stepping back from their roles as working royals

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle made their first joint public appearances in the UK since returning to the country, with their visit to Nottingham last week attracting significant attention. However, the reaction to the couple's return reportedly came as a surprise to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex.

‌



The couple were greeted by well-wishers as they visited Nottingham, where they made several public appearances on Thursday. But according to a royal expert who witnessed the visit, the response was not quite what they had anticipated.

Speaking on The Royals with Roya and Kate podcast, The Times royal editor Roya Nikkhah discussed the Sussexes' return with executive editor Jeremy Griffin, revealing how the public reacted to their appearance.

‌



Roya said: "From what I saw, they were very warmly received. Very warmly received."

She added: "And I was told they were quite surprised by that. And I was told they were quite emotional about it because they weren't expecting anyone to turn out."

View 3 Images The couple were greeted by well-wishers as they visited Nottingham (Image: Getty)

‌



Harry and Meghan visited the Community Recording Studio (CRS) in St Ann's, Nottingham, as part of three public engagements in the city. Although the appearances were not official engagements on behalf of the Royal Family, Roya suggested they closely resembled traditional royal visits.

She explained that despite the Sussexes' team reportedly expecting the appearances to remain private, crowds gathered to catch a glimpse of the couple, alongside a significant media presence.

‌



Roya said: "The very fact that a load of press did turn up, you know, an absolutely huge bank of photographers at that first engagement at the community recording studio, just goes to show that wherever Harry and Meghan go, you know, it's going to get a lot of coverage."

The visit also carried personal significance for the couple, as Nottingham was the location of their first joint public appearance following their engagement in 2017.

‌



Among those waiting to see them was 90-year-old Irene Hardman, who brought along a framed photograph of the Sussexes from that earlier visit.

View 3 Images Prince Harry and Meghan Markle (Image: Anadolu via Getty Images)

‌



Meghan was visibly touched by the gesture, kissing Irene on the cheek and embracing her as they reminisced about the occasion.

The Duchess said: "Oh my gosh. How sweet is that? This was our very first walkabout."

‌



Irene replied: "I remember you, my darling."

The couple also greeted schoolchildren, charity representatives and other members of the public, with flowers, photographs and selfies forming part of their visit.

‌



Meghan was heard telling one woman: "Oh, it's great to be back", while Harry complimented another well-wisher's bright pink jacket.

The appearance marked Meghan's first public events in Britain in four years, following her attendance at the late Queen's funeral in 2022.

‌



Harry and Meghan moved to the US after stepping back from their roles as working royals in 2020, triggering the crisis widely known as Megxit.

The high-profile appearances were not official royal engagements. A letter to government stakeholders authorised by the King last month clarified that the Sussexes remain "private citizens", although the visit appeared to bear many of the hallmarks of a traditional royal engagement.

News.title: 'Black alien' body modification addict shows what he looked like 15 years ago
News.content:
'Black alien' body modification addict shows what he looked like 15 years ago

Anthony Loffredo, who dubbed himself the 'black alien' after transforming himself to look as 'extra-terrestrial' as possible, showed what he looked like 15 years ago

View 2 Images The 'black alien' has spent decades on his appearance (Image: INSTAGRAM /@the_black_alien_project)

It's quite hard to believe what the 'black alien' tattoo modification addict once looked like. Having spent decades on altering his appearance, Anthony Loffredo looked completely different to what he's achieved now.

‌



‌



Despite trolls constantly slating him on social media, the Frenchman ignores the noise and in fact, loves the transformation he's completed so far. Although it seems like he doesn't have much left to do, he constantly assures fans that he's far from over. Now have you ever wondered what Anthony, who's in his late 30s, actually looked like?

‌



Ensure our latest headlines always appear at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as Preferred Source in your Google search settings...

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

In a post on Instagram, where he boasts one million followers, Anthony wrote: "BLACK ALIEN PROJECT – 15 YEARS OF EVOLUTION. For most, going this far in transforming their body is suicide. For me, it's audacity, a vision, and a dream I chose to realise.

"15 years of transformation, sacrifices, and conscious choices. I never sought to look like others, but to bring my own vision to life. My body became my canvas, my transformation became my identity.

‌



"Not everyone will understand my path, and that's not the point. I dared to live my dream... 3, 2, 1, let the hate comments begin!"

The upload shows Anthony pre-transformation alongside what he looks like today. Back then, he had dark hair, a goatee and a chiselled jawline. He also had piercing brown eyes, which he has since tattooed on a number of occasions.

‌



Now nearly two years on from his transformation, Anthony looks completely different and even fans can't believe it. One said: "You look much better now."

While another added: "Too many haters in the comment section... his life his choice... nobody should be judge his choice if this choice don't hurt others." And a third added: "Hmmm it's your life, live it man."

‌



View 2 Images You won't believe what he once looked like (Image: INSTAGRAM /@the_black_alien_project)

Who is Anthony Loffredo?

Known as the 'black alien', Anthony didn't start modifying his body until the age of 26 where he started by splitting his tongue. He now considers himself an artist who refers to his ongoing development as 'The Black Alien Project'.

‌



He's had a number of painful body modifications, like amputating his two fingers, removing his ear and skull implants. He also sharpened his teeth, inked his eyes and almost tattooed his entire body in black.

Anthony grew more fame when he appeared in a 2021 interview where he explained his modifications "made him feel better about himself".

Article continues below

Arthur Bruel made a documentary about Loffredo, I Transformed Myself Into An Alien (or The Black Alien Project ), which aired on Channel 4 digital in June 2023.

News.title: DWP gives new update on Universal Credit assessment '272-day wait'
News.content:
DWP gives new update on Universal Credit assessment '272-day wait'

A question has been answered

View 3 Images Liberal Democrat MP Lisa Smart (Image: Dave Benett, Tracey Welch/Dave Benett/Getty Images for Sky News)

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has given a new update on waiting times for Universal Credit claim assessments.

‌



‌



The Work Capability Assessment is a process used by the Department for Work and Pensions ( DWP ) to decide how a claimant's health condition or disability affects their ability to work for Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance. Asking a question in Parliament, Lisa Smart, Liberal Democrat MP for Hazel Grove, queired the situation regarding reassessments in particular.

‌



She asked: "To ask the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, what the average waiting time is for existing claimants awaiting a work capability reassessment; and what steps he is taking to reduce that time."

‌



View 3 Images The DWP assesses Universal Credit claims (Image: Mike Kemp, In Pictures via Getty Images)

On Thursday, Sir Stephen Timms, Minister of State in the Department for Work and Pensions and Minister of State (Minister for Equalities) in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government and Labour MP for East Ham, responded: "Demand for initial Work Capability Assessment (WCA) assessments has risen, so we continue to prioritise initial claims. This enables us to ensure that claimants receive the right level of benefit and we establish capability for work at the outset of a claim.

"The department is taking a number of steps to increase the capacity of the Health Assessment Advisory Service to deliver WCAs, including reassessments for existing Universal Credit (UC) claimants.

‌



"This includes the recruitment and training of additional healthcare professionals across all assessment suppliers, alongside improvements to workforce planning to better align available resources with demand.

"The department continues to monitor assessment volumes closely and works with suppliers to ensure sufficient capacity is in place to reduce waiting times and support timely reassessment activity.

‌



"The department prioritises WCAs for new claims in order to minimise waiting times and ensure that individuals receive the correct benefit entitlement as early as possible. We recognise that some existing claimants may experience delays when awaiting reassessment and continue to keep the impact of these arrangements under review while taking steps to improve overall assessment capacity and reduce waiting times.

View 3 Images Sir Stephen Timms (Image: WPA Pool, Getty Images)

Article continues below

"As of October 1, 2026, the average waiting time for a WCA reassessment was 272 working days. Claimants awaiting reassessment continue to receive their existing rate of benefit in the meantime. Where a reassessment results in entitlement to a higher rate of benefit, any increase due will be backdated in line with the date entitlement arose."

It was noted that figures had been rounded to the nearest whole number. Further, an addendum to Sir Stephen's response clarified that information on the average waiting time for existing claimants awaiting a WCA reassessment was derived from unpublished management information produced by assessment suppliers for internal departmental use and was not routinely published as official statistics.

News.title: Nearly 1,000 public swimming pools closed since 2010 amid record summer of drownings
News.content:
Nearly 1,000 public swimming pools closed since 2010 amid record summer of drownings

EXCLUSIVE: Among constituencies without swim facilities is Dewsbury and Batley, West Yorks. The area’s pool and sports centre shut in 2024 after the discovery of RAAC concrete, and there is no sign of a replacement

View 3 Images 915 leisure centres have closed their doors since 2010 (Image: Getty Images)

Nearly a thousand public swimming pools in England have closed in the last 16 years, Mirror analysis has found.

‌



‌



Some 915 leisure centres have closed their doors since 2010, and shockingly, 10 areas have been left without any public baths at all. In a further 126 voting areas, there’s just one pool to go around thousands of locals.

‌



Our shock findings come after at least 35 people lost their lives to drowning this summer – a record high. Last night Vanessa Abbess, whose son Joe, 17, died in a rip current off Bournemouth beach in 2023, said: “As a drowning bereaved mum, I feel it is imperative that everyone has the opportunity to learn to swim and practice in a safe and lifeguarded environment.

‌



View 3 Images Ten constituencies in England have no pool at all (Image: Stoke Sentinel)

Andy Burnham makes vow to families of drowning victims after heartbreaking pleas READ MORE :

“The closure of public pools and therefore the loss of this opportunity to gain life saving skills is shocking. Drowning is preventable and needs to be treated by the government as a public health emergency. Anyone can drown, but no one should.”

In June, we launched the Save Lives for Sam campaign in a bid to make our waters safer for everyone. It has been backed by MPs, Olympic champions, national water safety organisations and bereaved families.

‌



Among constituencies without swim facilities is Dewsbury and Batley, West Yorks. The area’s pool and sports centre shut in 2024 after the discovery of RAAC concrete, and there is no sign of a replacement.

‌



It’s a similar story in London’s Croydon South, where the only pool has been closed since 2020. And in west Bradford, west Yorks, the 127,000-strong population is served by just one pool after the Reform council scrapped plans to reopen a second facility this summer. The worst year for closures was 2020, when 84 public pools were permanently lost.

Rebecca Cox, Interim Chief Executive at Swim England, branded the situation a “tragedy” and called on the government to intervene. She added: “It has never been more important for the government to provide the investment needed to build the network of sustainable pools the country needs for the future. Recent tragic incidents of drowning have reinforced just how important it is that everyone can access a pool to learn to swim and get the skills and knowledge to be safe in, on and around the water.”

‌



View 3 Images Joe Abbess drowned off Bournemouth beach in 2023

Simon Haycock recently issued a heartfelt plea for the government to deliver on our Save Lives for Sam Campaign, in his son's name.

‌



Simon, whose son Sam was just 16 when he drowned in Ulley Reservoir in Rotherham, South Yorks, in 2021, said adopting the changes would mean he could sleep better at night knowing he had made a difference.

In response to the open letter from parents, Prime Minister Mr Burnham said: "No parent should ever have to go through what Vanessa and Simon have been through. My thoughts are with them, and with every family who has lost someone they love to drowning.

‌



"I want to thank them, and the Mirror, for turning their grief into a campaign that will help keep other people's children safe.

The Mirror launched the Save Lives for Sam campaign after a horrifying spate of drownings in May. At least 19 people lost their lives in open water during the heatwave that month, including 13 children. The Royal Life Saving Society warns that 90% of accidental drownings in the past five years have taken place in open water.

Article continues below

It is estimated that more than 30 children drown each year in open water - and if hotter temperatures become the norm, experts fear it could climb.

A government spokesperson said: “We recognise the important role that swimming pools play at the heart of so many communities, providing a space for people of all ages to stay fit and healthy. We’ve committed £400 million to transform sports facilities, including public leisure, over the next four years and are working closely with sporting bodies and local leaders to establish what communities need to get active. We will provide further details in due course.”

News.title: Forensic expert who attended 7/7 bombings says Shoreham air disaster site 'like a bomb scene'
News.content:
When Dr Julie Roberts was called to attend the Shoreham air disaster, she could never have predicted the devastation that awaited her.

A decade earlier she had forensically combed through the aftermath of the 7/7 bombings, a series of blasts that shook London and left 56 dead and more than 800 injured. Now, stood on the A27 in West Sussex, she was greeted with a similar scene.

Chaos and debris from pilot Andrew Hill's Hawker Hunter jet lay strewn across the dual carriageway after it slammed into the tarmac, sending a fireball raging down the road. And somewhere amid the twisted wreckage were the remains of 11 men who lost their lives when Mr Hill failed to pull out of an acrobatic loop-the-loop stunt.

View 10 Images Forensic anthropologist Dr Julie Roberts attended the 7/7 bombings and also the Shoreham airshow disaster (Image: ©5 Broadcasting Limited / ©Candour ProductionsPress Enquiries: press@channel5.com NOTE: Paramount images are for the use of Press outlets only. Any blogs requesting access to these images are required to seek approval from Paramount directly. Contact press@channel5.comWhile we will continue to send out the weekly PI booklet every Friday, we have now launched the ViacomCBS Media Hub. This is an all-encompassing press centre where you can find the latest PI, press releases and other relevant information.)

‌



Parents used Find My Phone app before discovering teenage son had taken his own life READ MORE :

Today, in her first interview since the 2015 disaster, Dr Roberts told how the crime scene was more akin to a terror attack. The forensic anthropologist said: "With the Shoreham Air Crash it was comparable in some ways to a bomb scene."

She added: "The first thing that struck me was the scale of it really. Debris everywhere. Bits of aeroplane all over the dual carriageway, fuel spillage, cars, bicycles, lots of broken trees.

"It was apparent from the early stages of the operation that multiple individuals had died as a result of the plane crash, but we didn't know how many. There were obviously a lot of people there, hundreds of officers, all trying to make order out of the chaos.

View 10 Images Shoreham Airshow disaster pilot Andrew Hill was charged with 11 counts of manslaughter by gross negligence but found not guilty on all counts in March 2019 (Image: PA)

‌



"The weather at Shoreham was really challenging. Heavy, heavy rainfall in the two days that immediately followed the incident. Difficult working conditions but also not great in terms of preservation.

"We can learn a lot even from very small fragments of bone or smaller body parts. We can determine biological sex; we can work out what their living height was. We can see any injuries on the bone. And ultimately determine the cause of death.

"So one of the things that myself and my colleague did was to go around the site trying to limit the amount of further damage to any remains - you can't make it better but you can make it worse. So we covered them over."

View 10 Images Bob and Caroline Schilt - whose son Jacob died in the fireball - attended the scene just days after the disaster (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

‌



In the days that followed, Dr Roberts' team collected more than 1,250 separate remains. In an intricate forensic operation, DNA and dental records were used to identify those who had lost their lives.

But each night before they left the disaster site, her team of experts would pay a haunting tribute to the dead. Dr Roberts said: "I was working on site on the A27 for probably about 10 days I think, prior to moving into the mortuary.

"Once I'd relocated to the mortuary in Brighton, we started the actual examination process. Documenting and describing the body parts and also taking the DNA samples as well. At the end of each day when the remains were taken off site for transfer to the mortuary, we always had a little ceremony, if you like.

View 10 Images Anthony Mallinson - whose dad James Graham Mallinson was killed - said he has a bond with the other Shoreham families (Image: Eddie Mitchell)

‌



"All personnel who were working on site would form a corridor and the remains would be driven down the corridor with a funeral director walking up front so everybody got the opportunity to pay their respects to the deceased before they left site.

"Seeing the victims as people is incredibly important and we should never ever forget that when we're working in this field."

Former British Airways pilot Mr Hill was attempting a loop manoeuvre in the vintage jet when he crashed on Saturday August 22, 2015. The 1950s aircraft broke into four parts, destroying eight vehicles on the dual carriageway in West Sussex.

View 10 Images Mr Hill was performing a stunt in a 1950s Hawker Hunter before it plummeted onto the A27 in West Sussex and exploded into a fireball killing 11 men (Image: PA)

‌



Mr Hill, 62, of Sandon, Herts, survived after being thrown clear but spent a week in an induced coma. As well as the 11 fatalities, a further 13 people were injured in the deadliest air show incident in the UK for more than 50 years.

Despite desperate efforts to find those who had perished in the disaster, it took weeks to formally identify the victims. But within hours of the tragedy, families believed to have been affected were allowed to visit the scene.

Among them was Caroline Schilt, 64, and her husband Bob, 73, whose son Jacob, 23, was killed in the inferno as he travelled to play football with his friend Matthew Grimstone, 23. Speaking as a new documentary - due to be broadcast on Channel 5 - examines the tragedy, Bob said: "We could see the car Jacob was travelling in under a yellow tarpaulin. What was powerful about it was that we were able to contextualise, not rationalise it, but contextualise it.

"It brings it home to you and by that time, I think we were certain we were going to do everything we could to see everything we could, to kind of bear witness to it. From our point of view, it was a completely earth shattering event. It completely destroyed our family, along with many other families."

‌



View 10 Images The crash sent an inferno raging down the A27, killing 11 men and injuring another 13 people (Image: Daily Mirror)

Caroline said: "It was important for us to see the scene. What really touched me was that at the end of each day, after the forensic team had been doing all this painstaking collecting, that they then formed a corridor as the vehicles drove off to the mortuary. They paid their respects as the vehicles left. It was incredible, because no families were there to watch it, they did it becauyse that's how they felt about it."

And Denise Morriss, the sister of victim Mark Reeves, 53, said: "I think it was on the Tuesday after the [crash] we were all taken to observe the scene. You could see where every vehicle was, every - It was as it was.

"Obviously that made it very real. But they still couldn't say they'd identified Mark's body. You are left in a moment of limbo. You can’t have a scenario like this happen and not want to know everything they’re capable of finding out.

‌



"I just wanted to know that Mark Died instantly. I wanted to know that he wouldn't have wouldn't have seen it coming. Wouldn't have had fear, wouldn't have known anything."

View 10 Images Jacob Schilt was killed alongside his friend, Matt Grimstone, when disaster struck on August 22 2015 (Image: Adam Gerrard / Daily Mirror)

Over the next seven years, after their loved ones were finally identified, the Shoreham families faced a desperate search for answers as watchdogs, police and the coroner carried out their own investigations.

In its final report on the disaster, the Air Accidents Investigation Branch (AAIB) listed a series of failings including poor risk assessments. The AAIB criticised risk assessments which did not adequately protect people in areas "outside the control of the organisers".

‌



And the report said the risk assessment "was not suitable and sufficient to manage the risks to the public". It also said the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) was not required to see or approve risk assessments before issuing a permission to hold a flying display.

View 10 Images Retired engineer James Mallinson, 72, died during the inferno, with an inquest later criticising Mr Hill's actions (Image: Sussex Police)

The AAIB made 31 safety recommendations for the CAA and one for the government. In 2022, a coroner ruled all 11 who died were unlawfully killed and blamed Mr Hill's poor flying. But he was cleared of 11 counts of gross negligence manslaughter charges during a trial at the Old Bailey.

The jury acquitted him of 11 counts of manslaughter after hearing he was cognitively impaired during the flight. It emerged that the year before the disaster, Mr Hill flouted CAA rules banning pilots from flying over Lancing College as he performed at Shoreham.

‌



During a practice run at Duxford in 2014, he flew just 200ft over the M11 - 300ft below the minimum level. And in the same year at the Southport airshow, Mr Hill was given a rare "stop" call from air traffic control for flying just 75ft above spectators.

View 10 Images Grandfather Mark Reeves, who was killed in the Shoreham Airshow disaster, was "the happiest he had ever been" (Image: Solent News)

He was interviewed by the CAA and put on a "watch list". Mr Hill blamed the error on cloud and "goldfish bowl" conditions. It meant Mr Hill retained his flying licence and was free to pilot the Hawker Hunter jet when it slammed into the A27 a decade ago.

Denise said: "As a relative of someone, you've just lost someone because of their actions, you want blame, you want someone to take responsibility for what's happened." She added: "Your life goes on and you try to dwell more on all your happy memories and all the lovely things and all the things that I loved about Mark."

‌



But despite the devastation, the families now have a shared bond. Anthony Mallinson, who lost his father, retired engineer James Graham Mallinson, 72, in the disaster, said: "Us 11 families, we've now become a collaborative group of families that look after one another and can support one another in good times and bad times."

The Shoreham air disaster claimed the lives of Anthony Brightwell, 53, from Hove; Daniele Polito, 23, from Goring-by-Sea; Dylan Archer, 42, from Brighton; Jacob Schilt, 23, from Brighton; James Mallinson, 72, from Newick; Mark Reeves, 53, from Seaford; Mark Trussler, 54, from Worthing; Matthew Grimstone, 23, from Brighton; Matthew Jones, 24, from Littlehampton; Maurice Abrahams, 76, from Brighton; and Richard Smith, 26, from Hove.

Cause of Death is on Wednesday October 28 at 9pm - Watch or stream on 5.

News.title: Mum can finally stop worrying her boys will be forgotten after horror double house fire murder
News.content:
Mum can finally stop worrying her boys will be forgotten after horror double house fire murder

EXCLUSIVE: Claire Throssell has endured an unbearable loss, but still fights for other families and is on the brink of seeing a vital law change

View 5 Images Jack and Paul Sykes who were murdered by their dad get a touching memorial as their mum faces the grim 12th anniversary of their deaths (Image: © Glen Minikin)

A mum whose two young boys were cruelly murdered by their evil father says she can now stop worrying about her sons being forgotten thanks to a touching memorial.

‌



‌



Twelve years ago Jack, 12, and nine-year-old Paul Sykes died after Darren Sykes, set more than 14 fires around the family home and barricaded them in the loft in October 2014.

‌



The twisted dad, 44, also died in the fire, after luring his innocent sons to the attic, promising them a new £600 train set and chocolate bars. On Friday, their mum, domestic abuse campaigner, Claire Throssell, fulfilled her wish to create a lasting tribute to her sons, as she faced the grim milestone, marking 12 years since her sons were murdered.

‌



“I have always worried that when I am no longer here, Jack and Paul’s names will be forgotten, but now there is a permanent memorial and they will be remembered forever,” she said. “This month marks the twelfth anniversary of when both my precious boys fell asleep for the last time, so the timing feels particularly poignant.”

The Victims Minister, Alex Davies-Jones alongside the Lord Chancellor and Secretary of State for Justice, Alex Norris, and the Labour MP for Bassetlaw, Jo White, were at the ceremony to support Claire.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

‌



View 5 Images A touching sculpture was unveiled at The Farr Centre in Worksop in remembrance of two murdered boys (Image: © Glen Minikin)

The white stone sculpture, shaped as a pair of hands holding a heart, sits outside the Farr Centre in Worksop, the home of Nottinghamshire Women’s Aid, who raised the funds for the memorial.

‌



Claire said: “The inspiration for the design of the memorial comes from the idea of loving parents holding children’s hearts in their hands. Behind the hands are angel wings, who we hope are now looking after our precious children.”

As well as the moving tribute to Jack and Paul, a plague in the shape of a butterfly remembers the 66 other children who have died at the hands of abusive parents over the last 30 years.

‌



On the memorial to her sons, it says: "Jack and Paul. There is a legacy in your names, that’s full of laughter, light and love…countless more will be saved in your names’. It continues ‘hope shines brightly and always will give light to those facing their darkest days."

After the moving unveiling, which saw many in tears, the song ‘Bring Him Home’, from the musical Les Miserables, was performed. The piece of music was played by Jack, a talented musician, just months before he died.

‌



View 5 Images Many were in tears as the memorial was revealed in front of their mum Claire Throssell (Image: © Glen Minikin)

Claire, 54, from Silkstone Common, South Yorkshire, has spent more than a decade campaigning to abolish presumption of parental involvement in the family courts. Since 1989, judges have been told by law to initially assume it is best for children to see both parents.

‌



Now new legislation repealing the law, will be heard at the House of Lords on Tuesday, after it was successfully passed by the House of Commons. Under ‘Jack and Paul’s Law’, which is part of Labour’s Courts and Tribunals Bill, judges will instead act in the child’s best interests.

Claire said: “In 2014, when I lost my boys no one in government was listening, now we are one step away from changing the law. Presumption has no place in the law. Children’s safety should always come first.”

‌



She told those gathered at the memorial: "Today is about Jack and Paul but it's also about 66 other children. Sixty-six other children's lives. And for 30 years children have been murdered due to unsafe contact.

"But unlike Jack and Paul they are a child A or a child B, they were put in a serious case reviews they are now in files in Whitehall gathering dust. Government after Government successfully just brushed what happened under the carpet..."

‌



5 View 5 Images Claire Trossell's sons Jack, 12 and Paul, nine, were killed in a house fire started by their father. (Image: © Glen Minikin) 5 View 5 Images The memorial to the boys (Image: © Glen Minikin)

‌



Poignantly, the bill goes before the Lords, on the 12th anniversary since Claire’s eldest son, Jack, passed away, after fighting for his life for five days.

Claire said: “Jack has now been sleeping for as long as he was alive. I really struggle to understand and cope with this. It breaks my heart as a mum.

Article continues below

“He died thinking he had saved his brother, Paul’s life, after he tried to pull him out of the attic. The last words he said, when firefighters pulled him from the blaze, was ‘My dad did this and he did it on purpose’.

“I promised Jack and Paul as they took their last breaths, as they lay in my arms, I would not stop fighting until children were safe and free from harm. Not only am I now one step closer to fulfilling that promise but there is a lasting memorial to my beautiful boys who were taken far too soon.”

News.title: Boy, 16, arrested after late night disorder near HMP Birmingham
News.content:
Boy, 16, arrested after late night disorder near HMP Birmingham

A disorder was reported on Lodge Road, near HMP Birmingham and the Devonshire Arms pub in the Winson Green area of the city

View Image (Image: Google )

A teenager has been arrested following reports of a disorder near a prison.

Officers from West Midlands Police were called to Lodge Road, close to HMP Birmingham and the Devonshire Arms pub, in the Winson Green area of Birmingham. The report was made at around 10pm last night.

The police have now confirmed that a teenager is being held on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon. No injuries were reported, the force added.

A police spokesman told BirminghamLive: "We were called to Lodge Road, Birmingham, shortly after 10pm last night after reports of a disorder.

"Officers attended and arrested a 16-year-old boy on suspicion of possession of an offensive weapon. He remains in custody today while our enquiries continue.

Article continues below

"No injuries were reported and we are keen to speak to anyone who was in the area at the time and may know more about what happened.

"If you know anything which could help with our investigation, call 101 quoting log 4287 of 24 October."

News.title: Burnham open to 'honest discussion' on EU free movement
News.content:
The prime minister says he would welcome an "honest discussion" about the prospect of returning to free movement between the UK and European Union.

Speaking to the Sunday Times, Andy Burnham said a new relationship with Brussels could include full EU membership or joining the single market, requiring free movement.

Asked about Burnham's remarks, Angela Rayner told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg "you can't take anything off the table", adding the prime minister was saying "we've got to be pragmatic to get the best deal for Britain and he wants to have the conversation."

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch responded that the prime minister "hasn't thought this through", while Reform UK's Robert Jenrick dismissed the idea as "mad".

Migration dominated debate during the 2016 Brexit campaign, with the Leave campaign raising issues about rules allowing any EU citizen to move to the UK.

Burnham has previously committed to Labour's 2024 election manifesto which ruled out a return of free movement, single market membership or a customs union.

He has said that any changes would require a mandate at a general election, would is due by 2029.

"I think you have to have a very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this," he told the Sunday Times, external, adding he believed the type of migration had changed from revolving door movement of young people.

"Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different," he said. "The balance of migration has changed, hasn't it, since then? I think we've just got to have an honest discussion about those things."

But he stressed: "I can't see myself ever recommending anything that would involve joining the euro or Schengen."

The Schengen Agreement allows passport-free travel across EU countries. The UK was able to keep the pound when it was an EU member, but the bloc has pushed new members to adopt the Euro.

His remarks were made ahead of an EU summit on 20 November in Brussels, where the prime minister is expected to pitch options for a reset of relations with the bloc.

On Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, Rayner said she wanted to see the best possible deal with the European Union, which may well involve concessions.

"What the prime minister is saying now, and what I want, is that we have an honest conversation about the facts of what the trade-offs are to get the best deal for Britain going forward," she said.

"The frustration for me in the previous debate we had when we had the referendum is that a lot of those facts didn't get the airtime... So I would like us to have an honest conversation about what the trade-offs could be and then put that to the people at a general election."

Writing on X, Badenoch dismissed it as "yet another example of Burnham's foot in mouth syndrome".

She added: "Most people who voted for Brexit did so because they didn't want free movement. Too many politicians have failed to understand the significance and impact of immigration on communities."

Conservative MP and former chancellor Jeremy Hunt, who backed Remain, warned the Brexit debate was "incredibly divisive" and insisted the current Brexit deal can still be made to work.

"I was at the top of a government that was paralysed for several years while we were trying to wrestle with the implications of that vote and I think, having made the decision, we should stick with it and make the most of it - I think we can make it a success," he told Kuenssberg.

Pointing to the one million young people not in work or training, he added: "Surely our priority in that situation is to get those jobs filled by the young people we have here instead of parking them on welfare.

"Which is why I think it's astonishing to lead on the issue of free movement... Something that is actually going to stop young people here getting jobs."

But Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper told Kuenssberg she believed allowing freedom of movement would be "a really good thing for growth" and pushed for the UK to rejoin the single market, the customs union, and also be involved in the bloc's defence pact.

The UK currently has "the worst of both worlds" on immigration, she said, as it was excluded from the EU's "new asylum pact with biometric data" that could be used to "tackle the small boats crisis".

Reform UK's economy spokesperson Robert Jenrick told Kuenssberg he had never believed freedom of movement "was a good thing", despite supporting the Remain position before the 2016 referendum when he was a Conservative MP.

"I think it's completely mad, the idea that this country needs more immigration," he said, claiming data shows mass migration "has been a disaster for working people, for Brits".

"The last thing they want is their wages being undercut by a load of low wage, low-skilled migrants from overseas," he added.

News.title: Couple were celebrating anniversary before Bahamas tragedy
News.content:
He said both boys had been so excited and had been snorkelling in shallow water as they sorted out their towels and bags on the beach when the boys got into difficulties.

Both parents went into the sea and tried to save them as they were swept out by the current, he added, and the whole ordeal happened in less than 10 minutes.

Nathan said the loss of his 36-year-old "childhood sweetheart" was "unimaginable", but she was a "hero... in life and in death" as she helped to rescue the two boys.

"I've known her since infant school," he told the BBC. " We first got together when we were 14... so 22 years."

"There are no words I can use to describe Leanne, same as anyone she has ever known.

"She was the purest of people, the most generous kind and beautiful person who ever walked the earth.

"Our relationship was perfect. She was the perfect mother, the perfect wife the foundation of our entire family."

Nathan said: "Royal Caribbean and Virgin Airlines were absolutely incredible to us and made an impossible journey home so much easier.

Now, as he "keeps strong for his boys", a gofundme has generated nearly Â£9,000 in donations to support them.

News.title: Meghan broke contact with father in letter citing abuse claims
News.content:
The Duchess of Sussex broke contact with her father last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls, the BBC understands.

Sources close to the duchess said Meghan warned Thomas Markle in a letter that he would never meet his grandchildren.

It is understood the letter was sent to Markle, 82, while he was in hospital in the Philippines after having his leg amputated.

It has been reported that images of child sexual abuse allegedly belonging to Markle had been found in his former home in the Philippines and UK police in 2019 told Meghan about claims of abuse against him. Markle, who is based in the US, denies all such allegations.

Meghan has been estranged from her father since 2018. He pulled out of his daughter's royal wedding that year, citing ill health.

The letter sent in 2025 appears to be the end of what has been a troubled relationship between father and daughter.

It is understood details of the letter, first reported in the Sun on Sunday, external, include Meghan telling Markle that he would never meet his grandchildren, Archie and Lillibet, with Meghan making it clear she would never contact her father again.

She also apparently told her father that authorities were aware of the claims made against him.

Meghan's half-brother Thomas Markle Jnr claimed to the Sun on Friday he found a stash of images belonging to his father at his former Philippines home.

He is said to have told police he discovered child abuse videos and pictures among the items. He is understood to have contacted the US Federal Bureau of Investigations (FBI) about it in July.

The FBI has since confirmed it is aware of the allegations.

On Sunday Markle Jnr, 60, apologised to Meghan in an interview with the Sun for initially siding with her father during their long-running estrangement.

"I now know I have been protecting the wrong person for the past nine years," he said.

Philippines officials have confirmed they are investigating the allegations about Meghan's father, telling the BBC on Friday that its anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force was investigating the matter.

Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately said national police had secured Thomas Markle's computer and would carry out a digital forensic examination.

Meanwhile, Thomas Markle has given an interview to the Mail on Sunday, external in which he acknowledged paying for sex in the Philippines on past visits but denies sleeping with underage girls and ever possessing child abuse images.

News.title: Why the charts are full of old songs - and so are your playlists
News.content:
More music is being created than at any other time in human history. Every day, more than 100,000 songs, external are being submitted to streaming services.

And despite the deluge of AI music, external - Spotify says it has removed 75 million "spammy tracks" from its catalogue - real music still makes up most of our listening. The streaming service Deezer says AI accounts for just 0.5% of streams on its platform.

The problem for all those artists creating new music is that our listening habits increasingly show a love for nostalgia.

Luminate, an independent entertainment data and analytics company that tracks music, film, and television consumption first started tracking music streaming in 2008.

This year, it recorded that the streaming of current music (released less than 18 months ago) was significantly dwarfed by older music in both the UK and US.

In the first half of 2026, almost two thirds of the music played (about 60%) was released five or more years ago.

So, if we're stuck in a streaming rut, what's to blame?

News.title: The bitter row over military service that could shape Israel's future
News.content:
Furious protesters are denouncing Israeli security forces as "Nazis" - but this is not a scene from a pro-Palestinian rally on the streets of London or Paris. This clash is in the heart of Israel, in which hundreds of ultra-Orthodox men in white shirts, black fedoras and long black frock coats face off against the military police.

The flashpoint is a building in the city of Modi'in, midway between Jerusalem and Tel Aviv, where a young ultra-Orthodox Jewish (or Haredi) man lives. The police have come to arrest him after he failed to report for military service.

The clash in early October, seen by the BBC in a video, is one of many in recent months in which one of the deepest schisms in Israeli society has become ever more exposed.

This widening fault line is playing out against the backdrop of the wars Israel is currently fighting, including the unresolved conflict against Hamas in Gaza - as well as increasing violence by extremist settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

Once a tiny minority, the ultra-Orthodox remain a group apart even as their numbers expand year by year. Currently, they are estimated to make up about 14% of the population, and the birth rate within the community remains far higher than among other Israelis. If their numbers continue to grow at a similar rate, they could make up one-third of the Jewish Israeli population by 2050.

As the ultra-Orthodox community becomes bigger, so has the debate around the expense of supporting them with stipends so they can devote themselves to full-time religious study. Subsidies to the group are estimated to cost the government 35bn shekels (Â£8.4bn) per year and, until recently, they were exempted from military service.

Now they're no longer an insignificant minority, they're facing pressure to engage more with wider Israeli society.

News.title: Why the King's Caribbean tour could be 'biggest risk of his reign'
News.content:
The King will make three significant speeches during the Caribbean trip and will follow government advice not to issue an official apology for Britain's role in the transatlantic slave trade.

A senior royal aide said that the King would "not shy away from the darkest days of our past" but stressed that decisions over apologies and reparations were matters for government.

The current Burnham administration, like those before it, will not pay reparations.

Buckingham Palace says that acknowledging the wrongs of the past will be built into the King's programme in all three countries.

But apologies, reparations, and republicanism are rich pickings for campaigners and protests are likely.

This is the reality for the King and Buckingham Palace, and they are accepting of it.

Those who've worked on the planning of the trip view protests as part of the open debate in the region and security preparations include their possibility.

Lurking in the back of Royal Household minds will also be memories of the last tour by senior royals to the Caribbean in the early part of 2022.

Then, as the Duke and Duchess of Cambridge, William and Catherine found themselves facing criticism over the optics of the trip - images of the royal couple reaching out to touch the outstretched hands of Jamaican children through a wire fence looked clumsy. Engagements designed as tributes to past royal visits appeared outdated. And protests also caused the cancellation of a small part of the schedule.

Everything will have been done to avoid those kinds of missteps on the 2026 Caribbean tour.

News.title: Rosebank: Life on the oil field at the centre of a political storm
News.content:
When we landed by helicopter at Rosebank, this oil field was at the centre of a political storm - and set to be in the path of a real one.

We arrived on Wednesday morning, just a few hours after the UK government had granted consent for the production of gas from the Jackdaw field in the North Sea.

But already attention was shifting to this wild and windy patch of the North Atlantic â the next big decision for Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

Rosebank is bigger than Jackdaw, it would generate higher greenhouse gas emissions, and it could be far more lucrative for its owners, Adura and Ithaca.

News.title: Four ways Labour could raise money in the Budget without hiking income tax
News.content:
We're likely to hear a lot about the chancellor's "headroom" in this Budget.

That is the cash buffer the government has to help meet its own fiscal rules and reduce borrowing.

Economists think the buffer might have halved in the last six months from around Â£24bn to as low as Â£11bn, in part because of rising interest rates the government has been paying to borrow money from private investors.

The Chancellor, John Healey, might need to raise money to restore it, which would show the government's plan to reduce borrowing by the end of this Parliament is still on track.

At the same time, he is under pressure to find money to help people with the rising cost of living and to fund spending on defence. However, Labour's 2024 election manifesto pledged not to raise the rates of income tax, VAT or National Insurance.

Increasing taxes on capital gains or extending the mansion tax had been raised as possible options but have since been ruled out by government sources.

BBC Verify has looked at what other options could be on the table for the chancellor to raise some more money, external on Wednesday.

News.title: Budget to include £1bn for social and affordable housing
News.content:
Under the plans for the regions, an initial Â£285m in transitional seed funding will be allocated by the government next year to support mayors and local leaders - and reduce reliance on "fragmented bidding pots" in Whitehall, the Treasury said.

The government will also confirm that it will work with mayors to design a new Â£1.5bn borrowing facility from 2028, which would allow them to access capital needed to support local priorities.

The Treasury said this could be put towards new homes, bringing High Streets back to life, or improving transport links.

Healey said: "Mayors and local leaders know what their communities need to grow, which is why we are giving them more money, more power and more capacity to get projects moving, build homes and make the right decisions for their areas."

Areas across the country which are not yet strategic authorities will be able to access a share of the Â£285m to "unlock projects which will contribute to growth in their areas".

The prime minister said: "I'm calling time on local leaders going cap in hand to Westminster. That is no way to run a country."

Claire Ward, chairwoman of the UK Mayors Network and Labour's East Midlands mayor, said that having the "right powers and resources through increased devolution" would help turn "ambitious plans into reality and deliver real, lasting change" for communities.

Lord Sadiq Khan, Labour's mayor of London, said greater ability to invest could "help unlock transformational infrastructure projects" including the West London Orbital route, the extension of the Bakerloo Underground line and Docklands Light Railway, and the development of Stratford International station.

Departing Treasury entrepreneurship adviser, Alex Depledge, has criticised the government's treatment of start-ups ahead of her last day on Thursday - the day after the Budget.

She told the Sunday Times, external, that start-ups were being treated as a "sideshow" and should not be pushed to the "margins of economic policy".

"Keeping scale-ups on the fringes underestimates the contribution of our greatest companies, and we need to support and develop them on British shores at all costs," she said.

Leading up to the Budget, defence has also remained a key talking point. Healey resigned in June from his role as defence secretary in the previous government over the defence investment plan, which he claimed fell "well short" of what was needed to fund the armed forces.

He had called for defence spending to rise to 3% of the country's GDP by 2030, on the way to reaching a Nato target of 3.5% in 2035.

But urging him to commit to setting out plans to spend 3% of GDP on defence, the shadow chancellor said: "We are living in an era of extraordinary threats, and yet the chancellor is dithering over finding the money to pay the country's insurance premium... you cannot have a strong economy without a strong defence".

Responding to Andrew Griffith's comments, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said the Conservatives were to blame for failing to invest in the military while in office.

Streeting said the prime minister had made it clear that his government was "determined to give our armed forces the investment needed to keep us safe".

News.title: Murder charge after body found in wheelie bin
News.content:
A man has been charged with murder after a body was found partially within a wheelie bin, police have said.

Devon and Cornwall Police said Mohamed Abotaka, 36, of Grand Parade, Plymouth, was charged with the murder of 52-year-old Ali Barzai. The force said Abotaka was due to appear in court on Monday.

Police said Barzai's body was found in a service lane off Grand Parade at about 06:40 BST on Wednesday.

Det Insp Chris Lithgow urged people not to speculate and said a heightened police presence would remain in the area in the coming days.

News.title: Mum who died trying to save sons was hero, husband says
News.content:
"She was the purest, most amazing wife, mother and friend to have ever walked this Earth," her husband said in a Facebook post.

"I will never get over this, she was my soulmate, my childhood sweetheart, my one and only. The foundation of my entire family and the strength that held us all together.

"My boys had to witness something nobody should ever have to see of any age, but they know Mum died an absolute hero."

Gregory said he had also set up a fundraising page "for my sons and security after the tragic loss".

In the post on that page he described how his wife, who he had been with for 22 years, had held on to their son until he was rescued "but didn't have the energy to save herself".

He added: "I just have to be thankful for the hero she was in life and in death, and totally grateful for the fact my boys got out safely."

News.title: Four-year-old girl dies after fall from tower block
News.content:
A four-year-old girl has died after falling from a tower block in East London.

The Metropolitan Police said officers were called to the scene at an address in St Paul's Road, Barking, at about 11:00 BST on Saturday morning, following reports that a child had fallen from height.

Paramedics from the London Ambulance Service gave first aid and the child was taken to hospital, but later died from her injuries.

A Met spokesperson said the incident was not believed to be suspicious.

"Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with the child's family and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time," they said.

"An investigation into the circumstances surrounding this tragic incident is ongoing. However, at this time, the incident is not believed to be suspicious.

"We urge anyone with information about the incident to contact police on 101, quoting CAD 2424/24OCT."

News.title: Plan for Northern Olympics to get £7m in Healey's Budget
News.content:
The report will look in closer detail at how hosting the games could work.

It will consider the kinds of venues and transport links required, how different cities could share the games, how communities could benefit.

Crucially it will also examine how much it could cost as well as assess the chances of a bid succeeding. The Conservative-Lib Dem coalition government said in 2013 it estimated hosting in London had cost Â£8.9bn.

A report in 2013 by the UK Trade and Investment, which has since been replaced by the Department for International Trade, said it had sparked a Â£9.9bn boost to the economy through new contracts, sales and foreign investments.

But the estimated amount was queried by some, including the Federation of Small Businesses and the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (NIESR).

Conservative shadow sports minister Louie French said that while hosting an Olympic Games would "likely provide a positive boost for the country", the cost of proposals would require "careful scrutiny".

He said the chancellor should use the Budget to bring down everyday costs before looking to "spend millions in taxpayer cash on reheated announcements made by his predecessor".

French added: "The irony is that Labour's new tourism tax will create a cost barrier for sports fans wanting to visit the North of England for an Olympic Games."

The new feasibility study for the Northern Games will be done by government, UK Sport, the Northern Mayors and include the British Olympic and Paralympic associations.

Healey said: "Olympic legacy lasts way beyond the celebration of sport over the summer. The North hosting an event as big as this would be truly unforgettable.

"Britain's experience of London 2012 is proof we can host the world. I'm picking up the pace on our work to potentially bid for these prestigious games. It will lift communities, create opportunities and give the UK a huge boost."

News of the funding for the study was welcomed by the British Olympic Association, ParalympicsGB and UK Sport.

"We welcome the government's continued support for exploring the potential of a future bid for the Olympic and Paralympic Games in the UK in the 2040s," they said in a joint statement.

"Building on the success and legacy of London 2012, we look forward to working in partnership to explore this exciting opportunity and the benefits it could deliver for the nation, and for the global Olympic and Paralympic movements."

News.title: Thousands of people gather in support of Drumcree Orangemen
News.content:
The first part of the parade was followed by a series of speeches, mainly from members of the Orange Order.

This was very much an Orange Order event and not a political rally but inevitably there was a political tone to many of the comments.

There was explicit criticism of the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) Chief Constable Jon Boutcher, the secretary of state and the first minister, but also implicit criticism of the leaders of the two biggest unionist parties - the DUP and Ulster Unionist Party.

Traditional Unionist Voice leader Jim Allister was applauded but by far the loudest cheers were for the Orange Order's legal adviser Jamie Bryson and the local MP Lockhart.

She was invited on to the stage and presented with a special gift for her support of the Orangemen.

Lockhart was the only politician to take to the stage, where she repeated her challenge to the DUP leadership: "Profound consequences must mean profound consequences. Michelle O'Neill must go.

"That's where I stand, and this lady is not for turning."

Portadown District Master Nigel Dawson warned politicians that they could face consequences at the next election over the Drumcree dispute.

"Politicians need to remember that we put them into office and we can take them out of office," he said.

He added that the Orange Order had won the right "to return home via our traditional route and Portadown District intends to exercise that right on a date and time of our choosing, and if necessary, without further recourse".

Orange Order Deputy District Master Alistair Power said Drumcree must not be allowed to divide unionism.

"It should not be used by parties to attack each other publicly over differences of opinion," he added. "We need to stand united."

News.title: Habitat destroyed by Cairngorms fire to be restored with government funding
News.content:
More than Â£1m is to be spent on nature recovery projects, including the restoration of habitats destroyed by a fire which ripped through a huge area of hillside in the Cairngorms.

The Scottish government funding will support habitat, species and river restoration, control of invasive non-native species and deer management across Scotland.

It includes Â£150,100 for recovery and nature restoration work following the Abernethy wildfire in the Cairngorms in July, to restore damaged habitats, help wildlife recover and reduce the risk of future wildfires.

News.title: Reward offered over murder in flat used as brothel
News.content:
A Â£20,000 reward is being offered by Crimestoppers in connection with the murder of a man who was found dead in a Birmingham flat in 2022.

Jinming Zhang had been stabbed multiple times before he was found in the property, which police said was being used as a brothel, in Moseley Street in Digbeth.

West Midlands Police previously released CCTV of a suspect, while a DNA sample from the suspected killer found at the scene did not produce a match on the national database.

The case was featured in the BBC series of Forensics: The Real CSI last year, which revealed police believed the murder suspect may have sustained a hand injury in the frenzied attack.

Jenny Birch, who has been overseeing the investigation, urged anyone with information "no matter how small" to contact police.

"Someone out there knows something, and we won't give up until we have answers," she said.

News.title: Larry David said he would rather ‘do time in prison’ than make another season of Seinfeld, biographer claims
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Larry David found it “torturous” to run the Emmy-winning sitcom Seinfeld, his biographer has said.

Blake J. Harris, the author behind the biography Emperor of Nothing: The Making of Larry David, said in a new interview that David put himself under extreme pressure when working on the sitcom that launched his career in the 90s.

Speaking to The Daily Beast’s Obsessed podcast, Harris said that ahead of the show's fifth season, which started airing in 1993, David told some associates during a lunch date that he would “rather spend a year in prison than do another season of Seinfeld.”

“Part of it is shtick or him being kind of funny, but part of it hints at how torturous it was for him to run Seinfeld,” Harris explained.

He continued: “That torture largely came from the pressure he put on himself to come up with good ideas, which is a constant theme in the book.”

open image in gallery Larry David found it ‘torturous’ to run the hit sitcom ‘Seinfeld,’ his biographer has said ( Getty )

According to Harris, David’s determination to make the show excellent was the source of his stress.

“To him, every second of every episode needed to hit a certain caliber of quality and trying to clear that bar – day after day after day – seemed unsustainable,” he added.

“Or put more succinctly, as one of Larry’s future Seinfeld colleagues would later tell The Hollywood Reporter, ‘[Larry’s] so consumed with perfection that doing episodes is as painful for him as passing kidney stones.”

Harris also recounted David reading a draft of the biography and saying, “I think we’ve done too much of this – of me being anxious and worried about coming up with ideas.”

Harris said: “And I said, ‘No, we haven’t, because that’s all that anyone talks about... you were always saying this.’”

David, who co-created the show with Jerry Seinfeld, served as the head writer and executive producer on the first seven seasons, and returned to co-write the series finale in season nine.

Elsewhere in the biography, Harris reveals that David and the late director Rob Reiner nearly made a movie together, but it never happened.

Harris recalls in the book that David had been working on the 1983 unproduced screenplay Prognosis: Negative, and had asked Reiner – who was then known for his Emmy-winning performance as Michael Stivic in All in the Family – to produce it.

Ultimately, Reiner was busy working on his directorial debut, the acclaimed mockumentary This Is Spinal Tap, about a fictional aging British heavy metal band on tour in the U.S.

Harris wrote: “And the project he wound up working on — his directorial debut — was a pretty risky venture: a fake documentary about a fictional rock band that Reiner co-wrote with three friends and then filmed over the course of only five weeks.”

News.title: How will the Israeli election work and when will the result be announced?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Israelis will head to the polls on Tuesday 27 October to cast their vote to elect the Knesset, after three years of war waged in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran, which have plunged the Middle East into turmoil.

Much of the election is centred around Benjamin Netanyahu, who is seeking another term after a combined 19 years in power, but neither he nor the opposition has a clear path to a governing majority.

Due to the fragmented political system, the country may have to wait weeks or even months before a new government is confirmed.

How do the elections work?

There are 38 different parties contesting the election, but most will not get enough votes to secure one of the 120 seats in the Knesset.

open image in gallery A cyclist passes a campaign billboard featuring Netanyahu, left, and his main rival, opposition candidate Gadi Eisenkot, with a message in Hebrew that reads ‘The race is tight’ ( AP )

Israeli elections are based on nationwide proportional representation. Citizens cast votes for a single party – not for individual candidates – and the party’s number of seats is determined by the proportion of the national vote it receives.

To actually enter the Knesset, a party must receive at least 3.25 per cent of the vote, or four seats.

Historically, no single party has won a majority, ​so governments are formed by a coalition. If no one manages to form a coalition with a 61-seat majority, citizens return to the ballot box.

open image in gallery A worker hangs a campaign billboard in Jerusalem featuring Gadi Eisenkot, leader of Yashar party, ahead of Israel’s general election ( AP )

When will the result be announced?

Polls open at 7am local time and close at 10pm that night. The official results will be confirmed on Tuesday 4 November.

But the whole process will take much longer, ranging from 20 to 100 days. In the past two decades, no government has been sworn in in less than 50 days.

After a coalition agreement is signed, the Knesset convenes a special session during which the designated prime minister presents the new government and its policy agenda.

open image in gallery People walk past election campaign banners in the Ben Yehuda Market area of Jerusalem on Thursday 22 October ( AFP/Getty )

A formal vote is then held, and if the new government wins the vote, it starts its tenure.

What are the main issues at stake?

The election is viewed domestically as one of the most consequential in the history of Israel.

The outcome could have profound consequences for Palestinians and Israel’s relations with neighbouring states, as well as international partners like the US and Europe.

open image in gallery An ultra-Orthodox Jewish man walks past a Palestinian flag painted on a wall at the Mea Shearim neighbourhood in Jerusalem ( AFP/Getty )

Some of the main issues centre on the debate over exemptions from military service for ultra-Orthodox Jews, how the state should investigate its inability to prevent the October 7 2023 Hamas attacks and future concessions in Gaza, the occupied West Bank and Lebanon.

Israel’s wars have also put pressure on the economy, so the cost of living will definitely weigh on people’s minds when casting their votes. For context, the state’s defence budget has doubled since 2023.

Who is leading the polls?

Two main blocs – of nearly equal weight – are facing off against each other. One is an alliance of far-right parties dominated by Netanyahu, and the other camp is led by Yashar’s Gadi Eisenkot, a former head of the Israel Defence Forces.

open image in gallery Israeli forces deploy at the scene following an exchange of fire with two Palestinian men at a northern checkpoint in Hebron, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank ( AFP/Getty )

Current polling puts the two in a tight race to become prime minister. But the PM’s coalition is likely to fall short of a majority, according to a new poll reported by The Independent .

Based on responses, the most likely scenario would see the right-wing “Haredi” bloc – including Netanyahu’s Likud and Shas – securing 52-54 seats. That includes a drop in seats for Likud from 32 to 19 and a decrease to six for Shas.

Meanwhile, the Eisenkot-led opposition is predicted to secure the most seats, although other liberal parties it could form a coalition with are forecast to collectively pool fewer votes than their right-wing partners.

Dr Nimrod Nir, of Agam Labs, said that “the real political drama will begin the morning after the election”.

“Israel’s election is not a single game, but a tournament – and election day is only the opening round,” he added.

“Our polling suggests that neither bloc is likely to secure a governing majority, leaving three possible outcomes: a unity government bringing Netanyahu together with more liberal parties, an alternative coalition backed by Arab parties, or yet another election.”

News.title: Brazilians head to the polls to vote in tense  Lula vs Bolsonaro runoff election
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Voting got underway across Brazil on Sunday in a deeply divided presidential runoff between incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and Flávio Bolsonaro, a contest set to decide whether the U.S. will substantially broaden its footprint in Latin America.

Pre-election surveys showed a tight race between the candidates, each needing over 50% of the vote to secure leadership of Brazil in January.

The ballot contrasts Lula, a veteran left-of-center figure, with Bolsonaro, an ally of U.S. President Donald Trump and the son of imprisoned former President Jair Bolsonaro.

Flávio Bolsonaro finished ahead of Lula by upwards of 2.2 million votes during the initial round earlier this month.

Even so, more than 33 million of the nearly 160 million eligible citizens abstained, despite voting being mandatory.

A sharp ideological divide separates the contenders. Lula and Bolsonaro hold opposing views across a range of issues, including social welfare initiatives, climate change, and U.S.-Brazil relations.

Victory for Bolsonaro would mark a rightward pivot for Latin America's largest economy and most populous country, capping a year in which Trump allies secured electoral victories in Chile, Peru, and Colombia.

Conversely, a Lula victory would ensure that both Brazil and Mexico, the region's second most populous nation led by President Claudia Sheinbaum, remain governed by left-of-center figures.

In many respects, the runoff represents a repeat battle between Brazil's deeply divided political camps, which evoke both fierce devotion and intense hostility.

Four years ago, Lula defeated Bolsonaro’s father by the smallest margin since the restoration of democracy in 1985, and polling suggests an even tighter finish this time.

Voters wait in line before polls open in Brazil ( Getty )

Security and cost-of-living concerns Lula, who previously served as president from 2003 to 2010, has navigated a difficult reelection fight centered on public anxiety over security and living expenses. Bolsonaro positioned a hardline stance on crime at the heart of his platform while promising to reduce food costs.

Both contenders have been dogged by corruption allegations tied to family members and allies, with Bolsonaro caught up in a major scandal currently sweeping the country. Lula spent over a year behind bars on corruption charges that were ultimately annulled.

Shadows have been cast over Bolsonaro's campaign following his admission that he received roughly $12 million from disgraced former banker Daniel Vorcaro to create a film about his father's life. Authorities are investigating him for tax evasion, money laundering, and corruption related to the funds.

When Bolsonaro arrived to vote at a Rio de Janeiro school around 8 a.m., his supporters shouted "Lula, thief, your place is in prison" while backing crowds for Lula responded with opposing chants.

"The time of real change has arrived," Bolsonaro told journalists. "Brazil can’t go on another four years on its current trajectory."

Fabianne Borges Santoro, a 45-year-old physiotherapist living in Rio de Janeiro, formerly voted for Lula’s party but now views it as linked to corruption.

"The Workers’ Party has been in power for a long time and the voice of the people is saying that we need change to see improvements in security and the cost of living," she said.

Leading up to election day, Lula repeatedly depicted Bolsonaro—whose father is under house arrest following an attempted coup—as a danger to democratic rule. Bolsonaro has promised to push for an amnesty for his father if he wins.

Pending retirements mean the incoming president will appoint at least three of the 11 Supreme Court justices during his term. Bolsonaro has frequently criticized the high court—which faces its own corruption scandal—and vowed to deliver judicial reform.

In a bid to win over undecided voters following his first-round defeat, Lula rolled out expensive policy incentives. His administration recently backed a small-business debt relief initiative and pledged free public transport on weekends. The incumbent also secured a boost when the Senate passed a popular government-supported measure to eliminate the six-day working week.

Speaking after voting in Sao Bernardo do Campo—the city where he launched his political journey as a labor leader in the 1960s—Lula expressed appreciation for the wave of support he received in the final days of the race.

"It is a lot of generosity, a lot of care, a lot of love. I will be forever grateful," Lula said.

"Lula is a man of the people and he knows what it’s like to be poor," said Luzia da Souza, who runs a bar in a middle-class neighborhood of Rio de Janeiro. "I find it impossible not to vote for him."

The Trump administration has loomed large Prior to the election, Lula raised concerns regarding potential U.S. interference in domestic politics after the Trump administration levied steep tariffs on Brazilian exports, penalized the Supreme Court justice who oversaw the case leading to Jair Bolsonaro's sentencing, and designated drug cartels as foreign terrorist organizations—a move analysts suggest was calculated to make Lula appear weak on crime.

Flávio Bolsonaro has highlighted his close connection to the White House, arguing that Brazil must negotiate more advantageous agreements with the Trump administration, particularly regarding the rare earth minerals sector. Brazil holds an estimated 21 million tons of these reserves, ranking behind only China. He rejects claims that he is receiving assistance from the U.S. government.

Balloting across Brazil is carried out electronically, with final outcomes typically available within hours after polling locations close at 5 p.m. in Brasilia.

News.title: Meghan cut off contact with her father Thomas Markle last year over sex abuse claims
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in
