The Duchess of Sussex last year wrote to her father last year telling him she knew about sex abuse claims against him and that she would never allow him to meet his grandchildren, it has been reported.

Meghan told Thomas Markle, 82, that it was the last time she would contact him in the letter, understood to have been sent while he was in hospital in the Philippines after having his leg amputated, sources close to her told the BBC.

Authorities in the Philippines are currently investigating allegations that Meghan’s estranged father kept a hoard of child sex abuse images at his former home there – claims he denies and has called a “bunch of lies”.

It is understood details of the letter sent by Meghan, first reported in The Sun on Sunday, included her telling him that he would never meet her children, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet, and and her insisting she would never contact her father again. She also reportedly told him that authorities were aware of the claims made against him.

The Metropolitan Police on Saturday confirmed it passed a letter featuring claims of alleged offending outside the UK by Thomas Markle Sr to Meghan and her husband Prince Harry, but in an astonishing admission, said it did not pass those claims on to other relevant law enforcement.

open image in gallery The Duchess of Sussex wrote a letter to her father last year saying she was cutting off contact over the claims ( Instagram )

The force said it received a letter in 2019 about a “number of claims” relating to Mr Markle, adding it was “reviewing the handling of this matter”, including whether it needs to be referred to the police watchdog over its conduct.

On Friday, Meghan revealed she was made aware of “disturbing allegations” about her father in 2018. She said she was shown a letter sent to Scotland Yard eight years ago making “troubling” allegations against Thomas Markle Sr and she was assured that these were being investigated.

A spokesperson for the Duchess of Sussex addressed the discrepancies in dates and said if police had a time-stamped record confirming the letter was reviewed in 2019, then that “should be treated as the accurate reference point for when it was received and shared with the Duchess”.

They said on Saturday afternoon that it was “understandable” because of the passage of time that Meghan “may have been mistaken by a few months”.

A Met Police spokesperson said on Saturday afternoon: “Following a thorough review of Met Police systems and records, we have confirmed that in January 2019, we received a letter containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.

“It was sent to the MPS Protection Command to raise concerns in relation to the security of the Duchess of Sussex. The letter was reviewed and a decision was made that it should be passed to the office of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for their awareness.

“The details of the allegations in the letter were not shared with other law enforcement agencies. The MPS is reviewing the handling of this matter in 2019 and considering whether a referral to the IOPC is necessary to review our approach.”

open image in gallery Thomas Markle has admitted paying for sex, but denies claims he has a stash of child sex abuse images ( Instagram )

Mr Markle has admitted to paying for sex in the Philippines, but has continued to deny allegations he had a hoard of child sex abuse images.

According to The Sun, Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, alleged that he found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.

He reportedly told police in the country that he discovered the child abuse pictures and videos mixed up with innocent family mementos. The newspaper said he also contacted FBI investigators in the US in July.

Authorities in the Philippines said they are investigating the allegations.

In an interview with the Mail on Sunday, Thomas Markle Sr said he has “never had sex with anyone under the age of 18”.

He told the paper that when he was single he travelled to the Philippines at least twice and “slept with prostitutes”.

“I like Asian women but that is not a crime,” he said.

“I am not well enough to go to the Philippines but I will speak to anyone who wants to talk to me. I have nothing to hide.”

Mr Markle is learning to walk again at a nursing facility in Florida after he had his leg amputated during life-saving surgery in 2025.

He said he would also welcome any forensic examination of his computer, telling the Mail on Sunday: “If there is anything bad on there, it was put there by someone else.”

Mr Markle’s eldest daughter, Samantha Markle, defended her father, telling the paper: “I believe this is a set-up.”

News.title: Rayner says ‘nothing off the table’ for Burnham to undo harms of Brexit
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Angela Rayner has confirmed that nothing is off the table for Andy Burnham as he looks to undo the harms of Brexit and secure a better deal with the EU.

The prime minister on Saturday admitted he is open to reintroducing freedom of movement in an intervention that has boosted hopes that the UK could look to rejoin the bloc after the next general election.

He said he wants to consider various options for a new relationship with Brussels, which could include a return to full EU membership or joining the single market – which would require free movement, and Ms Rayner suggested he is looking at options to include in Labour’s next manifesto.

The housing secretary said: “The prime minister is clear that you can’t take anything off the table when you’re having a conversation. But the prime minister is not saying we’re going back to where we were in 2016. He’s saying we’ve got to be pragmatic to get the best deal for Britain and he wants to have the conversation.”

It came as new data shared with The Independent ahead of Wednesday’s Budget reveals that chancellor John Healey would have far more money to deal with Britain’s problems if Brexit had not happened.

Research carried out by the pro-EU group European Movement UK suggests that the UK has missed out on between £180bn and £240bn of growth since leaving the EU in 2020, while campaign group Best for Britain estimates that there is a shortfall on annual tax receipts of about £40bn.

open image in gallery Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will meet again at a major UK-EU summit in November ( PA )

The campaign group estimated that rejoining the EU would boost UK growth by “at least £92bn.”

Ms Rayner was challenged by the BBC’s Laura Kuenssberg on her Sunday morning TV show over the prime minister telling voters in Makerfield before the summer when he fought the by-election there to return to parliament that “now is not the time” to reopen the Brexit debate.

Ms Rayner insisted there needs to be “an honest discussion” about Brexit while not turning the clock back 10 years to the referendum.

The approach is very different to the one taken by Sir Keir Starmer who refused to reconsider his “red lines” on not rejoining the EU, single market or customs union and ruled out freedom of movement.

It came after the prime minister told The Sunday Times that he is considering reintroducing freedom of movement – the biggest issue which saw voters back the Leave vote in 2016.

Mr Burnham said he wanted to have a “very factual, quite evidence-based debate about this”.

The prime minister will meet EU chiefs including European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen in Brussels on November 20 as he seeks to strike a better deal with the bloc. But he also wants a discussion about the long-term future of the UK-EU relationship, 10 years after the historic vote.

open image in gallery Angela Rayner has said Andy Burnham will not take anything off the table when discussing Brexit ( BBC )

Mr Burnham has committed to the red lines set out in Labour’s 2024 manifesto, meaning any change in relationship would have to wait until after an election.

Ms Rayner told Ms Kuenssberg: “I want to see the best deal for the people of my constituency and for Britain.

“We haven’t got the best deal at the moment because we’ve seen exports reduced by 20 per cent, we’ve seen the red tape and the friction that has meant that a lot of our businesses are not able to trade in the way that they would like with our biggest trading partners.

“So, I would like us to have an honest conversation about what the trade-offs could be and then put that to the people at a general election.”

The openness to revisit Brexit has been welcomed by campaigners and senior figures in Labour.

Stella Creasy, chair of the Labour Movement for Europe, said: “The prime minister is right – the UK is long overdue for a grown-up conversation about what EU freedom of movement actually means to our supply chains and for jobs for British citizens. If we want to negotiate our future with Europe we need to do so on facts not fiction.”

Pro-EU groups are pushing for Labour to include a pledge to rejoin the bloc in its next manifesto.

Europe: The Way Back We’re campaigning to rebuild Britain’s future in Europe JOIN US HERE

The European Movement UK recently published a plan with The Independent outlining how the UK could return as a member within 10 years.

The pressure group and Best for Britain have shared data on how Brexit is restricting Mr Healey’s economic plans as he tries to deliver a difficult Budget on Wednesday, with debt rising and pressure to find money to boost the defence budget as well as the prime minister’s other priorities, such as a free social care system.

It notes that Goldman Sachs and the National Bureau for Economic Research (NBER) has suggested the UK has missed out on 6 to 8 per cent of economic growth as a result of Brexit.

With the budget watchdog, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), suggesting that the 2026/27 size of the UK economy is £3.043 trillion, it would mean the UK has lost out on between £180bn and £240bn of economic growth – equating to between £30bn and £40bn a year since the UK left the EU.

A European Movement UK spokesman noted: “That's about £1,000 per household per year – or £5,000 poorer per household since Brexit, and counting.”

Dr Mike Galsworthy, Chair, European Movement UK, said: “The prime minister is right to ask for an honest debate, and honesty starts with the numbers. Brexit didn’t end migration, it swapped a fluid two-way exchange for a one-way visa ratchet leading to more permanent settling. Free movement is also the fairer system, where British people get the same rights in return, from school-leavers to pensioners. The new conversation is about a better kind of migration, one that fills dynamic gaps in our labour market whilst opening the full range of opportunity to our own citizens."

open image in gallery Farage claims Burnham is betraying his constituents in Leave voting Makerfield ( Getty )

Meanwhile, Tom Brufatto, policy and research director at Best for Britain, which campaigns for the UK to restore its place at the heart of Europe, told The Independent: “Brexit has actively lost the country £40bn in tax revenue that could have been spent on the schools, hospitals and defence systems we all rely on – and hit taxpayers squarely in the wallet with tax rises we could have avoided during a cost of living crisis.”

He added: “Taken together with the GDP growth of at least £92bn on offer from restoring our EU membership, and the urgent need to shore up our nation’s military, it's crystal clear: the next Budget would be a far less painful process if we even signalled our intent to rejoin.”

However, the Tories remain dismissive of Mr Burnham’s attempts to unpick the harms of Brexit.

Commenting on the revelations over freedom of movement, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch said: “This is yet another example of Burnham’s foot-in-mouth syndrome. He hasn’t thought this through or the implications.

“Most people who voted for Brexit did so because they didn’t want free movement. Too many politicians have failed to understand the significance and impact of immigration on communities.”

Reform UK also hit out at Mr Burnham, who said during the Makerfield by-election campaign which returned him to Westminster, that he would not re-run the Brexit arguments.

Nigel Farage said the prime minister’s comments were “a total betrayal of Brexit Britain and Burnham’s Makerfield pitch”.

But Liberal Democrat deputy leader Daisy Cooper said: “Freedom of movement, as well as freedom of capital and trade and ripping up red tape that has absolutely strangled British businesses, would be a really good thing for growth.”

As prime minister Andy Burnham looks at the way ahead for Britain's relationship with Europe, The Independent has been leading the charge, campaigning to secure the absolute best deal for Britain. News.title: Madrid festival reroutes thousands of sheep to avoid housing protest camp
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Thousands of sheep and goats thronged the streets of the Spanish capital on Sunday, drawing large crowds of tourists and locals alike to watch an annual festival recreating the pastoral practice of moving livestock to new grazing grounds.

Madrid sits on an ancient migration route that has always been part of a vast grid of farming paths covering the Iberian Peninsula. Open fields and woodland crisscrossed by droving routes once covered the area where the city now stands.

This year, the Transhumance Festival took a detour from its traditional historical route to avoid the city’s central square, the Puerta del Sol, where housing activists have set up a protest camp.

The housing protests gathered pace last month, fueled by outrage over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home of seven decades in downtown Madrid. The woman, María del Carmen Abascal, widely known as Maricarmen, died in hospital shortly after her eviction.

Avoiding the protest camp, the livestock were driven through the streets of central Madrid to the sound of bells and bleats. The festival also spotlights the environmental benefits of traditional grazing, in which livestock are used to clear brush and other flammable undergrowth, reducing the spread of wildfires.

The movement between seasonal pastures is called transhumance.

However, it is in decline as Spain’s interior experiences a population exodus, which started around 1950, as generations of young people left the countryside in search of work and opportunity in cities.

Madrid has held the festival since 1994. Towns and smaller cities in Italy, France and California hold similar events. In Spain, modern farming methods have reduced the practice of transhumance to a small group of farmers that keep the tradition alive not just for its environmental benefits but also for its cultural value.

News.title: Voices: This is what will happen after Israel’s most important election in years
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

On Tuesday, Israelis will vote in their first election since Hamas’s deadly October 2023 attacks and the unprecedented wars on Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

It has been billed as one of the most consequential elections in Israel’s history. Many see it as a referendum on Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.

Unseating Netanyahu is a very real possibility: most polls show the bloc of his main challenger, ex-army chief Gadi Eisenkot, securing a razor-thin lead.

But even with that outcome, the reality is very little fundamental change.

Very little will be different for the millions of Palestinians crammed into a destroyed Gaza, where, despite Israeli denials, a UN Commission of Inquiry found Israel is committing genocide.

Or for the millions of Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, surrounded by ever-growing settlements that are illegal under international law, where there is an unprecedented surge in settler violence and massive military operations.

Whatever happens, there is unlikely to be a speedy resolution to the numerous wars Israel is engaged in, including with Iran, that have killed thousands and caused the largest energy crisis ever recorded, impacting us all.

open image in gallery An Israeli soldier aims his weapon near where the houses of two alleged Palestinian gunmen are located, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank city of Hebron ( AFP/Getty )

Israel’s parliament, the Knesset, has 120 seats. To govern, you need 61. No party has ever won that alone, so governments are formed through a Tetris-like game of coalition building. If no one gets there, more elections are likely.

Netanyahu is running with his extreme right-wing bloc while on trial in Israel for corruption (charges he denies) and while facing heat from the Israeli public over the 7 October security failures. Three years on, his government has yet to form a state commission of inquiry, sparking fury.

His main challenger is Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief whose son and nephew were killed fighting in Gaza. In his bloc are former prime ministers Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, who briefly unseated Netanyahu in 2021.

Most polls show Eisenkot’s bloc slightly ahead of Netanyahu’s. As Dahlia Scheindlin, a prominent Tel Aviv-based pollster and journalist, points out, this tracks what most polls have consistently shown for the last three and a half years: “the majority of Israel is against this current government,” she explains.

Still, neither bloc looks able to reach the critical 61 seats to rule. Deadlock, and possible further elections, are a real possibility.

But whichever of the largest blocs wins, major fundamentals won’t change.

The key point to keep in mind is that more than 60 per cent of Jewish Israelis, and a clear majority of Israelis as a whole, self-identify as right-wing, Scheindlin continues.

“So regardless of the government, it’s very clear that the Knesset will be dominated by clearly ideological right-wing parties.”

open image in gallery An ad for an Israeli TV channel that will broadcast the election coverage, featuring Israeli prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot ( Reuters )

The Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs do differ on domestic issues such as draft exemptions for ultra-Orthodox religious students. Netanyahu, who is in a coalition with ultra-Orthodox parties, has supported this. His opponents have vehemently campaigned against it.

The other major sticking point is judicial reform. Netanyahu’s determination to severely curb the Supreme Court’s powers in favour of the executive has already sparked mass protests. Eisenkot’s party has said publicly it would oppose a Supreme Court override law.

But on everything else, there is not much daylight between either side.

On the wider Middle East region, Netanyahu has promised more war. Under his rule, Israeli forces have pushed deeper into occupied Lebanese and southern Syrian territory.

Eisenkot is widely seen as even more hawkish. He has repeatedly emphasised his security credentials on the campaign trail, citing his “Dahiyeh doctrine” of smashing enemies with disproportionate force. On Iran, Eisenkot and his coalition partners have talked of scaling up the response.

open image in gallery A child overlooks the destroyed Hamad family residential complex in Nuseirat Camp, central Gaza Strip, Palestine, on Friday 23 October ( AFP/Getty )

On Palestine, Netanyahu and Eisenkot also largely agree.

Both oppose an independent Palestinian state and insist Israel must maintain security control over all the land between the Jordan River and the Mediterranean.

In Gaza, Israeli troops still control around two-thirds of the besieged territory, a year into a so-called ceasefire during which Israeli strikes have killed 1,000 people. Both Netanyahu and Eisenkot say troops won’t leave until the Hamas militant group disarms, and both are ready to restart a full-scale offensive.

There are some differences over the occupied West Bank. Netanyahu’s partners, the sanctioned ministers Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, who are settlers themselves, have publicly demanded full formal annexation. There have been unprecedented levels of settler violence and forced displacement of Palestinians under their rule, according to the United Nations.

Eisenkot has rejected full annexation of the West Bank and promised to reduce settler violence. That said, he favours settlement in principle, despite settlements being illegal under international law. Under the 2021 government of his coalition partners, Bennett and Lapid, saw a significant increase in settlement expansion and demolitions of Palestinian houses, according to Israeli monitoring group Peace Now.

That is why Palestinians just aren’t following the Israeli elections, despite the fact that their lives and futures are determined by Israel, explains Zainah El-Haroun, a spokesperson for Palestinian human rights organisation al-Haq.

“It doesn’t make a difference to us, other than that it could get and probably will get worse,” she tells me bluntly.

“Our central concern isn’t really who’s forming Israel’s next government, but the continued policies of occupation, annexation, apartheid and continued genocide against the Palestinian that our people are enduring.”

(In 2024, the International Court of Justice found Israel responsible for apartheid, which Israel rejected).

“The fact [is] that Israel has pursued these policies across every single government, whether they’re left-wing, right-wing, supposed moderate centrist coalitions,” she adds.

Case in point is Al-Haq, she continues. The respected Palestinian human rights group was designated as a terrorist organisation by Israel, along with five other Palestinian civil society groups, in 2021, under Lapid and Bennett’s centrist “government of change”. That sparked international condemnation, including by UN experts, as “a frontal attack on the Palestinian human rights movement, and on human rights everywhere”.

open image in gallery Israeli soldiers patrol at the northern checkpoint in Hebron, in the occupied West Bank, on Saturday 24 October ( AFP/Getty )

Right now the situation is already bleaker in the occupied West Bank.

Just days before Tuesday’s election, Netanyahu ordered a full lockdown and a major military operation in Hebron, after reports that two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers at a checkpoint near the city on Friday. In a fiery speech, he vowed to “destroy this place, to change it completely”.

Hebron has been sealed off, Israeli bulldozers have begun demolishing homes, and the city’s mayor says thousands are already forced to flee their homes. Netanyahu’s rivals have not challenged this response.

This election may remove Netanyahu. But the alternatives are not massively different.

The fear is that nothing will change and further bloodshed is on the horizon.

News.title: Antonelli takes another step closer to F1 title with US GP pole position
News.content:
Welcome to our live coverage for qualifying for the 2026 United States Grand Prix at the Circuit of the Americas, just outside of Austin. This is one of the finest tracks that we have on the Formula One calendar and is a fitting place for the US Grand Prix. The races are usually entertaining, the drivers love the track (though have complained about the bumps this year) and it comfortably the best on-track action of the three races in the US.

What might we see this weekend? Well, Kimi Antonelli could be crowned world champion if results go his way. The way the results need to go make that fairly unlikely, but stranger things have happened in F1 and they often do. In any case, it would take a catastrophic implosion for Antonelli to lose the championship from here, so it is a case of when rather than if.

Who looks in good form? Well, Ferrari do. They have brought an updated car here this weekend it, so far, is paying off. Charles Leclerc had good pace yesterday and Lewis Hamilton, his team-mate, was fastest earlier today in final practice. Hamilton’s time of 1min34.893sec was a tenth or two quicker than the Red Bull of Max Verstappen, with Leclerc not too far behind. Then it was Antonelli, George Russell in the second Mercedes and Oscar Piastri making up the top six, though the Australian was nearly half a second off the ultimate pace of Hamilton.

Qualifying begins in about 50 minutes and we will be here with all the updates from that.

News.title: Sensational Spurs storm Stamford Bridge as Palmer loses his head
News.content:
Chelsea manager Xabi Alonso has told Cole Palmer he must learn from his red card that contributed to his team’s London derby defeat by Tottenham Hotspur.

Tottenham head coach Roberto De Zerbi insisted Palmer should have seen red for shoving his pelvis into the face of Mateus Fernandes. But, having got off with a yellow card, the Chelsea midfielder then fouled substitute Conor Gallagher.

“I haven’t seen them [the yellow cards] on TV, but as far as I have been told, he [the referee] probably got it right,” Alonso said. “So, for sure for Cole, but for everyone. We think [up until] now we haven’t received any red cards [this season] and we need to continue that way because we need to have this maturity to deal with difficult moments, when you have conceded 1-0, there was still 15-20 minutes to go, so we have to be calm. I need to check the action to talk with Cole, but it is one to learn for the future for sure.”

Asked if he thought Palmer should have been sent off for the first yellow card, De Zerbi, who was booked for his protests, replied: “Yep.”

Jordan Henderson had spoken to Palmer at the end of the previous week’s victory over Everton in which the forward could also have been booked for a second time and sent off.

But Alonso claimed he does not have any wider concerns about Palmer’s character. He said: “Today, for sure, yes, but it is not a [wider] concern. I think that Cole when he is focused on the game, when he is enjoying and today after the 1-0, it is a moment to keep calm, a moment to keep mature and for everyone.”

De Zerbi hailed his side’s character and claimed that Tottenham have “suffered enough” after two 17th-placed finishes and a slow start to the season until successive victories over Coventry City and Chelsea.

“We want to improve, improve and improve, to be better game by game, week by week. I think we have suffered enough,” De Zerbi said. “Changing the spirit of the group, changing the performance of the players, especially the more fragile players, maybe the younger players. We played very well. Great individual performances, great collective performance because we played very well. And then we put something different than Tottenham, I think, in the last period. Different attitude, different relationships with the players, different group.”

Chelsea were without João Pedro because of an injury and Alonso is waiting to find out how long the striker will be out.

“We don’t know yet because he has a lot of fluid,” Alonso said. “So he felt it yesterday [Friday] and we need to wait probably until tomorrow [Sunday] to do the test and to know the whole situation and the whole seriousness of the injury. We will know soon enough.”

News.title: Pollock at heart of scuffle that inspires Leicester to thumping win in feisty derby
News.content:
Hello and welcome to our live coverage of Leicester Tigers v Northampton Saints.

The Prem’s derby weekend continues today at Mattioli Woods Welford Road, where Geoff Parling’s side go head-to-head in with their East Midlands rivals.

Both Leicester and Northampton have two wins from the opening three rounds of the season and with both sides involved in a number of high-scoring encounters already in the new campaign, we could be in for a real treat.

Tigers started the season with a 38-40 loss at home to Saracens, but bounced back quickly with wins over Gloucester and Newcastle Red Bulls. They will be itching to right a few wrongs after suffering a chastening Champions Cup defeat in Pau last week.

Northampton, meanwhile, have notched up wins over Newcastle Red Bulls and Bath either side of loss to Bristol Bears.

A win today for Saints would be their first on the road since defeating Exeter Chiefs at Sandy Park in April.

“It (the East Midlands derby) means a lot to everyone, we know it will be a great atmosphere at Mattioli Woods Welford Road,” said Parling.

“I don’t think with this sort of game either team has to build it up too much emotionally because that just comes, so I think it’s actually about being really really calm in the moment.”

“Hopefully we can put the best of ourselves out there and I’m sure Saints will be able to do exactly the same.”

Saints are without a victory in Leicester since January 2023, when a single point decided the 18-19 result.

Since then, the last five meetings between the sides have been won by the hosts on the day – with Saints last taking home the bragging rights when a Tom Litchfield hat-trick helped Northampton to a 45-31 win on home soil in last season’s league play-off.

Kick-off gets underway at 3.05pm. Stay with us here for all the latest updates.

News.title: Saliba has fight on his hands to usurp ‘unbelievable’ Konsa
News.content:
Hello and welcome to coverage from the Emirates as Premier League champions Arsenal host Everton.

Mikel Arteta’s men produced a good performance in midweek to draw with Bayern Munich in the Champions League while David Moyes’s squad have had the week off following their 2-0 defeat by Chelsea last weekend.

Arteta said: “We’re having three games in six days so we know what’s happening, especially when the games are so demanding and the necessity is to win. We know that, so we prepare the players for those scenarios and do the best we possibly can.

“I know David so well and how he sets the team, the quality they have in their organisation and individually. It’s no coincidence they didn’t lose before their last game. They have a really good team, which we know because in recent clashes, it’s always been a really difficult game for us.”

Both teams enter this game having been beaten just once this season but eight points separate them with Arsenal in second and Everton in eighth.

Moyes said: “It’s not an easy game and never has been over many years. We look forward to it; they had a game in midweek, and we have to try and capitalise on that. I thought we did really well last year against them; we played really well down at Arsenal, and I hope we can do the same.

“When I look back at the team we had out, we were pretty threadbare at that time, but we did a good job, and I hope we can do it again. Obviously Arsenal have some many different tools in their bag and people they can use in different positions, so we’re fully aware of the team we’re up against and the level.”

Former Arsenal players Ainsley Maitland-Niles and Christian Norgaard could feature for Everton this afternoon.

News.title: ‘Tactical genius’ Emery outsmarts Maresca as City crash to first league defeat
News.content:
It was four years ago to the day that Emery grabbed this famous club by the shirt and collar and gave them an almighty shake. After a summer of much instability including many player sales, he appears to have already struck a formula with his newly assembled team.

There were a number of fine individual performances from many of the summer arrivals, such as Jackson, goalkeeper Zion Suzuki and Johan Manzambi.

Emery said: “We were very motivated and Manchester City is the best team in the world so this is the level. This year we started so poorly and we needed time to understand how we improve. The players showed the capacity to retrieve the level we’ve had over the last few years.

“Nicolas is more mature and very demanding of himself to improve. Earlier this season he was shooting over the crossbar but he is now finding the corners. There is still work to do and 11 points is not enough but we are feeling better.”

Villa were fierce from the start and ahead after six minutes. Guéhi’s mistake was punished by John McGinn, with the ball dropping to Jackson who crashed a shot into the roof of the net.

The home team did require Suzuki to produce saves to stop efforts from Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Abdukodir Khusanov as City responded. Ndiaye also struck the outside of the post and City were level seven minutes into the second half with Erling Haaland nodding in Ndiaye’s cross at the far post. Haaland had touched the ball just eight times in the opening 45 minutes but invariably only needs one chance.

News.title: England hammer France to keep Rugby League World Cup hopes alive
News.content:
With Samoa beating Papua New Guinea 64-6 earlier on Saturday, England’s task was put into stark and imposing focus. The Pacific Islanders have a points difference of plus-132. Courtesy of this mauling, England’s is plus-64. So they must see off Papua New Guinea by a big number next Friday and then pray that Tonga defeat Samoa two days later. That is their only route through.

In truth, that is as much as McDermott could hope after their initial shortcomings, as they seek to avoid missing out on the last four for the first time in the World Cup’s 72-year history.

“What we’ve done today, given the context, is just enormous,” McDermott said. “We had to win big but, as any coach will tell you, nobody thinks like that. You think, ‘we’ve got to win’.

“We had some real good, candid conversations this week about what that actually means and we’ve been able to do that without getting distracted in chasing points.”

It should be remembered that this was only McDermott’s second game in charge and, even allowing for the poor opposition, they were dramatically improved.

“We’ve been together for five field sessions only,” he said. “We’re building something here and there was a little bit of that on show today.

“Certainly the six tries we scored in the last 17 minutes or so before half-time are what we’ve been chasing. We can see how good that’s going to be.

“If this group’s together for a process or a long build-up to a tournament, we could achieve some special things but, over a short space of time, it’s been remarkable really.”

It is incredible to think that England took 22 minutes to break the deadlock, when the ever-excellent Dom Young burst through. From there, they averaged a try every four or so minutes, with France looking increasingly forlorn and fatigued.

News.title: How an aid initiative maimed thousands of children in war-torn Africa
News.content:
Tormented by pain from severe internal burns, Amza Kebbie is one of thousands of children in Sierra Leone damaged for life by an aid intervention which went horribly wrong.

It has been five days since the four-year-old boy drank caustic soda, one of the two main ingredients for making soap, after mistaking it for drinking water. The highly corrosive liquid, also known as sodium hydroxide, has stripped the lining of his oesophagus and part of his stomach, causing life changing damage.

He’s now in intensive care, clinging precariously to life. An intravenous drip provides fluids and there’s a nasal cannula that enables him to breathe. Medics and relatives look over him around the clock.

If he can gather enough strength (which the nurses say is by no means guaranteed) the dangerously sick child will undergo a gastrostomy, an operation that will see a tube directly inserted into his stomach so that he can be fed long term.

Amza drank caustic soda while being looked after by a neighbour who was making soap at home Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

He can no longer swallow properly and may never be able to do so again, say his doctors.

This is not an isolated tragedy. Across Sierra Leone, there are thousands of children like Amza, and their number is growing every year.

At the Goderich Surgical Centre in the capital Freetown, around 200 children are admitted annually with caustic soda poisoning. Many more are thought to die in remote regions where emergency medical treatment is unavailable.

Behind the calamity is a humanitarian initiative that has spectacularly backfired. It’s a prime example of the law of unintended consequences; of a seemingly sensible and undoubtedly well meaning public health intervention doing more harm than good.

Fatmata Kamara accidentally drank caustic soda at her grandmother’s house in 2014 and has had a feeding tube ever since Credit : SImon Townsley

The story starts in the aftermath of Sierra Leone’s vicious civil war, which ran between 1991 and 2002.

Fought between the government and the Revolutionary United Front – backed by Liberian warlord Charles Taylor – the war claimed an estimated 50,000 to 70,000 lives, displaced 2.5 million people and left the country brutalised and in ruins.

In its aftermath, international aid agencies and NGOs desperately sought ways to revive the country and alighted on DIY soap making as a way of killing two birds with one stone.

Siblings Aminata Fofana and Salieu Bangura help out with the family soap-making business Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Organisations including UNHCR, UNICEF and World Vision thought the practice would both improve sanitation in the country’s disease-ridden shanty towns and provide home-bound women with the means to earn a sustainable income.

It seemed like an obvious “win-win”, and schemes to help women set up in the soap making business rapidly proliferated.

An annual report by the International Federation of the Red Cross, published in May 2002, promoted a micro-finance scheme to fund small-scale soapmaking.

Saieu Bangura, 13, with a tub of soap flakes Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

In 2005, the Centre for War Affected Women in Sierra Leone’s Kono district, backed by the UNHCR, listed soap making as one of the main training courses for war widows and female amputees.

And at about the same time, the Freetown-based Safer Future Youth Development Programme, supported by UNICEF and the charity War Child, provided “a tool kit for soap production” at its training workshops.

As recently as 2020, Action Aid ran a promotional article on its Sierra Leone website showing how soap making had enabled women to become financially independent of their husbands.

The article ran under the headline: “With Soap Making Skills – I'm Empowered!”

Mabinty Bangura is taken to theatre for an endoscopy Credit : Simon Townsley

It is for good reason that the ancient Greek physician Hippocrates urged doctors “first, do no harm”.

To follow the rule literally is not possible as all health interventions entail some risk but it's a reminder never to underestimate the capacity of a new intervention to backfire.

There are plenty of examples from history to choose from.

During the British Raj in India, the government offered a cash bounty for every dead cobra as a way of reducing the danger of venomous snakes.

The surgical team examine the internal damage via an endoscopy Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

But rather than leading to a decline in snake numbers, the plan resulted in entrepreneurial individuals breeding cobras just so they could kill them and then claim the reward.

Once officials realised what was happening and the scheme was stopped, thousands of the then worthless cobras were released into the wild, greatly increasing the risk of snakebite.

In the late 1950s, the Chinese Communist regime introduced an equally calamitous public health campaign involving sparrows.

They issued a directive ordering the birds to be destroyed because they were thought to spread disease and destroy crops.

A child’s gastrostomy scar with a feeding tube in place Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

What those behind the idea failed to consider was that sparrows are natural predators. As their numbers declined, the locust population exploded, decimating agriculture and contributing to the Great Chinese Famine in which millions died.

So what went wrong in Sierra Leone? What did those behind the soap making scheme fail to foresee?

Experts say the initiative simply failed to consider the danger inherent in encouraging people to use toxic chemicals in their homes.

The brightly coloured buckets in which caustic soda is made, and then mixed with oil and scent to make soap, are the same buckets used across the country to fetch and hold drinking water. And just like drinking water, the lethal solution is cool, clear and inviting.

Just a drop is enough to cause the most horrific burns. So when a thirsty young child like Amza runs in from play and mistakenly scoops up a cup of it to quench their thirst they will lose their oesophagus, if not their lives.

Giuseppe Meucci, chief surgeon at the Goderich Surgical Centre Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Giuseppe Meucci, chief surgeon at the 56-bed Goderich hospital in Freetown where four year old Amza is being cared for, has been treating patients burned by sodium hydroxide nearly every day since arriving in Freetown in 2019.

Three quarters of patients seen by the hospital’s specialist programme for oesophageal burns, set up in response to the crisis and run by the Italian medical charity Emergency, are under five.

“It’s a struggle in this country,” says Dr Meucci. “Almost every family knows someone who has suffered because of this problem. But they just keep coming.”

Hospital director Jasna Sundic Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“In most countries you remove the source of danger for the child, but here that doesn’t seem to happen,” he says.

“It’s one of the main health problems of this country. Soda is there with malaria, malnutrition and typhoid complications. It’s one of the reasons why so many children die before they reach five years old.”

Hospital director Jasna Sundic agrees.

“This is a very severe issue but one which is very preventable,” she tells the Telegraph. “[But] however much we do here, we have not been able to decrease the overall number of soda patients being admitted.

“We cannot stop mothers who have no other source of income except making soap.”

Ibrahim Kerah is fed by his father Mohamed Credit : SImon Townsley

In a handful of rare cases, burns victims are sent abroad for complex oesophageal reconstruction surgery but this is not an option for the vast majority of children injured in Sierra Leone.

More than 60 per cent require surgery, but for these children, like Amza, a feeding tube that bypasses the oesophagus is the only option.

The hospital has many of these gastrostomy patients.

Critically underweight Mabinty Bangura Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

In a ward dedicated to soda burns, four-year-old Ibrahim Kerah is being fed through his stomach tube by his father Mohamed.

They travelled together on the back of a motorbike taxi for nearly 10 hours to get here for his third check-up appointment.

The Telegraph watches as Mohamed carefully prepares his son’s meal, adding spinach leaves to the porridge-like mix which is fed into a syringe at the end of the tube.

At an adjoining bed two-year-old Mabinty Bangura is critically underweight after ingesting soda about six months ago. Nurses have put her on a high protein drip so she can regain enough strength to undergo the same bypass surgery.

In the courtyard outside, mothers whose children have just had a gastrostomy are being taught how to prepare the liquid food.

Ibrahim and his father Mohamed endured a 10-hour motorbike journey to attend his hospital check-up Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Isatu Alie, 24, has been living with a stomach tube for 12 years, and now works for Emergency as a patient ambassador.

She is eight months pregnant with her second child and proud to have overcome her injury and the stigma of having to feed through a tube.

“I remember what happened so well,” she says. “I had just got back from school. I took my cup and dunked it into the water bucket. My aunt made soap and, on that day, I didn’t ask about the liquid in the bucket. The pain was incredible”.

More than a decade has passed since her surgery, and Isatu has adjusted well.

“I’m okay with it now. I feel like a normal human being; I’m blessed to be here,” she says.

“Now I speak to children and their parents who have just experienced the same thing and tell them not to lose hope.”

Pregnant Isatu Alie now works as a patient ambassador Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

A small proportion of the patients needing treatment following caustic soda burns are adults.

Among them is 21-year-old Junisa Bundeh, who is on a follow-up visit to check his stomach tube. He explains that he gulped down what he thought was a cup of water from a basin while eating at his grandmother’s house three months ago.

“It was so painful,” recalls Junisa. “I realised what it was straight away because it was so harsh. I tried to spit it all out but the liquid was already going down my throat.”

Mothers are taught how to prepare liquid food; Junisa Bundeh shows his feeding tube Credit : SImon Townsley

In the muddy lanes of Freetown’s Waterloo district there are makeshift soap making operations all over.

The coloured plastic buckets full of either soda or water are everywhere.

Against the backdrop of the rainy season’s persistent gloom, the containers symbolise a measure of cleanliness for families sheltering from torrential downpours under mouldy concrete awnings.

As the Telegraph watches Yabom Kapro, a village elder, making soap, the risks involved are immediately obvious.

Chief Yabom Kapro makes soap at her Waterloo town home, near Freetown Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

As she tips a purple bucket of caustic soda solution into a large basin and then adds palm oil from a plastic jerrycan, local children hover round the cluster of colourful containers.

Yabom uses a wooden paddle to stir the mixture into a creamy paste and then pours it into a mould held in place by an old motorcycle tyre.

Buckets containing caustic soda dissolving, top. Caustic soda crystals, below Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Once set, the beige-coloured cake of soap is cut into blocks which are then grated on a wire mesh contraption to be sold at the local market.

“When you dilute the caustic soda, it is completely clear like water at first,” says another soap maker, 43-year-old Cilina Bangura.

“Afterwards a white scum forms on the top, but you cannot be watching all of the time, [even] with all of these children around.”

Cilina knows the risks but says she can't afford to stop making soap. It has, as the NGOs intended, become an economic lifeline for her and her family.

“I want my children to continue making soap when I stop working,” she says. “I took out a loan to buy everything I needed, and now it is the only way I can make a living.

“Of course, I know how dangerous soda is – it has burned my skin many times – but I don’t have another option.”

Home-made soap, in Waterloo Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Maimunatu Sankoh, three, whose family lives in a nearby tin-roof shack, is sadly too well aware of that danger from her own bitter experience of soda poisoning.

As she feeds her daughter through a stomach tube, Maimunatu’s mum Iyesatu complains: “I have never seen any public information about soda.

“There are warnings on the packets but that is no use once the product is dissolved in water. They need to tell people to keep buckets out of the way.”

Iyesatu Kamara feeds her daughter Maimunatu Sankoh at their home Credit : SImon Townsley

Incidents of children consuming harmful chemicals are not confined to developing countries and were once common in the west.

In the US, the Poison Prevention Packaging Act was introduced in 1970, mandating childproof containers and the labelling of harmful household products.

The UK followed suit in 1975 with the introduction of child-resistant safety caps on containers of caustic soda and most other noxious household substances.

Despite the risks, Cilina says she can't afford to stop making soap Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Such legislation is still a long way off in Sierra Leone and is anyway far too late for four-year-old Amza.

Under heavy sedation in the intensive care unit, his glazed eyes open only occasionally.

The only visible evidence of his injuries is some scarring on his lips, but the doctors say his throat, oesophagus and stomach have all been seared by several large gulps of soda.

The boy’s mother, Mamie Kebbie, 30, keeps a watchful vigil, stroking his listless head tenderly. She says he used to be a playful and vivacious child.

If they are taken to hospital quickly, children with soda burns are normally given an oesophageal dilation endoscopy – a procedure which aims to keep the oesophagus open – but for Amza this has not been possible.

Freetown, Sierra Leone Credit : Simon Townsley

“This is a very severe case,” explains nurse Annette Turay, who heads the hospital’s intensive care unit. “When he was brought in, about 10 hours after he had ingested the soda, we were unable to conduct an endoscopy because he already had respiratory problems.

“He has pneumonia and he cannot feed through his mouth. He cannot even swallow his own saliva.

Mamie Kebbie keeps a vigil at her son's bedside Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“It will be a week before he is strong enough for us to be able to operate. We will insert a gastric tube into his stomach. He will have to keep this as his main way of being fed for a long time, potentially forever.”

But nurse Turay has seen worse.

“I have seen so many children suffering a lot after ingesting soda, so many dying too.

“A few weeks ago, we had a child in the ward who died because his stomach was completely gone”.

The Telegraph contacted all the NGOs involved in the setting up of and promotion of soap making schemes in Sierra Leone that are mentioned in this story for comment.

Protect yourself and your family by learning more about Global Health Security

As she tips a purple bucket of caustic soda solution into a large basin and then adds palm oil from a plastic jerrycan, local children hover round the cluster of colourful containers.

Yabom uses a wooden paddle to stir the mixture into a creamy paste and then pours it into a mould held in place by an old motorcycle tyre.

Buckets containing caustic soda dissolving, top. Caustic soda crystals, below Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Once set, the beige-coloured cake of soap is cut into blocks which are then grated on a wire mesh contraption to be sold at the local market.

“When you dilute the caustic soda, it is completely clear like water at first,” says another soap maker, 43-year-old Cilina Bangura.

“Afterwards a white scum forms on the top, but you cannot be watching all of the time, [even] with all of these children around.”

Cilina knows the risks but says she can't afford to stop making soap. It has, as the NGOs intended, become an economic lifeline for her and her family.

“I want my children to continue making soap when I stop working,” she says. “I took out a loan to buy everything I needed, and now it is the only way I can make a living.

“Of course, I know how dangerous soda is – it has burned my skin many times – but I don’t have another option.”

Home-made soap, in Waterloo Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Maimunatu Sankoh, three, whose family lives in a nearby tin-roof shack, is sadly too well aware of that danger from her own bitter experience of soda poisoning.

As she feeds her daughter through a stomach tube, Maimunatu’s mum Iyesatu complains: “I have never seen any public information about soda.

“There are warnings on the packets but that is no use once the product is dissolved in water. They need to tell people to keep buckets out of the way.”

Iyesatu Kamara feeds her daughter Maimunatu Sankoh at their home Credit : SImon Townsley

Incidents of children consuming harmful chemicals are not confined to developing countries and were once common in the west.

In the US, the Poison Prevention Packaging Act was introduced in 1970, mandating childproof containers and the labelling of harmful household products.

The UK followed suit in 1975 with the introduction of child-resistant safety caps on containers of caustic soda and most other noxious household substances.

Despite the risks, Cilina says she can't afford to stop making soap Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Such legislation is still a long way off in Sierra Leone and is anyway far too late for four-year-old Amza.

Under heavy sedation in the intensive care unit, his glazed eyes open only occasionally.

The only visible evidence of his injuries is some scarring on his lips, but the doctors say his throat, oesophagus and stomach have all been seared by several large gulps of soda.

The boy’s mother, Mamie Kebbie, 30, keeps a watchful vigil, stroking his listless head tenderly. She says he used to be a playful and vivacious child.

If they are taken to hospital quickly, children with soda burns are normally given an oesophageal dilation endoscopy – a procedure which aims to keep the oesophagus open – but for Amza this has not been possible.

Freetown, Sierra Leone Credit : Simon Townsley

“This is a very severe case,” explains nurse Annette Turay, who heads the hospital’s intensive care unit. “When he was brought in, about 10 hours after he had ingested the soda, we were unable to conduct an endoscopy because he already had respiratory problems.

“He has pneumonia and he cannot feed through his mouth. He cannot even swallow his own saliva.

Mamie Kebbie keeps a vigil at her son's bedside Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“It will be a week before he is strong enough for us to be able to operate. We will insert a gastric tube into his stomach. He will have to keep this as his main way of being fed for a long time, potentially forever.”

But nurse Turay has seen worse.

“I have seen so many children suffering a lot after ingesting soda, so many dying too.

“A few weeks ago, we had a child in the ward who died because his stomach was completely gone”.

The Telegraph contacted all the NGOs involved in the setting up of and promotion of soap making schemes in Sierra Leone that are mentioned in this story for comment.

The Eagles have conceded 17 goals in their opening seven league games, giving them the worst defensive record in the top flight.

Palace drew 2-2 with Besiktas in the Europa League on Thursday night, with Jean-Phillippe Mateta scoring on his first start since August.



Newcastle manager Matthias Jaissle is also facing scrutiny after his side fell to back-to-back defeats against Coventry and Aston Villa.

According to The Athletic, however, the Belgium international is still confident of making himself available for manager Jose Mourinho.

Sports.title: Bruno Fernandes dropped from Man Utd XI for first time in FIVE YEARS – with Michael Carrick last boss to axe him too
Sports.content:
Next

BRUNO FERNANDES has been dropped from Manchester United’s line-up just days after calling out Michael Carrick’s tactics.

The Old Trafford skipper is suffering his worst run of form as United are in the midst of a seven game winless run ahead of Bournemouth’s visit on Sunday afternoon.



Following the humiliating 4-1 defeat to Champions League new-boys Como on Wednesday, Fernandes gave a pointed interview about United’s lack of pressing.

He told TNT: “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave a little space in behind and try to get the ball in the first moment, to wait for them, to give them the ball.



“But sometimes when you give too much ball to these teams they get confident, they have so many bodies behind the ball that make you run a lot, make people get frustrated, and then obviously when you recover the ball the legs are, and the brain, much more difficult to make it work.”

Carrick has now dropped Fernandes, who sulked as he was dragged off in the 66th minute in Italy.

Fernandes has not been axed from the United starting XI – for non-fitness reasons – since back in November 2021 against Villarreal.

The man in charge at the time? None other than Michael Carrick.

Quizzed on the decision, Carrick said: “Team selection was a pure football decision.”

When asked earlier this week if he would consider taking the captaincy off Fernandes, Carrick said: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“First and foremost is the squad, the dynamics in the squad. And again, it’s about the club. And I’ll always do what’s best for the club.”

This will be the first Premier League game of the season that Fernandes has started on the bench.

He last started a league game as a sub in United’s 4-3 defeat at Brentford in May 2025, but that was injury related.

Since Carrick’s first game in charge in January, Fernandes has the most assists (14) and has created the most chances (96) of any player in Europe’s big-five leagues.

He has scored four in his 11 appearances across all competitions this season, but has gone five Prem matches without scoring or assisting – his longest run since April-May 2025.



He has started all 10 of United’s matches across the Premier League and Champions League to date this season, and was a sub in the Carabao Cup defeat to Brighton.

Sports.title: Man Utd and Bournemouth fans face ‘nightmare’ getting to Old Trafford as club announce travel alert ahead of huge clash
Sports.content:
Next

MANCHESTER UNITED and Bournemouth fans have been warned to allow extra time for their journey to Old Trafford today due to major tram closures across the city.

It has been announced that no tram services will run on the Altrincham, Eccles or Trafford Park lines, while East Didsbury and Airport line services will only run as far as Firswood, with no trams continuing into Manchester city centre.



Replacement buses will be available on match day, alongside additional Bee Network bus services to help supporters reach the ground.

Fans are being advised to leave an hour earlier than usual to account for potential traffic delays, with all Bee Network tickets accepted on the replacement services.



The disruption, which one fan on X described as a “nightmare” comes as major improvement works take place across the Bee Network, with the closures scheduled to continue until November 1.

Several tram stops close to Old Trafford will be affected, potentially making the journey to the stadium more difficult for supporters travelling from across Greater Manchester as well as away fans.



Trafford Bar, a nearby stop on the Altrincham line, will be closed, while Old Trafford tram stop – located directly outside the cricket ground and just a short walk from the football stadium — will also be affected.

Fans who usually travel on the Eccles line will also be unable to use Exchange Quay, which is around a 10-minute walk from the ground.

Meanwhile, the closure of the Trafford Park line means Wharfside, the closest tram stop to the stadium, will not be accessible.

Firswood will be the nearest available tram stop for supporters heading to the match, but it is around a 25-minute walk from the ground.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Although replacement buses will be running, they are likely to take longer than trams and could be caught up in the heavy traffic expected around Old Trafford on match day.

The additional Bee Network bus services are intended to help accommodate supporters, but fans are still being urged to plan their journeys carefully and allow extra time to avoid missing kick-off.

Manchester United welcome Bournemouth at 2pm, with the fixture having produced an eight-goal thriller last season as the sides played out a 4-4 draw.



Michael Carrick has made a huge call by dropping Bruno Fernandes for the game.

The Cherries have also enjoyed recent success at Old Trafford, winning 3-0 in each of the two seasons before that.

United’s last home victory over Bournemouth came in January 2023 in the days of Erik ten Hag.

It ended 3-0 thanks to goals from Casemiro, Luke Shaw and Marcus Rashford.

JAMES WARD-PROWSE finally got one over his old West Ham manager Nuno Espirito Santo.

The midfielder was largely snubbed by the Hammers boss before he returned to Southampton in the summer transfer window.



Ward-Prowse, 31, was a £30million signing for West Ham after Saints’ relegation in 2023.

Despite making a positive impression, he eventually fell down the pecking order and was sent out on loan to Nottingham Forest and Burnley.



It was during his time at the City Ground that Ward-Prowse’s path first crossed with Nuno.

The pair seemingly failed to see eye-to-eye with the loan move being labelled as a failure.

So when Nuno replaced Graham Potter at West Ham it seemed like it was only a matter of time before Ward-Prowse would be on his way out.

He had the last laugh though as Southampton beat the Hammers 3-2 at the London Stadium on Saturday.



Ward-Prowse was asked about getting one over his former boss by Troy Deeney after the game.

Speaking on CBS Sports, Deeney asked: “Just because it is me, does it feel a little bit better when the gaffer of the previous club didn’t want you, it feels a bit better?”

Sports.title: Jamie Carragher claims Man Utd stars 'don't like playing' with Bruno Fernandes as star axed
Sports.content:
Jamie Carragher claims Man Utd stars 'don't like playing' with Bruno Fernandes as star axed

In light of Bruno Fernandes being dropped to the bench Jamie Carragher believed several Manchester United players would enjoy playing without him

View 2 Images (Image: Sky Sports)

Jamie Carragher claims that several Manchester United players will relish playing without Bruno Fernandes after he was axed by Michael Carrick.

‌



‌



The Portuguese star, in light of Wednesday night's rant that called into question the United manager's tactics, has been dropped to the bench for the clash with Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

‌



Fernandes, last year's Player of the Year, has long been the team's talisman but will now start from the bench for just the fifth time since joining the club in January 2020.

‌



For all his quality the former Sporting Lisbon man has copped criticism for how he conducts himself on the pitch. Carragher claimed that his antics, which often see him lamenting his teammates, are a sign that he's not convinced they're good enough to play with him, but they would now look to embrace the chance to run out minus the Portugal star.

The ex-Liverpool man said on Sky Sports: "You don't want it to blow up in your face, he is Manchester United's best player, we can't get away from that. PFA Player of the Year last year, but Carrick had to make a stand.

"And you're hoping that this brings us together as a group because there's no doubt about it, even though he's their best player, there will be a lot of people who don't actually like playing with Fernandes. He's always throwing his arms up at people, he's basically saying 'you lot aren't good enough to play with me'. We see that a lot from Fernandes.

And if things aren't going well, or someone gives a pass away, you get together, keep encouraging and push each other on."

United will start with a front three of Amad, Mason Mount and Bryan Mbeumo. Fernandes is joined on the bench by the likes of Matheus Cunha and Joshua Zirkzee.

Sports.title: Bruno Fernandes DROPPED as Man Utd boss Michael Carrick reacts to midweek outburst
Sports.content:
Bruno Fernandes DROPPED as Man Utd boss Michael Carrick reacts to midweek outburst

Bruno Fernandes has been dropped to the bench for Manchester United's clash with Bournemouth as Michael Carrick reacts to his public outburst on Wednesday night

View 2 Images Bruno Fernandes has been dropped to the bench

Bruno Fernandes has been dropped by Manchester United just days after he took aim at Michael Carrick.

‌



‌



The Red Devils skipper, who by his own high standards has underperformed this season, laid the blame for the team's failed press on his manager in the aftermath of the 4-1 defeat in Como.

‌



He became the second United player to go public with his frustrations after Lisandro Martinez had done likewise. But whilst the defender retained his starting role for last weekend's draw at Leeds, Fernandes has been benched by Carrick for the game against Bournemouth.

‌



Carrick said there were "always difficult decisions" when picking a team, and that his call to snub Fernandes was "purely football" as he was quizzed on whether his comments influenced his selection.

Fernandes has previously been the team's talisman but, during a run of just two wins in 11 games, even the Portuguese's performances have come in for criticism.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌

Fernandes had started all 24 Premier League games under Carrick, but in his absence Bryan Mbeumo, Amad and Mason Mount will be United's attacking trio in front of a midfield three featuring all of their summer signings.

‌



Carrick began Friday's press conference by not taking any questions, instead launching into a five minutes speech where he acknowledged the results were not up to standard, but made it known that he wanted more graft from his player.

He said, with multiple references to the past: "It was never about Ryan Giggs, it was never about Ryan Giggs, it was about Manchester United. Wayne Rooney, the greatest goalscorer in the club’s history, he played for team.

‌



"Sir Alex Ferguson, the greatest manager in the club’s history... Sir Matt [Busby] and Sir Bobby [Charlton], their resilience was beyond belief what they showed and how they rebuilt this football club. It was built on hard work, and we should never forget that."

View 2 Images Bruno Fernandes' midweek interview took aim at Michael Carrick

‌



After losing in midweek, which was their second Champions League reverse in three games, Fernandes said: "It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave space behind and try to get the ball, but sometimes when you give space to these teams they get confidence."

Asked directly whether Carrick got his tactics wrong, the playmaker added: "That's on the manager and staff to see, not me. Sometimes you have to be more brave under pressure, take the risk of pressing high and making them uncomfortable."

Article continues below

Told of Fernandes' comments in his post-match press conference, Carrick offered a curt response: "There's a little bit of whatever system you play, whatever tactics you play, if you don't run, and you don't run forward, and you don't run back, you aren't going to win."

Sports.title: Ex-Premier League boss stuns with Marc Cucurella Ballon d'Or pick as Harry Kane eyes award
Sports.content:
Ex-Premier League boss stuns with Marc Cucurella Ballon d'Or pick as Harry Kane eyes award

The Ballon d'Or will be handed out on Monday night with Harry Kane and Lamine Yamal among the favourites, but Marc Cucurella's name has been thrown in by a former Premier League manager

View 2 Images Marc Cucurella has been tipped to be a shock winner of the Ballon d'Or

Former Premier League boss Felix Magath has produced a sensational pick by naming Marc Cucurella as his winner of the Ballon d'Or.

‌



‌



The prestigious award will be handed out in London on Monday night with Harry Kane the favourite to scoop the award for the first time. He spearheaded Bayern Munich's continued dominance domestically but fell at the semi-final hurdle in the Champions League and at the World Cup.

‌



PSG's success at club level and Spain's win on the global stage gives their players a potential shot at glory with the likes of Lamine Yamal and Ousmane Dembele also in the Ballon d'Or mix.

‌



But Magath, who led Bayern to Bundesliga titles but also presided over Fulham's relegation in 2014, has picked Cucurella, the Real Madrid right-back as his winner.

Magath had Rodri in second and Fabian Ruiz, the only player to win the World Cup and the Champions League, in third. Despite claiming the World Cup almost no one has tipped the former Chelsea defender to win the Golden Ball. No defender has claimed the prize since Fabio Cannavaro in 2006.

‌



Magath's tip came from within German media, where five pundits and ex-players were asked to name their top three. Magath was the only man to overlook Kane, not even putting him in the top three, despite him scoring 61 times last season.

Kylian Mbappe, Michael Olise and Lionel Messi featured as the picks for third spot. Mbappe became the World Cup's all-time leading scorer in the summr whilst Olise, despite playing alongside Kane, was named the Footballer of the Year in Germany.

Sports.title: Andoni Iraola puts limit on Florian Wirtz as Liverpool boss defends goalless run
Sports.content:
Andoni Iraola puts limit on Florian Wirtz as Liverpool boss defends goalless run

Florian Wirtz remains without a goal in the Premier League this season and Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola admits his position will not lend itself to him scoring regularly

View 2 Images Liverpool star Florian Wirtz has found himself under the spotlight for months (Image: Richard Sellers/Sportsphoto/Allstar via Getty Images)

Andoni Iraola admits that Florian Wirtz is "not going to score 15 goals a season" as he launched another defence of the Liverpool playmaker.

‌



‌



Now into his second season at Anfield, more is being expected of the German, who cost a British record £116million when he moved to the Premier League from Bayer Leverkusen.

‌



He was part of a hugely underwhelming Liverpool team that finished fifth last season, which resulted in Arne Slot's sacking, and now Iraola is tasked with getting the most out of Wirtz. He has been regularly criticised with the Reds yet to find a position that routinely gets the best out of him.

‌



Wirtz has been hauled off after 70 minutes or earlier in three of Liverpool's seven games, but Iraola has claimed that the role that the German plays means he's never going to be regularly scoring.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



“I’m delighted with Florian,” Iraola told the El Boro podcast. “He’s coming off three very good performances and I trust this is the start of finding his confidence again. We believe in him a lot. He is judged a lot in terms of goals and assists, but he is a player for whom that won’t be his strength.

“He’s not a No.10 or a second striker who is going to score 15 goals this year. No. I mean if he can do that, even better, but he’s a player who gives us a lot of control over the matches. He has a lot of confidence on the ball. Ultimately, we have to make him feel comfortable but he’s probably feeling more comfortable in Champions League matches.

‌



“In the Premier League, he has to get used to those duels. Here, duels are really hard to win. He’s in that process. It’s true he’s been here a year but he’s still acclimatising to this competition. But in terms of talent I have no doubt about him and in terms of attitude either. He is a player who works a lot.”

View 2 Images Andoni Iraola has continued to back his German playmaker

‌



Wirtz's performance in the Champions League win over LASK recently was arguably his best performance in a Liverpool shirt. The German was hugely creative with Bradley Barcola among the beneficiaries.

The Premier League has been a different story and he's come up with just the two assists domestically so far, and remains without a goal. Last term Wirtz equally found it difficult to regularly influence games in the final third.

Article continues below

Fitting the ex-Leverkusen man into the line-up is also having notable knock on affects. If he plays as the No 10 then only two midfield slots are available, leaving big names missing out. Equally if he were to play from out wide, which is an option, then he is playing instead of one of the number of wingers in the Liverpool squad.

Sports.title: Michael Carrick in regular contact with Sir Alex Ferguson and sacked Man Utd boss
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick in regular contact with Sir Alex Ferguson and sacked Man Utd boss

Michael Carrick is a man under pressure at Manchester United but is regularly talking to his former boss Sir Alex Ferguson and Ole Gunnar Solskjaer

View 2 Images Michael Carrick is chatting to Sir Alex Ferguson during his difficult spell as Man Utd boss (Image: John Peters/Manchester United via Getty Images)

Michael Carrick admits he's in regular contact with Manchester United icon Sir Alex Ferguson as well as Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, who is one of the many managers to follow the Scot.

‌



‌



It was Ferguson who signed Carrick back in 2006 and the now manager had a spell as Solskjaer's No 2 when the Norwegian was in charge at Old Trafford. The pair never won a trophy together before Solskjaer was shown the door.

‌



Carrick is in dialogue with his former boss as well as Solskjaer as he tries to navigate the current challenges on the red side of Manchester. The 45-year-old has presided over two wins in 11 to begin the season, making him a man under pressure.

‌



Carrick beat Solskjaer to the job of head coach in January when the club were, initially, looking for an interim. But the pair remain in talks with Ferguson also at the end of the phone.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



He said: "I speak to both of them quite regularly, to be honest. There's nothing in particular from that. I'm close to both of them and we do have regular conversations. It's nothing different this week."

Solskjaer is among the men who have been unable to bring the success of yesteryear back to United. He came after the likes of Louis van Gaal and Jose Mourinho, and since his dismissal in late 2021 Erik ten Hag and Ruben Amorim have had underwhelming stints.

‌



Carrick needs to improve results of face the prospect of losing his job and in a rallying cry on Friday he referenced Ferguson during an emotional speech.

View 2 Images Former Man Utd boss Ole Gunnar Solskjaer had Michael Carrick as his assistant (Image: Clive Brunskill/Getty Images)

‌



Pressed on why he spoke for five minutes before his weekly press conference on Friday he replied: "Because I understand the situation, and I understand my position and I know what this football club means to so, so many people.

"The history doesn't give you the right to keep winning. Teams that win earn the right to win. So it's important that we draw inspiration from history and the past of what's gone on. But our responsibility is to carry that forward, and it's so important to me that we do that."

Article continues below

United host Bournemouth on Sunday at Old Trafford - the Cherries are unbeaten in their last three visits to the Red Devils, scoring ten goals in that time.
