Sports.title: Gary Neville demands Xabi Alonso action after 'ludicrous' Morgan Rogers moment vs Tottenham
Sports.content:
Gary Neville demands Xabi Alonso action after 'ludicrous' Morgan Rogers moment vs Tottenham

Gary Neville believes Morgan Rogers should have been shown a red card for a "ludicrous" challenge during Chelsea's 2-0 defeat to Tottenham at Stamford Bridge

View 2 Images Chelsea star Morgan Rogers escaped a red card against Tottenham

Gary Neville insisted Morgan Rogers ought to have seen red for a 'ludicrous' challenge during Chelsea's defeat to Tottenham. The midfielder was shown a yellow card in added time of the fixture for bringing down Conor Gallagher. Referee Chris Kavanagh cautioned the 24-year-old, but Neville felt the punishment was insufficient.

‌



‌



While providing commentary for Sky Sports, the former Manchester United defender remarked: "I think that's a red. I do. He's absolutely wellied him with no intent. That's ludicrous from Rogers."

‌



Neville also urged the Chelsea manager to regain control of his squad, stating: "They have lost it. Xabi Alonso needs to get them off."

‌



The Blues suffered a 2-0 reverse against their capital rivals at Stamford Bridge, handing Spurs their first victory at the venue since 2018. Young goalkeeper Mike Penders punched the ball into his own net to gift the visitors a crucial advantage before Mathys Tel fired home from distance to wrap up the three points.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



Between the two strikes, Cole Palmer received his marching orders after collecting two yellow cards, though Neville also suggested the midfielder was fortunate not to be dismissed outright. For his initial booking, the 24-year-old barged into Mateus Fernandes on the floor and knocked him over as the Spurs player attempted to stand up.

It was this flashpoint that ignited a 14-man brawl between the two London clubs, resulting in bookings for Conor Gallagher, Micky van de Ven, Fernandes and Palmer.

‌



Neville felt the latter was fortunate to remain on the pitch, saying: "Palmer's reaction was silly. He's asking for trouble, that's not great. He's asking for trouble. That's not great from Cole Palmer.

"No idea why he's doing that. He was no doubt [sailing close to the wind]. I think that could be a red. Into the chest you'll get away with it but Fernandes is on the ground. He's got no way to defend himself. It's a stupid thing to do."

‌



View 2 Images Cole Palmer was sent off (Image: Glyn KIRK / AFP via Getty Images)

FOLLOW OUR CHELSEA FB PAGE! Latest Blues news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



In the wake of the defeat, Alonso acknowledged that emotional discipline is an area he wants his Chelsea side to address, and confirmed he would be speaking to Palmer privately about his dismissal.

He said: "Yes we need to work and we need to improve on that. I think we spoke yesterday about those things and to know that in those situations that one first yellow card can be decisive as we have seen, it is a process of the maturity of the team and of the individual players as well.

‌



"We think [up until] now we haven't received any red card and we need to continue that way because we need to have this maturity to deal with difficult moments, when you have conceded 1-0, still probably was 15-20 minutes to go, so we have to be on the way.

"I need to check the action to talk with Cole but it is one to learn for the future for sure."

Sports.title: Are Man Utd unmanageable? Michael Carrick speaks as club face prospect of another sacking
Sports.content:
Are Man Utd unmanageable? Michael Carrick speaks as club face prospect of another sacking

Michael Carrick is the latest man to try and make Manchester United the force of old, but he is nowhere close as results leave in under pressure whilst he has to cop public criticism from his captain

View 2 Images Michael Carrick is under pressure at Man Utd (Image: Martin Rickett/PA Wire)

Seven permanent managers in 13 years. A fair few interims in between that as well. Manchester United have tried it all, but with little to no success.

‌



‌



The odd FA Cup, a Carabao Cup here and there, Europa League success was perhaps as good as it got. But sandwiched in with all that is managers having to deal with constant outside noise, often from former United players, and issues of in-fighting, often between themselves and members of the squad.

‌



Michael Carrick is the latest to see his players call out issues within the club. He's had it twice in the space of a fortnight. Lisandro Martinez took aim, largely at the hierarchy, but the attack from Bruno Fernandes was very much aimed at Carrick.

‌



This is a team with two wins in 11, accusations of cultural problems that have spanned years and an environment that has been described as a "graveyard" for talent.

So are Manchester United an unmanageable club? "No," was Carrick's simple answer.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Of course, he kind of has to say that. Would be a bit of a paradox had he himself chosen to manage a club that he deems is beyond managing.

‌



He's been part of the post-Sir Alex Ferguson era as a player. He was there for David Moyes' short-lived reign. He remained for the two years of Louis van Gaal, with the Dutchman bringing glamour and an FA Cup, but a style of football that was highly criticised.

Jose Mourinho had his two and a bit seasons. During that period he'd called out record signing Paul Pogba, that famous clip in training still living on. He'd claimed that United's history wasn't as stellar as they'd like to think during his infamous "football heritage" rant. He also felt he wasn't sufficiently backed in the market.

‌



View 2 Images Louis van Gaal and Jose Mourinho are two managerial heavyweights of the 21st century, but both found it difficult in Manchester

Ole Gunnar Solskjaer was red through and through, very rarely complained about the state of the club, but undoubtedly lost the dressing room with the players' performance nosediving before his sacking.

‌



Erik ten Hag was almost given too much room to manage the club, which meant he was allowed to spend £81million on Antony, £72m on Ramus Hojlund and £47m on Andre Onana. So whether the manager gets all the say, or very little of the say, it seems to make no difference to the club's fortunes.

Ruben Amorim left, with a dire record, after a fiery press conference where he demanded to work as a manager "not the coach" - but equally was ready to leave when his contract expired in 18 months' time. He was sacked the following day.

‌



And so to Carrick, whose sensational interim spell landed him the top job. This year though he's found it much tougher going, perhaps owing to the fact he has to prepare for multiple competitions and not just one game a week.

‌



The poor results off the back of that have led to clear signs of dressing room chaos. Body language tells its own story with Carrick taking the lead in Friday's press conference to demand a greater work ethic if they were to turn their fortunes around.

If they don't start soon then Carrick will be the man to pay, even if the Old Trafford hierarchy will be loathed to make another change in the dugout, which would be another admission they have, yet again, got it wrong.

Sports.title: 'Dream come true!' - Britain's Palmowski becomes 2026 F1 Academy champion
Sports.content:
Britain's Alisha Palmowski became the 2026 F1 Academy champion with three races to spare after building an unassailable lead in Austin.

Palmowski followed up victory in Friday's Opening Race at the Circuit of the Americas with second in the Reverse Grid Race behind Alba Larsen to take a 70-point lead over her closest championship challenger, Emma Felbermayr, with only a maximum of 67 points remaining.

The Red Bull-backed driver has dominated this season by winning five of the 11 races so far with six pole positions to become the second Briton after Abbi Pulling in 2024 to win the F1 Academy title.

Palmowski, 20, is the youngest F1 Academy champion and praised the team and her family, who were in attendance in Austin.

"We did it guys! It's incredible. I don't know what to say. I'm trying not to cry!" she said.

"There's so much hard work gone on behind the scenes, not just from myself, but all the people you won't see. They have lived it day and night.

"We have worked so hard as a team, Campos Racing and Red Bull Racing. We have left no stone unturned. I don't want to name names but my engineer Diego has lived this with me every day and night."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the second F1 Academy race at the 2026 United States Grand Prix

Palmowski has won the title in her second full campaign after an impressive rookie season where she won the 2025 season-opener and took another four podiums.

She has been backed by Red Bull since the start of last year after finishing as runner-up in the 2024 GB4 Championship.

"I've learned so much in the last 18 months to two years being with Red Bull," she said.

"I learned about things I didn't know. I've developed so much, not only as a driver but a person as well. I've matured so much in the last 12 months. It's a dream come true."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Watch Alisha Palmowski get the biggest winning margin in F1 Academy history in Canada earlier this year, and then broke it again a few races later!

What next for Palmowski?

Previous F1 Academy champions Marta Garcia, Pulling and Doriane Pin have gone on to race in other motorsport categories in endurance racing and Formula Regional.

Palmowski, who starts on pole for Sunday's main race in Austin at 5pm, live on Sky Sports F1, may now look to make a similar move in 2027.

"There are conversations happening in the background but I'm leaving that to my management team," she told Sky Sports F1.

"I want to go as far up the single-seater ladder as possible but I'm aware motorsport is a results-based business.

"I'm a big believer that when you go in a car, the helmet goes on, the car doesn't have a gender and we are fighting for the same thing."

Sports.title: Antonelli takes surprise pole to boost chances of sealing title in USA
Sports.content:
Kimi Antonelli beat Max Verstappen to pole position for the United States Grand Prix to boost his chances of sealing a maiden world championship in Sunday's race.

The 20-year-old Mercedes driver is all but certain to become Formula 1's youngest ever champion but could clinch the title with five rounds to spare if he wins in Austin on Sunday and other placings go his way.

It was perhaps the most unlikely of Antonelli's seven poles this season as he came from nowhere in Q3 to surge ahead of Verstappen, who had appeared for most of the weekend to be battling Ferrari for the front-row positions.

Antonelli's pole time of 1:34.035s was good enough to beat Verstappen by 0.179s, with neither driver managing to improve on the second of their two Q3 flying laps.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Craig Slater explains how Kimi Antonelli can clinch the F1 world title this weekend at the United States Grand Prix

Verstappen's Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar equalled his best qualifying result by taking third, leaving Ferrari's Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton a hugely disappointing fourth and fifth, respectively.

George Russell will start from sixth, with the Brit needing to finish in the top eight to ensure Antonelli won't be crowned champion if he wins on Sunday. Hamilton would also need to finish fifth or lower in the event of an Antonelli victory for the title to be confirmed.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli admits taking pole at the United States GP was 'tricky' and eyes up a 'tough' battle with Max Verstappen

"We got pole, so we will try to win tomorrow," Antonelli said. "Max has been very quick and Isack did an incredible job, so it won't be easy.

"We will try to get a good start and hopefully we lead into Turn 1, then set the pace, even though it will be very tight.

"Very happy with qualifying. Q3 was very tough with the wind. Very gusty and unpredictable but happy to put it on pole."

United States GP Qualifying: Top 10 1) Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes



2) Max Verstappen, Red Bull



3) Isack Hadjar, Red Bull



4) Charles Leclerc, Ferrari



5) Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari



6) George Russell, Mercedes



7) Oscar Piastri, McLaren



8) Lando Norris, McLaren



9) Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls*



10) Liam Lawson, Racing Bulls



*five-place grid penalty to be applied

Oscar Piastri took seventh ahead of his McLaren team-mate Lando Norris as the latter was demoted from sixth after having his final effort deleted for breaching track limits.

Racing Bulls took the final two top-10 places but Liam Lawson will inherit ninth from his team-mate Arvid Lindblad, who has a five-place grid penalty for exceeding his engine component allowance.

Antonelli delivers as Ferrari fall away

Ferrari came into the session as favourites for pole having topped all three practice sessions, and the only driver who appeared to be capable of challenging them was the in-form Verstappen.

That form appeared to be holding as qualifying began with Leclerc setting the early pace. It was only an extra run at the end of Q1 from Norris that knocked the Ferrari driver and Verstappen down from the top two places.

It was in Q2 that the picture began to change, with Verstappen appearing to separate himself from his rivals as he eased through with just one run on a used set of tyres.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli takes pole for the United States Grand Prix - could this be a championship winning drive?

Leclerc finished the period fastest ahead of Antonelli and Russell, who had shown improvement for Mercedes but still couldn't match the Ferrari as all three ran on fresh tyres.

The Silver Arrows' dominance during the first half of the season enabled Antonelli to build a big championship lead and his team to do the same in the constructors' standings, but the recent upgrade package they brought had to this point failed to deliver.

That all changed on the first runs in Q3 when Antonelli put together a fine lap to sit almost two tenths clear of Verstappen, with Leclerc behind Hadjar, three tenths down and seemingly suddenly out of contention.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Toto Wolff admits the car is still 'on the edge' despite encouraging signs of their Mercedes upgrades.

With gusting winds making for challenging conditions, Antonelli made a mistake in the final sector on his second run that appeared to have opened the door for Verstappen to snatch pole, but the Dutchman was also caught out and failed to improve his time, before the lap was deleted in any case for a track limits breach.

"Just Q3 was not good," Verstappen said. "Q1, Q2 was nice but then, for whatever reason on both sets [of tyres], just didn't have a good balance.

"There were no mistakes but just no grip and started to slide a lot and then the final lap, you can see that it's not really happening with the tail wind in places so you try to push a bit more, you hit the bump wrong the car is like a kangaroo and you have a massive slide so you know the lap is over."

Behind the top two on track, Leclerc managed to improve but not enough to improve his position, while Hamilton could only get above Russell for fifth.

Hamilton questioned over team radio whether Ferrari's rivals 'turning up their engines' had caused the turnaround, but Leclerc insisted after the session that it was down to other factors.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton explain what went wrong for Ferrari during qualifying, despite them looking on pace

"This time I think it's slightly different in that I don't think the others have changed anything from Q2 to Q3," Leclerc said. "Where we have lost is on ourselves and that is mostly the tyres.

"The out lap was extremely difficult. There was a bit more cloud in Q3. We lost one or two degrees of track temp and, for us, it was night and day different and already from the out lap I felt I was having lots of difficulties.

"It's a shame that it happened in Q3 because I strongly believe that we had the pace to be fighting in front but unfortunately not today again."

Sports.title: Glitch in Chelsea’s coding costs Alonso while resurgent Spurs are all systems go | Barney Ronay
Sports.content:
There was an odd interlude at Stamford Bridge with 76 minutes gone and the score still 0-0, one of those moments where suddenly your brain seems to be on inside out, like trying to walk the wrong way down an escalator.

Tottenham had a corner on the left-hand side, in a game that had felt to that point like an extended practice session, a refinement of systems, the football equivalent of watching two middle-aged men methodically emptying the dishwasher, adding salt, descaling the hoses, tutting over knives incorrectly slotted, cups in the wrong row.

Fittingly it took a glitch in the coding to break this game open. Austin MacPhee, Chelsea’s set-piece coach, was, as ever, up on his touchline semaphoring his instructions. Except this time he was ordering Chelsea players out of their own box. Get upfield. We need fewer people defending. We must, for some reason, vacate that space and initiate some kind of counterattack chess game.

This had already happened at another corner on 52 minutes. On that occasion 10 players were arranged in various upfield positions, leaving just a small gaggle in the box doing the actual try-to-score stuff. The ball landed in one of the huge vacant spaces. Everyone cheered.

Who started this habit? It seems like one of those things that just happens and you don’t know how or why, like driverless cars, or Howard Webb suddenly having his own ref-based TV show. But it was decisive here.

The second corner came howling in right through that vacated area. Again it looked strange, not least on a wet, blustery day, the kind of day where the rain just seems to want to get inside the neck of your coat, up your trouser turn-ups, in your pockets. The ball kept travelling, right through all that open space. At which point Mike Penders punched it into his own net.

MacPhee came to Chelsea in the summer after the club activated his release clause at Aston Villa, the most remarkable part of which is that the bloke who waves at corners actually has a release clause (fee: undisclosed). Here his response to the goal was to walk pensively down the touchline, stroking his chin. Hmm, yes, need to log this. Look at the data on that.

To be fair, this was a goalkeeping mistake by Penders, a random variable. Although not really if you zoom out. Penders is not best equipped to deal with no protection, with rain, wind and a soaking ball. Penders is good with his feet, famous for stepping out to play centre-half sometimes at Strasbourg. Maybe he should have been waved upfield by MacPhee to mark the counterattack. Anything but this in fact.

MacPhee’s gambit, now safely in the data bank as Counter-Bluff Own Goal No 34, did at least open up the game. A few minutes later Cole Palmer was sent off for a second yellow after a foul on Conor Gallagher. And on 87 minutes Mathys Tel scored a lovely goal, surging upfield and shooting low inside the near post, signal for Roberto De Zerbi to invade the pitch in a strange capering run, cramped over at the waist, cackling provocatively, like a stylised martial arts pose. Enter: Haemorrhoid Warrior.

View image in fullscreen Roberto De Zerbi was wild, passionate, his heart on his sleeve, but also obsessed with patterns and systems. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Until that point the entire afternoon had felt like an overload of systems-ball. Sometimes games like this are described as a fascinating tactical battle. This was something else, a dull tactical battle. At times in the first half the Stamford Bridge crowd got to watch a press being baited when there was no press, just a bait. Essentially, just people standing around.

By the end two things had happened. First, Chelsea were terrible. Maybe this is still a structural thing. After the years of wild overspend this has now become a high-speed talent trading house, new faces, old faces, faces you didn’t know were there, all simultaneously coming and going. End result: Chelsea had no cutting edge at all here in the absence of João Pedro, an entire system thrown by the lack of a focal point in attack. Danny Welbeck stayed on the bench for whatever reason.

Xabi Alonso played Palmer and Morgan Rogers in a strange, liminal forward role, ghost tens, nonexistent nines. There has been a lot of talk about the freedom Alonso likes to give his attack, the hard positional stuff reserved for the block behind. Sometimes freedom’s just another word for standing around in the rain, not sure which run to make.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Chelsea were static all game, lacking in edge, fire or urgency. There was even something a little sad in the crowd reaction on 69 minutes as Palmer earned his first yellow card, signal for a bust-up between the benches, basically a load of men in puffer jackets jostling and prancing. The home crowd leapt up, absolutely delighted to see some kind of edge finally. This is what they like here. In the end people just want to feel something.

Instead Chelsea had kicked off this London derby in cold systems-ball mode, and never got the engine hot. Forty minutes in Palmer had touched the ball eight times, Chelsea were on 27 per cent possession at home to Spurs, and the only real element of tension was the sight of Alonso’s weirdly inadequate golfing blouson steadily saturating with rainwater. Not his only misjudgment of the afternoon.

The second thing, Tottenham were good. Allowed to dominate the ball, and with Mateus Fernandes very good in deep midfield, this turned into their best result of the season, and a huge tick for the manager, who clearly loved every second.

De Zerbi is a funny concept. Wild, passionate, heart on his sleeve. But also obsessed with patterns and systems. He’s basically wildly excited about maths. But he was great to watch here. On the hour mark something complex happened in his team’s movements. Someone stood in the wrong space. A chance to swarm-press was passed up.

In response De Zerbi leapt in the air and let out a strange baying noise, the sound of an alpaca being garrotted. Moments later, Omar Marmoush passed straight to a Chelsea player and De Zerbi didn’t even flinch. We see things you’ll never see.

For a while James Maddison seemed to be playing a different game to everyone else, one where you’re allowed to make forward passes, carry the ball and make the game up in front of you a little. With 49 minutes gone he sat down in the centre-circle, his game done, which will be a concern. But this was still an excellent afternoon for De Zerbi’s Spurs; albeit one that turned on a missed punch and a moment of unnecessary helicopter coaching.

Sports.title: Ballon d’Or ceremony returns to England in nod to ‘revolutionary’ Stanley Matthews
Sports.content:
When football’s dignitaries assemble on Monday at the London Palladium for the Ballon d’Or ceremony it will be a far cry from the first awards 70 years ago. That was held in the slightly less glamorous surroundings of Blackpool town hall, where Stanley Matthews was presented with the prize by Gabriel Hanot, the visionary editor of L’Équipe who came up with the idea of crowning the world’s best player every year.

A specially commissioned china plate was also handed over by the town’s mayor before the 41-year-old Matthews, who was famously teetotal, gave a short speech. “He might have had a double carrot juice that day,” says his son, Stanley Matthews Jr, who will attend this year’s awards with his sister, Jean, and her two daughters. “There was no ceremony. ‘Here’s your Ballon d’Or, well done’, sort of thing. But obviously it’s grown over the years, and now it’s a huge event. We’re very excited.”

The switch of venue to England from its usual home in Paris is a mark of respect to the man who became the first active player to receive a knighthood in 1965, a few months before retiring at the age of 50. It also provides an opportunity to recall an astonishing career that began with his local side Stoke in 1932 and made the “Wizard of Dribble” the most famous player on the planet.

View image in fullscreen In September 1956, Stanley Matthews shows his son Stanley Jr a scrapbook of cuttings from newspapers and magazines going back over 25 years of his career in football. Photograph: Popperfoto/Getty Images

“He was so far ahead of his time,” says Matthews Jr, a former winner of junior Wimbledon who had a successful tennis career. “The way he trained, his football boots … they were so light, they were like slippers so that he could move quicker. Towards the end of his career, when he was back at Stoke, he had the fire brigade come and water the pitch before the game so it would be a little slick, which was better for him. Now they water the pitches all the time, you know. So he was very revolutionary in all the things he did, plus his diet and his training.”

Matthews’ father, Jack, was a renowned boxer known as the Fighting Barber of Hanley and it was from him that he is said to have developed his work ethic. Matthews owned a Blackpool hotel that regularly welcomed celebrities including the comedian Charlie Chester, and was known for his early morning fitness routines on the beach that helped to prolong his career.

View image in fullscreen Stanley Matthews (right) visits a boot and shoe factory in 1951 where he is pictured discussing his own design with two experts. Photograph: Popperfoto/Getty Images

He remains the oldest Ballon d’Or winner and won the last of his 54 England caps – a number that would have been higher but for the second world war – in 1957 at the age of 42. Matthews Jr thinks his father could have lasted even longer in today’s possession-based game. “He would probably have thought: ‘My goodness, if all I had to do was pass the ball around, I could have played until I was 70,’ because a lot of the players just seem to be doing that, passing out from the back,” he says.

Whereas Harry Kane and the rest of the favourites for this year’s Ballon d’Or are all multimillionaires, Matthews had to make do with at most £20 a week until the maximum wage was abolished in 1961. “We compared it to the top sportsman in the US at the time, which was [baseball player] Joe DiMaggio” says Joe Pierce, who produced the 2017 film Matthews. “He was at the height of his career, and he had just signed a contract for $100,000 a year.”

View image in fullscreen Stoke City’s Sir Stanley Matthews is chaired off the pitch by World Stars XI’s Lev Yashin and Ferenc Puskas as Josef Masopust (left) leads the applause for the Wizard of Dribble after his testimonial in April 1965. Photograph: Empics/PA/Alamy

That meant there were a few successful and not so successful business ventures, including his own football boot brand, hats and various books, not to mention vegetable juice. “He tried to do it in cans, but it didn’t work out,” says Pierce. “There was a problem because it went bad in the cans.”

Another way of supplementing his income was coaching overseas in the off-season and between 1953 and 1978 Matthews visited an African country each summer. His love affair with the continent grew a few months after he had won the Ballon d’Or when he arrived in Ghana to play a series of exhibition matches to celebrate its independence. He was presented with an ivory sword and crowned as a “soccerhene” (soccer chief). “The King of Ghana – that’s what they called him,” says Matthews Jr. “My sister still has the stool that he was crowned on.”

Matthews developed a particular affinity for South Africa. He started coaching a team in Soweto during the mid-70s who became known as Stan’s Men and secured them sponsorship from Coca-Cola before taking them to play in a tournament in Brazil. Pierce was surprised when he discovered the lengths Matthews went to under significant pressure from the apartheid government not to travel.

View image in fullscreen Stanley Matthews coaching in Soweto. Photograph: Courtesy of Stanley Matthews Jr

“There was real drama and back and forth. The UK government was involved. The South African government was involved. There were spies involved – the South African spies at the camps and around – and he just kept pushing forward. He was good friends with the Duke of Edinburgh – they would get invited over for tea and things like that. So he had connections in high places that probably helped quite a bit.”

Matthews Jr says: “He was very proud of the fact that at one stage he was banned. He said: ‘Frank Sinatra was banned as well.’ So he thought that was kind of funny. I remember him saying that the South African players had so much speed and so much talent. Dad just liked people. And he knew that they had or he thought that they had a good talent. He just wanted to see if he could help them improve.”

His association with Stan’s Men ended after the 1976 Soweto Uprising, with one player in the film describing how ending contact with Matthews left a “hole in my heart”. Matthews’ death in 2000 at the age of 85 also evoked strong emotions, with more than 100,000 people turning out in Stoke for what the Guardian called the biggest public funeral since Winston Churchill.

View image in fullscreen Some former members of Stan’s Men. Photograph: Courtesy of Stanley Matthews Jr

“He’s probably sitting there saying: ‘I told you so,’” Pierce says of the record 78 African players in the Premier League last season. Only one African player – George Weah – and three Englishmen – Bobby Charlton, Kevin Keegan and Michael Owen – have followed Matthews in winning the Ballon d’Or. Whoever is chosen this year will be following in the footsteps of one of the sport’s most celebrated figures.

Sports.title: Ian Holloway’s circus: why the manager’s outbursts are no laughing matter for fans
Sports.content:
In Ian Holloway’s often madcap managerial orbit, this was simply the latest in a steady succession of eccentric outbursts. Eyes bulging as he spoke, he boomed the letter “D” and promptly stabbed himself in the chest with an imaginary dagger. Next came the letter “M” alongside a blow from another invisible knife. Finally, a “W” followed by a jab to the heart. “Dead. Man. Walking,” he declared, pausing for effect between words and briefly falling into an Oscar-worthy zombie stupor. “That’s how it feels.”

To an offbeat press conference genre containing seagulls following trawlers and self-proclaimed special ones, it was a crazy new entry worthy of its subsequent viral nature. Holloway at his finest.

The clip was widely shared, there is every chance you saw it earlier this month. The general perception, from those of a neutral stance, was that one of football’s great characters had lost the plot. To those in the room, there was a sense that it was merely the exuberant mannerisms of a quirky manager during a tricky period. But for a large section of Swindon fans, it prompted an unamused eye roll. Here we go again. The circus tent is pitched firmly in town.

Supporting a Holloway-led club is an interesting assignment. Within weeks of taking the Swindon job two years ago on Sunday, he began constructing a hostile wall towards fans by reminding them that they could “go bowling” if they did not like his methods. Last December, he had to be restrained by his players during an altercation with a fan, while he has made a habit of telling them to “jog on” if overly vocal in their criticism.

When his side picked up a much-needed point against Walsall last week, the goalkeeping coach held him back from another confrontation with supporters. Asked about it, he goaded reporters into putting his address online so that disgruntled fans could have it out with him: “I don’t really care anymore.” So, when season-ticket holders found their phones pinging with amused messages containing the same viral Holloway zombie clip, their lack of laughter could be forgiven.

“When you get these soundbites from Ian Holloway, outside the Swindon Town world it’s all about what a great character he is, how he says it like it is, and how it must be great to have him as manager,” says Rich Pullen, founder and co-host of the largest Swindon podcast, Loathed Strangers. “But, to a growing percentage of the Swindon community, it’s exhausting and it takes away from any of the good.

“If Swindon win, post-match he often uses it as an opportunity to have a go at the fans. It’s got to the stage where you can’t even enjoy a win without Ian Holloway being unable to hold himself from criticising fans. The easy thing to do is ignore him, but it’s almost impossible because he is everywhere. He goes viral and everyone always thinks: ‘Oh, isn’t that funny.’ Well, no. People are tired of the excess noise.”

This time last week, there was a thought that Saturday’s M4 derby homecoming trip to Bristol Rovers might hasten a possible end to Holloway’s Swindon tenure. Winless in eight games in all competitions, the discontent was not expected to abate on the preceding midweek trip to high-flying Barnet. The 3-1 victory that followed – Barnet’s first league defeat of the season – was a huge shock, thanks in no small part to the heroics of the goalkeeper, Connor Ripley, who recently declared the whole squad would “run through a brick wall” for Holloway.

View image in fullscreen Disheartened Swindon fans stand solemnly in the pouring rain at the Memorial Stadium. Photograph: Jeremy Landey/Focus Images Ltd/Shutterstock

Swindon might have followed it with another win, at Rovers’ Memorial Stadium, only for Matty Virtue to miss an open goal 90 seconds into the match. The forgettable goalless draw that played out at least extended Swindon’s unbeaten run to three games and kept them safely mid-table in League Two. Holloway was right to savour the improved performances, but the malaise runs deeper.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

The manager had said something far more significant immediately after his viral soundbite when he continued: “The owner’s a dead man walking as well and that over-complicates everything here.”

Even those seeking a more composed figure in Holloway’s place agree the manager is just one cog in a machine many argue has been misfiring for some time. Days after the zombie rant, the Swindon Town Supporters Trust declared the club had “lost our soul, our hope, our passion”, and urged Holloway’s comments about the Australian owner, Clem Morfuni, to “be a wake-up call”.

Since saving the club from probable administration in 2021, Morfuni has become a target of increasing fan indignation, failing to sell up and adding millions to the club’s debt. “Whilst the short-term focus may be on Ian Holloway, the bigger picture is above the role of the manager,” concluded the Trust, pointing to “a wedge with supporters so obvious that even the manager openly talks about it”.

In such a context, the uptick in form is merely one – albeit very welcome – aspect among wider misgivings. Because what fans really want is a united club and manager they can get behind; not to go jogging on.

Sports.title: Clinical Arsenal earn precious win against Everton thanks to Konsa and Gabriel
Sports.content:
The wait goes on for David Moyes. The 63-year-old Scot must have been hoping that on his 14th visit to this stadium as Everton’s manager, his luck would change. Yet from the moment Ezri Konsa slammed home his first goal for Arsenal as the Premier League champions rediscovered their knack of scoring from set pieces, the writing was on the wall.

While it took until midway through the second half for Gabriel Magalhães to make sure of the victory, Arsenal were never going to let slip the chance of moving level on points at the top with Manchester City after their defeat by Aston Villa earlier in the day.

Asked whether it was strange that his side are again going toe-to-toe with their great rivals but with the added uncertainty of what punishment City will receive after being found guilty of 115 charges by the Premier League, Mikel Arteta said: “[We are] just focusing on what we can do. We are very pleased with 90% of the results and performances that we have.”

This was hardly a vintage performance from the clinical home side after a testing week but it did not need to be against opponents who offered precious little in attack, even if they defended for their lives at times.

Having gone six matches without defeat to start the season, a second in succession will only add to Everton’s concerns after confirmation that the club’s American owners want out.

“It was always going to be hard after conceding the early goal,” said Moyes, whose solitary victory at the Emirates was as West Ham’s manager in 2023. “I want us to challenge the top teams but it’s difficult when you see the strength of their bench.”

Everton’s record at this stadium is almost as bad as their manager’s. They arrived in north London having won twice in 35 matches here and had to do without Jarrad Branthwaite and Jack Grealish, who was ruled out with illness. It did not bode well for them when Arsenal took the lead in the seventh minute with a third corner in succession.

View image in fullscreen Ezri Konsa (No 15) squeezes the ball home for Arsenal’s early first goal against Everton. Photograph: Adam Davy/PA

Gabriel made the crucial first contact at the near post and Jordan Pickford tipped the ball on to the crossbar, only for Vitaliy Mykolenko’s failed clearance under pressure from Viktor Gyökeres to allow Konsa to ram home from close range. After a record-breaking 25 goals from set pieces last season, it was their first of this campaign.

It was a measure of Arsenal’s exertions against Bayern Munich on Wednesday that Arteta rotated his side more than usual for a Premier League match, making five changes.

Eberechi Eze and Noni Madueke spurned good opportunities to extend the lead in front of the watching England head coach, Thomas Tuchel. The latter was left out of the last squad, but could well benefit from Bukayo Saka’s expected long absence due to a thigh injury. He was inches away with an instinctive effort with his right foot from the edge of the area on the half-hour mark and was consistently Arsenal’s most dangerous threat.

Everton must have feared the worst as yet another Arsenal corner – 10 during the first half – was launched into the area. Yet the defence just about stood firm.

A moment’s lapse of concentration from Ben White just before half-time almost gave Everton an equaliser but Thierno Barry could not get enough on his attempt to flick the ball past David Raya in their clearest opening.

Gyökeres looked determined to make an impression on his first Premier League start of the season but the Sweden striker, who has yet to score for his club this term, looked laboured.

Quick Guide Arsenal 2-0 Everton key facts Show • With both Arsenal and Manchester City doing so this season, this is just the third top-flight campaign to have two teams win at least seven of their opening eight matches after 1892-93 (Preston and Sunderland) and 1913-14 (Blackburn and Manchester United). • This was David Moyes’s 400th defeat across all competitions in his managerial career with all clubs. 31 of these have come against Arsenal, more than against any other opponent. • The opener from Ezri Konsa (pictured celebrating) was Arsenal’s first set piece goal (excluding penalties) since May against Crystal Palace, ending a run of 13 games without one. Opta Photograph: Adam Davy/PA Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

He could not believe it when Tony Harrington penalised him for a foul on James Tarkowski and a sheepish Arteta earned himself a booking for protesting. Unsurprisingly, Gyökeres’ number was up soon after as Arsenal turned to their bench.

It took less than 60 seconds for Gabriel to head in at the back post as White offered Tuchel a timely reminder of his qualities with a brilliant cross.

Moyes’ frustration meant he joined Arteta in the referee’s notebook. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall could have made things interesting but his header fizzed just wide of a post.

Arsenal are now breathing down City’s necks, although whether this title race lasts the course remains unknown.

Sports.title: Relief for Slegers as Russo rescues Arsenal against Tottenham in WSL
Sports.content:
Alessia Russo’s contentious second-half penalty delivered relief, a reprieve and a chance for a reset as Arsenal came from a goal down to earn their second win of the WSL season in the north London derby.

At a rain-lashed Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, the Gunners were again their own worst enemy, forced to come from behind after Cathinka Tandberg’s headed opener. Georgia Stanway levelled and Russo powered in the penalty that gave them the lead they protected defiantly.

The Tottenham manager, Martin Ho, queried the penalty decision, with the ball hitting the raised arm of substitute Ella Morris from the clearance of one of her teammates. “My interpretation of the rule is if your teammate hits it and it hits your player, if you’re one yard away, the time and distance is taken into account, so there’s no penalty,” he said. “That’s my understanding of it, from when we were told to start the season. I want to understand what they’re saying, because then I can accept the decision.

“I don’t want the game to be about that, but when it decides a game it’s frustrating because it’s not within the law of the game.”

Arsenal’s manager, Renée Slegers, said she was glad to give the fans a win. “They sing us and fight us through the game,” she said. “At the end it’s scrappy, it’s game management and it’s scenarios, and they’re all with us.”

With the pressure building on her and her players after five games without a win, at times it felt like they were trying to disprove the phrase “you can’t dig yourself out of a hole”.

Quick Guide Brighton cruise to victory against West Ham Show Maisie Symonds’ first-half stunner sent Brighton on their way to a 3-0 win against West Ham at the Amex Stadium. The midfielder Symonds’ thunderbolt gave the Seagulls a half-time lead before Fran Kirby and Kiko Seike struck quickfire goals midway through the second period. It was a first clean sheet this season for Arturo Ruiz’s side and lifts them up to eighth in the table, two points above West Ham, who slipped to 12th after their fifth league defeat of the campaign. Press Association Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Arsenal had looked a little shaky in the opening few minutes but they settled, built possession and started to pose a threat. A failure to carve out clearcut chances and capitalise on any period of dominance has been the running theme of their season. They lacked fight and there was sloppiness too, with too many overhit passes putting the ball out of play or giving away possession.

That the opener came from a Tottenham corner was unsurprising. Victoria Pelova swung the ball in and Tandberg rose above her two markers, Stanway and Emily Fox, who failed to even to jump and challenge, and headed home.

Spurs’ joy was short lived as Stanway made up for her marking error four minutes later by arriving to meet Russo’s cut back and powered the ball in off the crossbar.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Georgia Stanway equalises for Arsenal in the 17th minute. Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/Reuters

After the break there was concern for Tottenham when Alice Sombath’s leg seemed to twist awkwardly as she stretched for the ball. The club’s record signing left on a stretcher to be replaced by Morris, who made her return from an anterior cruciate ligament injury towards the end of last season.

After the lengthy stoppage, Russo forced a huge save from Lize Kop as she attempted to turn in Caitlin Foord’s cross from close range, the forward putting her hands to her head and screaming in frustration at the missed opportunity.

It did not take long for that frustration to transform into elation. The resulting corner from Kyra Cooney-Cross was headed on by Leah Williamson at the near post and Lisa Baum’s effort came back off the post. Spurs’ clearance bounced off the raised arm of Morris and the referee pointed to the spot. Russo sent Kop the wrong way and drove the ball low into the corner.

Arsenal were clinging on as the final whistle loomed but they had “found their fight,” said Slegers. “We had a run of games where results haven’t been good enough. It was frustrating for everyone. I’m so happy we got to win on this occasion, in the north London derby, away from home in the rain and we showed that character in the team.

“This will definitely energise us. We need to back this up in the next couple of games.”

Sports.title: Maresca ‘not worried’ by Guéhi’s gaffes as Aston Villa end City’s flawless start
Sports.content:
Enzo Maresca is not concerned by the form of Marc Guéhi despite the defender costing his side three goals in the past two Premier League matches, the Manchester City manager said after seeing his side lose in the league for the first time this season.

Nicolas Jackson’s double earned Aston Villa a 2-1 victory at Villa Park after Guéhi was unable to control the ball for the opener. Instead he spilled it into the path of John McGinn, who played it to Jackson, allowing him to score the first of two goals. The defender was then substituted at half-time having been booked on 32 minutes. Guéhi’s errors allowed Ipswich to score twice against City last weekend.

“No, I’m not worried about Marc at all,” Maresca said. “I know that he’s played every minute since the season started with us, with the international team, so it’s not easy. But again, the change was also because he was on a yellow card and in the way we want to be aggressive, sometimes to have one yellow card can be dangerous, but I’m not worried at all.”

City had 15 shots to Villa’s eight as they dropped points for the first time this season. Zion Suzuki made a number of important saves to keep City at bay in the second half, and Villa scored with their only two shots on target.

“I think we deserved more from the game, for the amount of chances that we created and for the chances that we conceded,” Maresca said. “We lost because probably we have not been clinical enough in their box and sometimes when you concede the first goal because of the mistake, the second goal again comes from transition in 45 minutes. It’s difficult to avoid that every time, but we learn from the game and we try to move on and to improve.”

View image in fullscreen Nicolas Jackson scores Aston Villa’s first goal past Gianluigi Donnarumma. Photograph: Tony O Brien/Reuters

Jackson’s double takes him to seven goals since his move from Chelsea. He was a constant threat to the City centre-backs, who were unable to cope with his speed, physical presence and clinical finishing. Unai Emery said of his forward: “He’s very demanding of himself to improve things. Today he scored two goals, in the last matches he scored goals – but at the beginning of the season, what happened to us was more difficult and he was shooting a lot of balls over the corner.

“Now, he’s getting better at shooting. He’s working fantastically tactically, he’s understanding as well where we need him. Today, he scored two goals, but the most important thing is how he did his work, his task.”

His fellow summer signing Suzuki challenged Jackson for the player of the match award and is starting to show why Villa were so keen to acquire him as Emiliano Martínez’s replacement. Matty Cash told TNT Sport: “He’s brilliant, his first session when he came in, in the possession drill I thought we’d signed a midfielder. His vision is unbelievable, he catches crosses really well which as a full-back is a dream.”

Sports.title: Burnley sack Nicky Hayen after Lincoln rout leaves them in bottom three
Sports.content:
Burnley have sacked Nicky Hayen after only 14 games in charge, in the wake of a 4-1 defeat at Lincoln that left the Clarets in the Championship’s relegation zone.

The Belgian was appointed in the summer as the permanent successor to Scott Parker, who left in April with relegation from the Premier League inevitable. He leaves having won just one match, a 4-0 league victory at Watford on 10 October.

Burnley edged past Notts County on penalties in the Carabao Cup in his first match in charge and recovered in the last seven minutes from 2-0 down to draw at home to West Ham in their opening game of the Championship season. However, they then lost badly at West Brom and Norwich, sandwiching a shootout exit from the Carabao Cup at Bradford, and the pattern was set.

Burnley were fancied to push for promotion, which was achieved in their past two Championship seasons, but are now at risk of relegation. Wolves’ come-from-behind win at Turf Moor last weekend left Hayen on the brink and now the club have acted.

A terse, two-sentence statement on the club website said: “Burnley Football Club has dismissed head coach Nicky Hayen with immediate effect. The board has taken the decision following a disappointing start to the Championship season.”

Hayen had earlier said in his post-match press conference, before news of his dismissal emerged: “It’s frustrating for everyone, especially the fans. I want to apologise to them, but I know it doesn’t matter because it’s another hard defeat for them and I can understand their criticism.

“We haven’t got the results. I will keep on working hard as long as I have the chance. But there will be a day if it carries on like this that it stops. I know it’s a really tough defeat and something to think about for the board.”

Sports.title: Dele Alli pokes fun at Chelsea legend John Terry with video from Stamford Bridge as he watches former club Tottenham earn surprise 2-0 win... just weeks after going viral for his Twitch calls with Harry Kane and Co
Sports.content:
Dele Alli pokes fun at Chelsea legend John Terry with video from Stamford Bridge as he watches former club Tottenham earn surprise 2-0 win... just weeks after going viral for his Twitch calls with Harry Kane and Co

Dele Alli enjoyed a trip to Stamford Bridge to see his former club Tottenham inflict a surprise defeat on rivals Chelsea – and entertained his followers on social media by poking fun at John Terry.

The 30-year-old midfielder, who played 269 games for Spurs between 2015 and 2022, kept his Instagram followers posted throughout the game - and posted a video of himself laughing while filming the Chelsea legend's reaction when Tottenham took the lead through an own goal from keeper Mike Penders.

Cole Palmer was later sent off for the hosts, and Mathys Tel’s brilliant goal sealed a 2-0 victory.

Dele also filmed the scoreboard and Spurs celebrations at Stamford Bridge and later put up a picture of Terry’s empty seat beside him with the caption: ‘Empty seat here now?’

He finished a story on Instagram by posting a celebratory photo alongside fellow former Tottenham midfielder Jermaine Jenas.

It was a momentous evening for Spurs – and just their second league win at Stamford Bridge since 1990. They now sit 12th after back-to-back victories following just three points from their first six games.

Dele Alli's Instagram story of his day out at Stamford Bridge included him sitting next to Chelsea legend John Terry

He tagged Terry into his video of the scoreboard once Spurs went 1-0 ahead

... and then mocked the former Chelsea star who appeared to have left

Alli finished off his story with a selfie alongside fellow ex-Spurs star Jermaine Jenas

Dele is having something of a reinvention as a social-media personality, having been without a club since leaving Como last year.

He has played just ten minutes of professional football since February 2023 and earlier this month hit the headlines when he live-streamed himself on Twitch calling footballers from his contacts book such as Jack Grealish, Ashley Cole and Harry Kane.

Kane and Alli played together in an eye-catching Spurs team under Mauricio Pochettino which finished runners up in the Premier League in 2017 and reached Champions League final two years later.

After Alli tipped Kane for the Ballon d’Or in the unscheduled call, the Bayern Munich striker appeared concerned, asking Alli where he was living now and expressed his hope that he is still ‘working hard’.

Sports.title: 'I am a good dad': Snooker star Mark Allen shares handwritten pages of 'positive affirmations' as he vows to shine light on mental health struggles - days after revealing he has spent 10 weeks in a clinic
Sports.content:
Snooker star Mark Allen has thanked fans for their 'overwhelming' support after he revealed his mental health battles – and shared two handwritten notes detailing 'positive affirmations' which help him deal with his struggles.

Allen, 40, revealed last week that he had spent ten weeks in a mental health clinic after an emotional interview where he revealed he could quit the sport.

Speaking after his defeat in the first round of the Northern Ireland Open on Tuesday, the former world No1 told TNT Sports that his career may be over as he deals with a lot of 'problems within' that mean he is 'just trying to survive'.

The interview sparked a wave of concern from fans and Allen posted a statement on X where he said 'I'm not OK,' but insisted he was in a better place than he had been.

On Sunday morning, Allen then took to social media again to outline his determination to recover, before he shared his gratitude to fans for their response to him opening up on his struggles.

'Completely overwhelmed by all the messages I have received since my statement,' Allen wrote. 'As I continue my treatment and my recovery now I know that I simply have to raise more awareness around mental health in the future.

'Best part of 6 weeks before the UK Championships starts and all being well I’ll be in a better place by then but for now it’s just one day at a time. Thanks again for all your support. It’s meant so so much to myself and my family.'

A few hours later, Allen then demonstrated one of the ways he is trying to deal with things.

Mark Allen returned the sport in Belfast last week for his first match since May

I do these every morning with a cup of tea out of my positive mindset cup. Been doing this for 2 months now. You don’t have to believe it all at the start!!! It’ll come pic.twitter.com/YBjlfhvxkU — Mark Allen (@pistol147) October 25, 2026

The former World Championship semi-finalist brushed away a tear at the end of his interview following his defeat and was consoled by TNT Sport's Rachel Casey

Sharing two photos of handwritten notes, Allen said: 'I do these every morning with a cup of tea out of my positive mindset cup. Been doing this for 2 months now. You don’t have to believe it all at the start!!! It’ll come.'

The notes, titled 'positive affirmations', showed Allen writing down aspects of life that he was 'grateful for', 'things from yesterday that made me happy/smile' and he also had a series of words to describe himself.

These included Allen saying he was grateful for 'my health', 'Harleigh (his nine-year-old daughter) being my shining light', while a 'nice dinner with my parents and Harleigh' made him happy on Saturday.

Another page saw Allen write down a series of things about himself.

The list of 32 affirmations included reminding himself he is 'a good dad', 'a good person', 'loyal', 'enjoying living in the present', while he also wrote that 'I am deserving of love', 'I am not my mistakes' and 'I am not a failure - I have failed at times'.

He also added: 'I am strong,' 'I am brave,' 'I am a good friend' and 'I am OK just being.'

Allen's notes, dated on Sunday, detail 'things that made me happy/smile' from the previous day... as well as a list of 32 'positive affirmations'

Allen's emotional social media posts earlier in the week received swathes of positive responses, with several fans sharing messages of support for him.

In the TNT interview, Allen had indicated he could be set to take another long, and potentially permanent, break from the sport.

The 40-year-old was close to tears and received comforting support from his interviewer Rachel Casey after saying 'the problems are within.'

That came after he lost 4-2 to Jordan Brown, a close friend and compatriot.

'I think if I wasn't playing Jordan I wouldn't have come back,' he said. 'I felt like if I was going to play one last time, playing here at the Waterfront, where it all started in 2005, against one of my best mates, I thought that was a better way to sign out.'

Asked if he was serious about his threat to retire, Allen confirmed his view and continued: 'I've been flooded with support but the problems are within. I just don't see a future with snooker in it, if I'm honest.

The 40-year-old tied the knot with Sarah Herald last year and highlighted 'Sarah's intervention' as something he was grateful for in his notes shared on X on Sunday

'It's sad to say, because it's all I've loved to do since I was 12 but the last few months have been really difficult and it's put snooker into perspective for me. At the minute I'm just trying to survive.'

Allen had previously stayed silent on his reasons for staying away from the tour.

However, in the past six years he has had to contend with bankruptcy and a divorce – with the latter prompting a five-stone weight loss.

It was in January 2021 when Allen declared himself bankrupt – citing that he spent his £3.5million in career prize money as fast as he earned it.

Allen's financial situation was affected by his split from his ex-wife Kyla McGuigan. The pair had been married for seven years and share a daughter, Harleigh, born in 2017.

As well as Harleigh, Allen has a daughter with his former girlfriend Reanne Evans – another snooker star.

The duo, who have publicly feuded in the past, had a three-year relationship that ended in 2008.

Allen is now a married man once more after tying the knot with Sara Herald last year. They are understood to have first dated in 2023.

Sports.title: Bruno Fernandes is DROPPED from Manchester United's starting XI for Bournemouth - with Red Devils captain on the bench for the first time in almost five years after questioning Michael Carrick's tactics following Como loss
Sports.content:
Bruno Fernandes has been DROPPED from Manchester United's line-up for the first time in almost five years just days after he publicly questioned boss Michael Carrick's tactics. Following the shambolic 4-1 defeat away to Como in the Champions League, Carrick has ruled with an iron fist by dropping his ever-present captain to the bench for Sunday's clash against AFC Bournemouth at Old Trafford. Fernandes is usually the first name on the teamsheet and is rarely ever taken off, never mind left out from the start. It represents the first time Fernandes has been pulled from the line-up for non-fitness reasons since Carrick, again, took him out against Villarreal in November 2021. In truth, Carrick had to cement his power as the manager of the football club and the public criticism of the tactics in Como could not go unpunished. Speaking at a defiant press conference on Friday, Carrick laid bare that no individual is bigger than the club. Bruno Fernandes has been dropped from Manchester United's starting XI to face Bournemouth He cut a downcast figure as he arrived at Old Trafford on Sunday ahead of United's must-win United head coach Michael Carrick made the decision after Fernandes questioned his tactics 'The most important thing for me is the team, first and foremost,' Carrick said. 'I'll always do what's best for the football club.' Fernandes, who is usually very deliberate in what he says in the media, was scathing in his criticism of coaches after the Como debacle. 'It's a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man and sometimes leave a little space in behind and try to get the ball in the first moment, to wait for them, to give them the ball,' he said. 'But sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confident, they have so many bodies behind the ball that make you run a lot, make people get frustrated, and then obviously when you recover the ball the legs are, and the brain, much more difficult to make it work.'
