Sports.title: Fabio Wardley reveals why he wanted to get straight back into the ring with Daniel Dubois as he defends his team after they came under fire for not pulling him out earlier in first defeat
Sports.content:
Fabio Wardley reveals why he wanted to get straight back into the ring with Daniel Dubois as he defends his team after they came under fire for not pulling him out earlier in first defeat

Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon.

Not, at least, according to those who watched him endure 11 gruelling rounds against Daniel Dubois in Manchester in May. Not according to those who questioned whether his corner should have pulled him out earlier, as his face became increasingly battered and his right eye swelled shut. And certainly not according to those who believe the punishment he absorbed makes a rematch a risk too far.

But Wardley has never been one to follow the script.

When the 31-year-old first faced Dubois, 29, he did so as the WBO heavyweight champion. He dropped his opponent twice in the opening three rounds, threatening to produce one of the biggest victories of his career before Dubois fought his way back into the contest and eventually stopped him in the 11th.

Now, with the WBO title back on the line, Wardley finds himself in more familiar territory in one respect: he is the challenger, the underdog and the man many expect to lose again.

And, as he explains when we sit down ahead of the rematch, he rather likes it that way.

Fabio Wardley is not supposed to be here again so soon but he's never one to follow the script

Dubois (right) and Wardley (left) will go toe-to-toe for a second time on Saturday evening

'It's been the staple of my career for as long as I can remember, well, since I started. It has been the main focal point. After the first five or six fights, when I started to step up the level, even incrementally, even slightly, people were saying I was going to lose, that it was a step too far, and all the rest of it. It's all the stuff everyone's heard before,' he says.

'It's a side of the coin I'm very much used to, and the pressure's off. I'm the challenger here. I'm expected to lose and expected to go even quicker, and Daniel's supposed to put on a better performance, and all the rest of it. So there's no pressure on me. There's nothing on my shoulders.'

It is a strikingly relaxed assessment from a fighter preparing to walk back into the ring with the man who inflicted the first defeat of his professional career.

Wardley, however, insists that defeat has done little to change him. He is not pretending that losing a world title is enjoyable, but nor does he regard it as a defining moment in his life.

'Not a lot has changed. I'm not that different. Don't get me wrong, a loss is never fun. It's never nice, it's never enjoyable. But for me, at least, it wasn't soul-crushing or devastating, and it hasn't had any effect on me as a person, my character or anything else.

'The job’s the job, the game’s the game. From the very beginning, I’ve accepted that getting through heavyweight boxing unscathed isn’t guaranteed, especially given the way I compete at the highest level and my desire to take on the biggest challengers out there.

'I think people forget that the first time around, I picked Daniel. I asked for that fight because I looked at the crop of heavyweights and thought, "That's the best one to challenge myself against."

'Knowing that about myself, and knowing that's my angle, was I ever going to get through this undefeated like Floyd Mayweather? Probably not. So, look, it comes how it comes. But as long as I'm happy with myself in terms of the performances, that I've given my all and all the rest of it, I can sleep at night.'

Their first fight in May was a brutal affair, with the contest being stopped in the 11th round

Wardley took a lot of punishment in the latter rounds of their first encounter in May (above)

It is that willingness to put himself in the firing line which has made Wardley such a compelling heavyweight. His fights are rarely short on drama, and the first meeting with Dubois was no exception. He started at a blistering pace, dropping DDD in the opening 10 seconds, only for the momentum to swing as the punishment began to accumulate.

By the later rounds, Wardley was absorbing heavy shots and fighting through considerable damage. His condition between rounds prompted questions about whether the contest should have been stopped sooner, with particular scrutiny falling on his corner for allowing him out ahead of the 10th.

Wardley disagrees with the suggestion that his team failed him. He regards the people around him as family and trusts them to put his welfare first, even when the decisions they make are questioned from the outside.

He is equally dismissive of the noise surrounding the timing of the rematch, arguing that those watching from the outside cannot know the full picture of his recovery. His position is that he and his team are best placed to judge the damage he sustained and whether he is ready to fight again.

For Wardley, the prospect of another brutal encounter is not something he has brushed aside or refused to think about. It is a reality he has had to confront with himself, knowing that by stepping back into the ring with Dubois, he is willingly putting himself in a position where he could once again withstand a frightening amount of punishment.

It is a remarkable thought process: to acknowledge the possibility of enduring the same damage all over again, to ask himself whether he is prepared to go through it, and then to make peace with the answer before he has even thrown a punch.

'It's a level of early acceptance. The second I triggered the rematch clause, even before that, I had to have a conversation with myself and ask, "This could go the exact same way. Are you ready for that? Are you OK with that?"

'As long as the answer is yes from me to me, then cool, let's go. But by now, it's nowhere near my brain as a question mark or something I'm having to deal with, battle with or anything else. It's already been ticked off, boxed and put away. It is what it is.'

Wardley was checked by the doctor and spoken to by the referee multiple times in the fight

As a result, Dubois became a two-time heavyweight champion and will now defend his belt

There is little melodrama in his delivery. When the possibility of going through the same ordeal again is put to him, Wardley does not attempt to dress it up as fearlessness or pretend that the risks do not exist.

'It's an acceptance of the game and the sport we got into, and especially the way I fight as well,' he says.

That approach is perhaps best illustrated by what goes through his mind when he is taking punishment in the ring. Wardley is not a heavyweight who is inclined to retreat quietly after being caught cleanly. His instinct is to make sure his opponent knows there will be a response.

'Especially in those moments, it's about getting back at them. All right, you took one… let your hands go. Don't just let them get away with it for free. At least let them know. Let them have it in their brain that if they get off a few shots, I'm not just going to take them, run away and roll over.'

It is a mindset that makes for spectacular viewing, but one which also places enormous demands on a fighter's corner.

Wardley describes those 60 seconds between rounds as almost too precious to waste on anything other than the information he needs to continue. With the clock ticking and another round approaching, he wants tactical instruction rather than an emotional check-in.

'No, I think it's 90 per cent tactical, 10 per cent everything else, because in those moments, compassion doesn't need to come into it. That's not where the compassion needs to be.

'Those 60 seconds are so precious, such a small moment. It feels like a click. It feels like nothing. It feels like it's done and gone so quickly that you're on your stool, you're off your stool and the next round has started.

'In that time, you need to get the information. It's not time for, "Oh, a little rub on the shoulder. Are you doing OK, Fab? Is everything alright? Are you going to be alright, mate? Do you want me to dab your face a bit?" No. Let me know what I need to know. Let's get this going again.'

Wardley knows that the rematch will be gruelling. He knows his durability will continue to be questioned. But he also knows why he wanted the first fight in the first place.

For Wardley, the pursuit of the biggest challenges has always mattered more than protecting an unbeaten record. Defeat by Dubois has not changed that. He is back because in his mind, the possibility of the same ending has already been accepted and because it’s a risk worth taking.

Sports.title: Daniel Dubois' second clash with Fabio Wardley promises to be even MORE brutal than their first, writes JEFF POWELL MBE - as May's champion vows to 'bash and smash' his rival
Sports.content:
Even the most hardened boxing fans can be taken aback by the depths of brutality which two men are capable of inflicting on each other. Especially the heavyweights.

So it was on the Saturday night this May when Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley battered hell's bells out of each other in Manchester’s Co-op Live Arena. Wardley dropped his world title challenger twice in the first three rounds. Just 28 seconds into the 11th, Dubois had to be pulled off the champion he had reduced to a bleeding and battered but still-standing wreck.

We mere mortals can only ask: How on earth do they do it? ‘We’re fighters,’ says Dubois. ‘Honoured to share a ring with him.’

‘Born to do it,’ says Wardley, who found out that truth of himself when he tried white collar boxing. ‘Love being in with such a great fighter.’

What in heaven goes through their minds at the prospect of doing it again, as they are on Saturday night at the O2? Do they not realise the danger this sledgehammer head-banging presents to their health?

Prepare yourselves, dear gentle readers, for this stunning answer from Dubois: ‘Dementia? If you’re talking about dementia, no point worrying. We’ve probably got it already.’

Daniel Dubois and Fabio Wardley have both spoken of their love for stepping into the ring with one another ahead of their rematch on Saturday

But as brutal as their meeting in May was, tomorrow night's clash at the O2 has been teased as even bloodier

A chilling insight, this, into the mentality of men who fight not only for a living but for the lust for glory, the thrill of battle, the roar of the crowd, the smell of the greasepaint, the glare of the lights and not least their manly pride.

And on nights like this, for a world championship. This time the WBO belt which Dubois ripped from Wardley’s fairy-tale grasp five months ago.

What, no nerves? ‘I live with the chaos,’ says Dubois. ‘Chaos all day every day and specially on the night. I love the fear. It gives me the power. I hold the chaos in until it’s at its peak when the first bell goes. Then it explodes as I let it out. Which brings power and clarity.’

Wardley comes not only from his different background in commerce but also with an opposite mindset. He says: ‘No one wants to lose a world title but if it has to be, then what really matters is how it happens.

‘I feel more relaxed and confident having proved I can engage a top-level fighter in a great fight, which everyone expected me to lose easily. Calm makes me better.’

That and the lessons he learned in the five months since his gladiatorial — and only — defeat thus far. ‘We’ve studied every critical moment of the first fight,’ he says. ‘And I’ve adapted where necessary. Had to because I have more to work on than Daniel with all his experience.

‘But we’ve not only looked at me. We’ve looked at him. He’s not as adaptable as me. He’s not suddenly going to become light-footed and free moving. I’ll give him something different.’

To which Dubois says: ‘I’ll give him another beating. Bash him up. Smash him worse than before. And quicker. We didn’t know quite what he might do in the first fight. Now I know what to expect.

‘I also know that he’s not good enough to adapt. I’m his daddy now.’ That is clarity, Dubois style. He also discounts those two knock-downs. As a man who has been a slow starter at times — although not when he demolished Anthony Joshua from the get-go — he says: ‘Things happen in boxing. You can get caught. But I also know now that he doesn’t have the power. No real power.’

Wardley, for his part, denies that he was as badly hurt as it appeared in fight one. Their respective trainers have disagreed about the 11th-hour stoppage. Dubois’ coach Don Charles says the towel should have been thrown in earlier.

Wardley supports his man Ben Davison’s assertion that he was still in the fight throwing punches, saying: ‘The optics looked bad, what with the blood and the bruising and the punches. But I trust my team to take care of me. Trust them with my life.

‘A lot of the punches were glancing and in the 10th round I shook him with an uppercut. If the big right that followed had connected cleanly we might have had a different ending.’

This man who escaped office drudgery to chase his dream hopes to go on to meet the December winner of Joshua v Tyson Fury. Dubois fancies some of that big money but is also looking beyond, to unifying all the other world titles vacated by Oleksandr Usyk.

Will the ending on Saturday be different from Wardley v Dubois One? Probably not. Dynamite Dan likely added the more valuable knowledge to his wider experience and has never looked this bullish before a fight.

What we do know for sure is that this pair will give us another thriller.

Sports.title: Inside COTA's Turn 1 clubhouse and its plans to build a second track
Sports.content:
For spectators and TV viewers tuning into coverage of F1's US Grand Prix, it's been hard to miss. Turn 1 of the Circuit of the Americas has a distinctly different look to it this year with the addition of a mammoth multi-storey clubhouse. Connected to the main paddock area via a cable car that crosses the track, this weekend the new hospitality structure serves as an extension of F1's swanky Paddock Club. From January 2 it becomes a year-round members-only club, dubbed 'The Circuit', as the venue turns private at the start of next year.

"It isn’t an annual membership in the traditional sense," says Parris Mullins, COTA’s Senior Vice President of Motorsports. It’s much more like a country club. There are annual dues to maintain the facilities and cover staffing, but the initiation fee is a one-time payment that essentially provides a lifetime membership.

"We’ve had more than 50 additional submissions in the past 24 hours, and that was before this race weekend. Before this race weekend, around 600 people had reached out. We’ve had one-to-one conversations with approximately 140 of them, and many have started putting down deposits and signing contracts.

"There will never be more than 300 members. We’re limiting North American membership to 250. The remaining 50 places will be a mix of international and corporate memberships."

A view from COTA's new Turn 1 clubhouse. Photo by: Filip Cleeren

The new facility isn't just COTA president Bobby Epstein's brainchild alone, though. It fits a calendar-wide push by F1 management for races to significantly ramp up their hospitality offerings. "A lot of our contract renewal was dependent on this as well," Mullins adds. "We needed to improve both the members’ experience and the experience for the Paddock Club guests. F1 has made a big commitment to it. The sport has grown, and certain markets demand these kinds of amenities. They have to keep improving what they offer."

Why COTA is building a second circuit

COTA's decision to go private has some side effects, with the venue now no longer available for track days or for regional driving clubs. But there's a solution on the horizon. On an empty plot of land to the north of the existing F1 track, COTA has crafted advanced plans to build a second, shorter circuit designed for both cars and motorcycles.

"A second track will be built, primarily because we recognise that we’re displacing a number of people and organisations that have been partners of ours since the circuit opened," Mullins explains. "Growing motorsport, particularly in the local area, is very important to us. We’re not going to build another FIA Grade 1 facility because there’s no need for one. Instead, we want to build something that suits the local motorsport community, allows them to continue using a circuit and gives them access at a much lower price point.

"There’s obviously prestige associated with COTA. I know people love being able to say they’ve driven their car on the Grand Prix circuit, and we’re sorry that this won’t always be possible unless they’re members. But we want to give people somewhere they can drive, enjoy motorsport and continue participating at a grassroots level."

While details remain sparse, the circuit's undisclosed layout has already been defined. COTA is also open to the new circuit, built to FIA Grade 3 standards suitable for touring cars, sportscars and entry-level single-seaters, hosting smaller motorsports series. But by not having to cater to F1 cars, Mullins feels there is an opportunity to come up with a track more suited to high-performance sports cars and the people who drive them.

"We want to create something fun with a different personality from the Grand Prix circuit. COTA was built around the requirements of a single major race weekend. I’d like it to have corners we don’t have here. We don’t have a banked corner, for example, so I think the new circuit should have one. It should also have an iconic chicane. We want features that people can enjoy in the kinds of cars they bring to the track. The layout should suit them much better."

When asked about the timelines for the secondary track, Mullins didn't want to commit to a firm date, but there is a sense of urgency not to leave local driving and car clubs without a track for too long.

"We still need to finalise everything and work through the process with the city," he says. "We’re far enough along that we’re comfortable saying we want to get it done sooner rather than later. We don’t want the local motorsport community to go without a facility for too long, but we also need to get the project right."

Oliver Bearman, Haas F1 Team Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

COTA still sees itself as the "people's race" with its enormous spectator numbers of up to 440,000 across the F1 weekend, and by gradually turning the entire venue into one giant theme park the organisers want to lean into F1's changed demographic in the post-Netflix era. Some of that can be taken quite literally, with the rollercoaster rides of the new COTALAND amusement running alongside the circuit's third sector. But the grand prix also continues its tradition of big-name end-of-day concerts, roping in Austin's popular college sports and food culture.

Earning a new F1 deal to 2034 gives COTA the long-term stability to write off those investments, and turn them into ways to make the circuit a year-round source of revenue alongside hosting the likes of F1, MotoGP, WEC and - from 2027 - Formula E. COTALAND fits into that picture, and so does the exclusive members club and the secondary track.

But COTA hasn't forgotten that its core business is to keep the hordes of F1 fans entertained over a weekend. "Formula 1 provides the on-track action. Our job is to complement that between sessions," Mullins acknowledges. The concerts were the first step. What Bobby did with those was really groundbreaking.

"At the end of the day, this is sport, but it’s also entertainment. We want to entertain people."

Sports.title: Red Bull no longer falls away on difficult days: What Austin qualifying reveals about its progress
Sports.content:
In Austin, the battle for pole position looked for a long time as though it would be between Max Verstappen and Ferrari. By the end of qualifying, however, the Scuderia had failed to get either car into the top three, while Kimi Antonelli emerged as a surprise contender.

Verstappen had to settle for second place, making his conclusion during the Dutch media session in the paddock clear: yes, the Red Bull driver could certainly live with that starting position, but there was still more potential to be unlocked.

That was especially evident from the Q2 lap with which Verstappen impressed his rivals. On a set of scrubbed tyres, the Dutchman was faster than some drivers from the other top teams on fresh rubber, making a third consecutive pole position seem within reach.

When Autosport asked Verstappen why the picture in Q3 was so different from the second qualifying segment, the four-time world champion explained: "I just didn't have the same grip anymore. It's as simple as that.

"I simply couldn't carry the speed that I wanted through the slow corners anymore. That's something we obviously need to understand, because there was for sure more in it. I just couldn't get it out of the car in Q3."

The wind appears to have been an important factor in that story. In the closing minutes of Q3, many drivers were caught out by gusts of wind, explaining why there were only three improvements on the second runs. Lando Norris spoke of the worst gusts of wind he had ever experienced behind the wheel, which caused him to lock up despite braking earlier as a precaution.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Ronaldo Schemidt / AFP via Getty Images

Verstappen clarified, however, that this could not explain the whole story of Q3.

"On the final run, the wind was really bad, but not on the first run. So I don't really understand why it was so disappointing. But anyway, if that's still good enough for second place, then that's okay."

Ferrari's pace also dropped away in Q3, with Charles Leclerc – like George Russell, incidentally – pointing to the increased cloud cover and falling track temperature, which pushed the Pirelli tyres slightly outside the ideal operating window for them.

Red Bull no longer falls away on challenging days

Qualifying in Austin was nevertheless revealing about the progress Red Bull has made in recent weeks, particularly since the Baku upgrade. On a day when neither driver was particularly happy with the feeling in the car, the team still managed to secure second and third places on the grid.

That marks a considerable contrast with the first half of this season, when Red Bull would often slip towards seventh and eighth on a difficult day – right at the back of the group comprising the four leading teams.

Verstappen acknowledged this too and recognised that qualifying in Austin was, in that sense, representative of the team's recent resurgence.

"Yes, absolutely. The car has been a lot better over the last few weekends, that's clear. And as I've said over the past few weekends as well, some circuits will simply suit us a little better than others. I think this one is still okay, but I think Singapore and Malaysia were clearly better for our car."

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Rudy Carezzevoli / Getty Images

Nevertheless, Verstappen's race pace in Austin looked more than respectable on Friday, giving him confidence heading into Sunday.

"Normally, yes. It's a bit difficult to judge who's really the fastest in race pace, but over the last few weekends it's been pretty good for us. I hope the set-up we have on the car is the right direction for the race."

The start remains a major question mark for Red Bull, although second place on the inside of the grid offers opportunities if Verstappen manages to get away well.

"Yes, but I don't think about that too much. If an overtake happens in the first corner, then it happens. And if it doesn't, then it's still such a long race in which so many things can go right or wrong. If you have a good balance and enough speed in the car, you can race here through strategy or even by overtaking someone on track."

Read Also: Formula 1 Verstappen responds to COTA boss and proposes drastic measures to tackle bumps

Sports.title: Verstappen responds to COTA boss and proposes drastic measures to tackle bumps
Sports.content:
It is one of the main talking points in the Formula 1 paddock this weekend: the extreme bumps at the Circuit of the Americas. Drivers raised their concerns during Friday evening's drivers' briefing, after which Verstappen stayed behind for some time to speak further with representatives of the FIA and the circuit.

Because the track was built on Texas' infamous high-plasticity clay, it suffers from a severe shrink-swell effect. Two years ago, it was completely resurfaced, while two further interventions were carried out ahead of this year's event. The section between Turns 9 and 11 was resurfaced again, while efforts were made to remove the worst bumps between Turns 12 and 19.

According to the drivers, however, that is not enough. Verstappen already described the track conditions as "unacceptable" and "out of control" on Thursday, adding on Saturday that he is taking painkillers every day in Austin, just as Lando Norris needs headache tablets for every session.

When the bumps came up again after qualifying during Verstappen’s Dutch media round in the paddock, he said: "There are a few corners here that are simply really unacceptable."

That appears to refer primarily to the enormous bump under braking for Turn 1 and a rather dangerous one at Turn 19, but when Autosport put that to Verstappen, he explained that there are more problem areas.

"Turns 1 and 19 are indeed really bad, but also that whole fast section between Turns 4 and 5, there are such big bumps there... Of course I understand that the ground here is a problem, but that's something you should have looked at beforehand. That really shouldn't be an excuse."

Besides placing considerable physical strain on the drivers, the bumps through the Esses are also potentially dangerous. Several drivers have already come close to losing control of their cars at that point during the practice sessions in Austin, and if things actually go wrong through the sequence of high-speed corners, the consequences could be immense.

"Yes, those are things that really shouldn't happen at such high speeds, when the car bottoms out like that", Verstappen said.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

Verstappen proposes far-reaching measures

Bobby Epstein, chairman of the Circuit of the Americas, responded to Verstappen's initial comments by suggesting that the situation was not as bad in practice as the Dutchman had made it sound.

"We don't feel good that there's a bump at the bottom of Turn 1. We didn't know about it until this week. We would have fixed it. But the other things Max spoke about, all the bumps around the track, we've fixed them. The track is in really good shape", Epstein told ESPN.

He even expressed the expectation that Verstappen would change his mind after Friday practice.

"Max doesn't say I'm wrong a lot, but he's also right a lot. He's usually very frank, and I appreciate that about him. I had no problem with him saying what he said, but I think he might be surprised in some areas that bumps he thought were here aren't [there] anymore."

However, when those comments were put to Verstappen during the Dutch media session, that proved to be anything but the case. The four-time world champion is still far from impressed with the condition of the circuit and believes Epstein would say the same if he were to drive the RB22.

"I invite him to drive my car", Verstappen said. "I think he'd have to get out after five laps and wouldn't be able to walk anymore."

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Clive Rose / Formula 1 via Getty Images

According to Verstappen, far-reaching measures will be needed in the coming years. On Thursday, he had already said that F1 drivers should no longer have to accept such conditions because of the damage to their spines, and after qualifying the Dutchman put forward a concrete proposal for the years ahead.

"You can put down a new layer of asphalt again, but a year or two later you'll have the same problem, so you need to look deeper.

"I think the FIA and Formula 1 should also be stricter about that. I understand that it all costs a lot of money, but this is really just putting a plaster over the problem. You need to dig the whole thing up and put in a proper foundation if you know the ground underneath is moving."

Sports.title: Antonelli pole shows Mercedes is 'finally seeing the results' of car upgrades
Sports.content:
Formula 1 championship leader Kimi Antonelli reckons his United States Grand Prix pole is the reward for Mercedes' efforts to finetune its comprehensive but troubled Malaysia upgrade.

Antonelli held off Red Bull tandem Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar on Austin's Circuit of the Americas as Ferrari flattered to deceive in Saturday's qualifying shootout by taking fourth and fifth.

With the gusty conditions only getting worse throughout Q3, nailing the first of two qualifying runs proved to be pivotal. And following a weekend that had been building up as a battle between Verstappen and Ferrari duo Charles Leclerc plus Lewis Hamilton, Antonelli sprung somewhat of a surprise by taking his first pole since July's Belgian Grand Prix.

It was a reward for Mercedes' efforts to exploit its big Malaysia upgrade, which has made the W17 faster but also more difficult to set up. That struggle looked set to continue in Austin's first practice session, but the team gradually chipped away to improve the balance. A new front wing for Austin, which was trialled in Singapore practice, was intended to further improve the package.

"I'm happy because we've been working really hard on this package, and we're still trying to understand it fully," said Antonelli, after denying Verstappen a third consecutive pole.

"Since Singapore, we've taken a big step further, and now we've just got to keep working on it, keep understanding. But it's a good result for the team because they've done a tremendous job on bringing this package. Finally, we're seeing the results.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Mark Sutton / Formula 1 via Getty Images

"It was surprising, but also one of the biggest achievements for me today is that I didn't do track limits! That also made our life a little bit easier. I didn't put myself in a difficult situation, and we were able to just progress throughout the session and build from there."

Antonelli gets a first, if remote, opportunity to tie up the championship on Sunday if he wins the race and team-mate George Russell finishes ninth or lower, and Hamilton is no higher than fifth.

With Hamilton and Russell only starting fifth and sixth respectively, the chances of Antonelli celebrating a maiden title in Texas may still be small, but they are not negligible either.

"I'm just going to try to do the best race I can. I'm going to try to win, and then we'll see what happens," said the 20-year-old Italian.

"It does feel a little bit different, but the goal stays the same. I just need to keep doing my job, and actually, I feel like I can enjoy the driving and everything more because I'm in a very good position. But still, the mindset is always the same."

Sports.title: Leclerc and Hamilton's differing theories behind Ferrari's Austin qualifying disappointment
Sports.content:
Ferrari had been pegged as the team to beat after practice at the United States Grand Prix, but ultimately found itself wanting when it came to qualifying and failed to find enough progression through Q3.

Charles Leclerc had headlined both Friday practice sessions, while Lewis Hamilton took the honours in FP3 after Leclerc's best lap was deleted, and it looked as though the team was primed to battle against Red Bull's Max Verstappen for pole position.

As the session unfolded, Mercedes entered the fray; Kimi Antonelli then reeled off a strong first effort in Q3 which proved good enough to clinch pole over Verstappen. Leclerc could only manage fourth, with Hamilton fifth on Sunday's Formula 1 grid as its pace appeared to plateau at the business end of qualifying.

There were two strands to this: Ferrari's straightline speed, and its difficulty in getting the tyres sufficiently prepared for the final part of qualifying.

The Ferrari demonstrated strong performance in the low-speed corners, and through practice had also been able to find time between Turns 6-10 at the end of the esses section, and through the high-speed Turns 16-19. But as the pace ratcheted up through the qualifying session, the Ferraris couldn't quite respond.

Leclerc reckons the source of Ferrari's flat end to Q3 was partly down to the change in track temperature. The Ferrari chassis manages to maintain reasonably cool tyre temperatures in race trim, but this comes at the expense of single-lap pace in qualifying as it becomes much harder to load them with the right level of heat. When the track dropped in temperature, it made the right tyre window more difficult to find.

"It's very disappointing because I think there are some other weekends where we've been strong in free practice, but then coming to quali it's very clear that the others are just having a lot more in the straights and it's very difficult for us to match that," the Monegasque explained.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Kym Illman / Getty Images

"I feel like today it's a qualifying where we had the potential in the car, but the car also includes tyres and in Q3 unfortunately we were not in the right place. It was like one or two degrees less in Q3 and for me it was a huge difference; I just really struggled in the out-lap, I was sliding quite a lot already from the out-lap and that made it very difficult after that.

"There are reasons for [the plateau] and so at the same time I think we just need to work harder and try and understand those tyres even better than what we are doing now. The others I think normally have a bit more, it's a bit easier for them to extract the lap time in Q3 than it is for us and as soon as we are a tiny bit outside the window, we pay a lot the price, so this is something that we need to look into.

"Our car for some reason, it's very difficult to put some heat in those tyres which is a good thing for us on a Sunday, but in qualifying it makes it very tricky when the track temp goes down."

Hamilton, on the other hand, didn't experience the same issues as Leclerc; conversely, he felt that he'd had a "really good" out-lap to prepare the tyres and had enjoyed a relatively clean run with his final lap of the session.

Instead, he theorised that it was simply a matter of how Ferrari was running its power unit - partly due to overall power, and partly due to the cut-off in power from the electrical systems.

"I haven't looked at the data," said Hamilton, "but we know through the weekend we look at the straight, like just up to Turn 1 [compared to] Max, when we cut power they just keep pulling. That's similar in other places like going into Turn 11.

"I think we might be similar in maybe Turn 12 within the rest of the lap. You see it on the overlay. I don't know what happened, my car felt really good. Lap was solid, so they were just quicker.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Angela Weiss / AFP via Getty Images

"I think [power unit is] the only place we lose. I think our car is really solid: at least as good, maybe slightly better than the others, but I think they have closed up on chassis.

"We've seen the Red Bull closed up on their downforce. Mercedes took a three-tenths step of upgrade at least from a couple of races ago. I think they're starting to figure out how to utilise that.

"They're now matching us through the corners, we're not able to take that step in this season to close that speed on the straight."

Putting a number to that powertrain deficit to the Red Bull-Ford unit, Hamilton's assessment was that the practice pace suggested a swing of around three to four tenths of a second on the straights, and that Ferrari simply couldn't match up to that through its cornering speed alone.

If the situation is indeed tyre-related, then Ferrari will be confident that it can manage temperatures through the course of the grand prix - but engine power, especially on the lengthy back straight, will be harder to compensate for.

Sports.title: Norris frustrated after United States GP qualifying: "I did a very bad job"
Sports.content:
Lando Norris was incredibly frustrated by his “very bad job” in qualifying for Formula 1’s United States Grand Prix as he took eighth despite thinking a front row was possible.

The reigning world champion will share row four with McLaren team-mate Oscar Piastri, despite briefly taking sixth with his second Q3 run before that time was struck off because he had exceeded track limits at Turn 19. The time he had set on his first run was only good for eighth.

It continues a disappointing run for McLaren which has failed to score a podium in the last three grands prix, having been outdeveloped by Red Bull behind Mercedes and Ferrari.

But despite the weaknesses of the MCL40 in straightline speed and slow-corner performance, Norris still reckons he could have achieved much more in Austin.

“The car was very strong today in terms of pace,” he said. “Insanely difficult to drive.

“Probably the hardest car I've ever had to drive in my life. But good enough for P2, so I should be P2 and I'm P8, so clearly, I did a very bad job today.”

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Chris Graythen / Getty Images

So Norris still reckons a good points return is possible in Sunday’s race, especially having topped Q1 - though many others used medium rubber and not softs.

Nevertheless, the Briton ultimately qualified a second off Mercedes polesitter Kimi Antonelli and 0.835s behind second-placed Max Verstappen for Red Bull.

“The car was quick, it's just nasty to drive,” added Norris. “I saw a good result, it's possible. I think I still have faith that we can get a good result tomorrow.

“I don't know how easy it's going to be to overtake and things like that. But, for a lot of the track, we seem on par.

“We struggle a lot in sector three and there's very slow speed. We're pretty dreadful, honestly. But tomorrow is a new day.”

What makes it more frustrating for the 26-year-old is that McLaren has brought the first stage of its final upgrade package of the year to Texas, featuring a revised front suspension geometry and an altered diffuser profile.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing, Isack Hadjar, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Rudy Carezzevoli / Getty Images

“We try and improve it every time,” said Norris. “We improve the car, we bring upgrades.

“But it's something we're not completely... I don't know, it might be that the car is just not quick enough and therefore there's always hope that I can do a mega lap and I can be P1.

“But you improve three corners and the other three are a nightmare all of a sudden. It's just impossible. It's an impossible car to achieve the perfection that I want to achieve at the minute.

“Which is a struggle, because I want to go for pole, and I need to tell myself to settle for a P5, and I don't want to do that.”

The woes were present on Piastri’s side as well, with the Australian claiming “I’ve not been anywhere near as competitive as what I wanted to be”.

Sports.title: F1 United States GP: Antonelli beats Verstappen to pole with Russell only sixth
Sports.content:
Championship leader Kimi Antonelli has claimed his seventh pole of 2026 at Formula 1's United States Grand Prix, defeating Max Verstappen in a thrillingly close qualifying session in Austin.

Antonelli surged to pole with his first of two Q3 runs, which yielded a 1m34.035s as he headed Red Bull tandem Verstappen and Isack Hadjar by around two tenths, as few frontrunners improved on their final lap.

It was Antonelli's first pole since the summer break as he denied Verstappen a third consecutive pole, breaking this weekend's trend of Verstappen and the two Ferraris looking to have a slight edge on Mercedes across the demanding 5.5km Circuit of the Americas.

After impressing in practice and leading the way in Q2, Leclerc only managed fourth when it mattered, with Ferrari team-mate Lewis Hamilton in fifth.

George Russell was a disappointing sixth ahead of McLaren duo Oscar Piastri and Lando Norris, who lost two spots after seeing his final lap deleted for track limits.

Meanwhile, Racing Bulls pairing Arvid Lindblad and Liam Lawson further helped their squad's bid to cement fifth in the standings.

With Lindblad facing a five-place penalty for taking a new combustion engine, Lawson opted to sit out Q3 to minimise the damage for his team-mate. Lawson will start ninth anyway now, with Lindblad set for a start from 14th.

Q2 - Ferrari quickest

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari Photo by: Chris Graythen / Getty Images

Leclerc headed Q2 with a 1m34.198s on his second run, beating Antonelli and Russell as well as an early Verstappen benchmark.

The battle for the remaining Q3 spots featured Piastri, who couldn't string a good first lap together and needed a second effort to move up to sixth after taking provisional 10th. Lindblad and Lawson also found late improvements to move into the top 10 in a dramatic end to the segment, knocking out the Alpine and Audi cars.

So Pierre Gasly was the first driver to miss the cutoff by just 0.022s for Alpine, ahead of Audi's Nico Hulkenberg and Gabriel Bortoleto, with Franco Colapinto, Fernando Alonso and Oliver Bearman also eliminated. Haas man Bearman saw a lap that was quick enough for 13th scratched for track limits at Turn 11.

Bortoleto is facing a back-of-the-grid start for taking a new Audi power unit anyway, but the Brazilian advanced to Q2 to try and hand Hulkenberg a valuable slipstream on COTA's long straight. Alpine's Colapinto will be docked 10 grid places for installing new engine control electronics, joining Bortoleto on the back row of Sunday's grid.

Q1 - Double Williams exit while Norris goes fastest

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

Norris led the way in a tight Q1 session by setting a 1m35.029s, with the reigning world champion conducting two runs to cement his place, heading the four cars from Ferrari and Red Bull.

Behind them, Antonelli and Russell, as well as the second McLaren of Piastri, all advanced using a set of medium tyres, saving a set of softs.

In the background, Alonso's strong 1m36.240s lap got him through to Q2 in 16th at the expense of Haas man Esteban Ocon and his Aston Martin team-mate Lance Stroll, who lamented a lack of rear grip.

Aston Martin's improved performance relegated Williams to F1's slowest team outside of newcomer Cadillac. Carlos Sainz headed a frustrated Alex Albon in 19th, while 21st-placed Sergio Perez again had the measure of Cadillac team-mate Valtteri Bottas.

Sports.title: F1 United States GP: Ferrari completes perfect practice record as Hamilton tops FP3
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton finished final practice on top at Formula 1's United States Grand Prix, leading Max Verstappen and Charles Leclerc into qualifying at Austin.

Hamilton was the only driver to break the 1m35s barrier in the final 20 minutes of third practice, as frequent track limits transgressions kept Ferrari team-mate Leclerc from leapfrogging him on the leaderboard.

Following an opening quarter of the session which can only be described as pedestrian, action picked up as Hamilton set a 1m36.716s on softs to get ahead of a number of medium-tyred install laps.

His time was soon beaten by Liam Lawson in the Racing Bulls and McLaren's Oscar Piastri, while several heavy hitters kept turning laps on medium tyres instead.

Verstappen even went top courtesy of a 1m35.702s on the yellow sidewall tyre, despite recurring complaints about his unsettling downshifts.

Hamilton swiftly improved upon the Dutchman's lap, using softs to set a 1m35.561s. But when Leclerc took over command with a 1m35.127s despite using the slower mediums, that underlined there was still a lot more pace to find.

Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Anni Graf - Formula 1 via Getty Images

Entering the final 20 minutes, Antonelli took a tenth out of Leclerc's time on softs, but his lap was scratched for breaking track limits at Turn 9.

Verstappen did adhere to the white lines to set a 1m35.061s and go top, with Red Bull the quickest car through sector one, only for Hamilton to dip below the 1m35s barrier with a 1m34.893s.

Track limits, which have been a recurring theme throughout practice, also kept Leclerc from reclaiming first as he dipped over the white line at Turn 10.

That meant the Monegasque had to settle for third behind Hamilton and Verstappen, setting up a finely poised qualifying session on Saturday afternoon.

Championship leader Antonelli was fourth ahead of Mercedes team-mate George Russell, as the Silver Arrows appears to be a half-step behind on pure pace, with Piastri sixth in the difficult to tame MCL40.

In the Audi, Nico Hulkenberg kept McLaren’s Lando Norris from seventh, with the world champion’s 1m35.2s also deleted for track limits at Turn 10.

Alpine driver Pierre Gasly was ninth, a full second behind Hamilton, with Isack Hadjar 10th in the second Red Bull as the Frenchman was left frustrated by his car's handling.

Sports.title: “It does feels different” Antonelli admits ahead of first chance to seal title | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli admitted this weekend’s race has a different feel because he has his first chance to clinch the world championship.

The 20-year-old will only claim the title today if he wins the race and team mate George Russell finishes no higher than ninth. But after taking pole position for the race, while Russell only managed sixth on the grid, Antonelli said the opportunity to win the championship was on his mind.

“It does feel a little bit different,” said Antonelli, who will become the youngest world champion in F1 history if he takes the title this year. “But the goal stays the same. I just need to keep doing my job.

“Actually, I feel like I can enjoy the driving and everything more. But of course, we still have to do the race tomorrow, still have to try and win, and then, of course, we’ll see what happens.

“I feel like I can enjoy it a bit more because obviously I’m in a very good position. But still, the mindset is always the same.”

Antonelli will start today’s race immediately in front of the two Red Bull drivers, who he expects will be competitive.

“I’m just going to try to do the best race I can: I’m going to try to win, and then we’ll see what happens,” he said after qualifying on Saturday. “But it’s good to finish the day like this.

“Of course, tomorrow is going to be a new day. Max [Verstappen] has been very quick, Isack [Hadjar] also has been very quick, so just need to get a good start, and then we’ll see from there what we can do.”

“I have a great group of people around me,” he added. “I have a lot of friends here as well, so we enjoy the evenings together. We play cards in the evening, so we’re just doing the fun stuff, and that all helps to relax a little bit and disconnect mentally.

“Then, once you go on track, you’re back fully focused.”

Sports.title: Loss of pace in Q3 ‘something we have to look at because it’s very odd’ – Verstappen | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen admitted he thought he was on course for pole position after his strong run in the second round of qualifying for the United States Grand Prix.

The Red Bull driver used the same set of tyres to progress through the first two rounds of qualifying and expected a significant gain in performance when he switched to new tyres for his final run.

“In Q1 and Q2, I felt really good,” he explained. “I did my fastest lap in Q2 on a used set, so when I went to Q3, I had high hopes.

“But unfortunately, it just felt bad. I just didn’t really have the grip that I wanted, so I couldn’t lean on the rear the way I wanted in the final sector, and that just cost me too much time.

“Of course, when you look at the sheets and you’re starting P2, it’s nice and it’s a good result, but I was hoping for more, and this was just not it. But if it’s not a great feeling in qualifying and then that’s a P2, I’ll take it. But there’s no need to then smile and be super-happy about it.”

Most drivers failed to improve their lap times on their final runs in Q3 as the weather conditions changed. But Verstappen suspects there was more to Red Bull’s difficulties than that.

“The wind, for sure, picked up. But even with that, it’s not an excuse for why Q3 felt the way it felt for me in the first run.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“The second run, for sure, was influenced by the wind, but it just didn’t feel the same.

“Q2 felt great on a used set, and then you think, okay, you put a new set on, now it’s time to really push, and it just didn’t come alive. That was my feeling, but that can happen.”

Verstappen does not believe he was disadvantaged by not running a new set of tyres in Q2.

“I’ve done that many times before. I’ve even qualified once with only two sets, so there is no explanation why in Q3 it just didn’t come together, apart from the last lap, where I think everyone struggled for lap time,” he said.

“But it’s something that we have to look at because it’s very odd, of course, that you have the best feeling on a used set.”

Sports.title: Antonelli pleased and surprised to avoid another track limits breach in qualifying | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli admitted he was pleased to avoid a penalty for exceeding track limits after claiming pole position for the United States Grand Prix.

The Mercedes driver has collected several penalties this year for exceeding track limits. Seven drivers lost lap times for running off-track in qualifying including both Red Bull drivers and McLaren’s Lando Norris on their final runs in Q3.

Antonelli, who claimed his first pole position since the Belgian Grand Prix in July, said he was relieved to avoid the same mistake.

“It was surprising [to take pole], but also one of the biggest achievements for me today is that I didn’t [exceed] track limits,” he said. “That also made our life a little bit easier.

“I didn’t put myself in a difficult situation and we were able to just progress throughout the session and build from there. But definitely [pole] was unexpected. We knew we’d be close, but it was a good surprise.”

While other tracks have added small gravel traps to deter track limits breaches in recent years, the Circuit of the Americas has not. Lines were repainted at some corners after Friday’s running in a bid to reduce the number of breaches, but the generous asphalt run-offs mean they are still common.

Antonelli said the windy conditions in qualifying made it especially difficult.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“It was not an easy session,” he said. “The wind was picking up and was being quite gusty, and Q3 was a little bit tricky because the wind was a bit unpredictable. It picked up as well, especially on that last lap it felt a bit worse.”

Following a difficult debut for Mercedes’ recent upgrade package in Sepang two rounds earlier, Antonelli said he was pleased with their result this weekend.

“I’m happy because we’ve been working really hard on this package and we’re still trying to understand it fully. But since Singapore, we’ve taken a big step further, and now we’ve just got to keep working on it, keep understanding it.

“But it’s a good result for the team because they’ve done a tremendous job on bringing this package, and finally we’re seeing the results.”

Sports.title: Norris says he’s “scared in every single corner” after “terrible” qualifying | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lando Norris says he should have put his car on the front row of the grid after qualifying eighth.

The McLaren driver’s final lap time in Q3 was deleted because he exceeded track limits infringement at turn 15. Had that time stood, Norris would have qualified sixth.

However he believes he could have qualified much higher than that.

“I should be P2 and I’m P8,” Norris told Viaplay. He said his session had been “terrible.”

“It was a very difficult car, but it can still be P2, and I should drive it to P2. I didn’t do it today, so I’m not happy with the job that I did.”

Norris, who scored back-to-back wins earlier this year, said he has “zero confidence” in the car at the moment. “I’m just scared in every single corner,” he said.

“Every corner I’m scared something’s going to happen, I’m going to make a mistake because it’s such a struggle.”

He told the official F1 channel he did a “crap job” in qualifying and faces a difficult task to make up ground in the race. “The pace is not bad,” he said. “It’s better than what it looks, but it’s going to be hard from P8, I guess.”

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

His team mate Oscar Piastri said he is also struggling to tap the potential of McLaren’s car. The team enjoyed a strong run of form in the middle of the season but have struggled in recent races.

Piastri qualified seventh for this weekend’s race over three-quarters of a second behind pole-winner Andrea Kimi Antonelli.

“It’s been tough all weekend,” said Piastri after qualifying. “There’s just not been any pace so it’s a bit of a head-scratcher.

“I think the car has the potential to be quick but it’s just incredibly difficult to drive. It’s been a challenge from the first lap yesterday until now so it’s not a massive surprise to end up where we are.”

The team introduced a few aerodynamic changes to its car for this weekend’s race. But Piastri said the team had not expected to make significant gains.

“We’ve tried a lot of stuff but nothing’s really seemed to be the fix,” he said. “We didn’t really expect any of the changes we made to make a massive difference but it’s just been incredibly difficult to get lap time out of the car.

“It’s just one of those weekends at the moment.”

Sports.title: Team’s tactical decision not to run in Q3 was “a shame” for Lawson | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Liam Lawson said he wanted to set a lap in Q3 after Racing Bulls told him not to run in order to help his team mate.

Both Racing Bulls drivers made the cut for Q3. However with Arvid Lindblad due to take a five-place grid penalty, and Racing Bulls unlikely to out-qualify any of the other eight cars in the session, the team made a tactical decision.

While Lindblad set a time which put him ninth on the grid, Lawson remained in the garage. That ensured Lawson would start ninth and Lindblad 14th; had both drivers set times and Lawson qualified ninth ahead of his team mate, Lindblad would be 15th on the grid.

“We decided that, if we got both cars into Q3, considering Arvid has a penalty for tomorrow, we wouldn’t run,” Lawson explained. “Even if we out-qualified one of the top guys, we’re not really fighting them in the race tomorrow, so it just makes sense to do this.”

Lawson reached as high as eighth in Q1 and was eager to run in Q3. “It’s a shame,” he said, “I managed to get through Q1 on one set [of tyres] and we had two new sets for Q3 so I was ready to have a proper go at it.

“But unfortunately, or fortunately, now we have plenty of tyres for tomorrow.”

Racing Bulls’ chief technical officer Tim Goss said the team chose to prioritise the race result. “The bigger prize is the race on Sunday for which we decided we would benefit from saving a new soft tyre set for each driver, rather than using them in Q3,” he explained. “We completed a steady lap with Arvid on used tyres, just to place him ahead of Liam and limit his grid penalty by one place.”

Sports.title: Ferrari were in contention “until the last corner of Q3” after strong practice – Vasseur | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur admitted he expected more from qualifying after neither of his drivers claimed places in the top three.

The team headed all three practice sessions at the Circuit of the Americas but managed no higher than fourth and fifth on the grid for Sunday’s race.

Charles Leclerc, who qualified fourth, blamed the drop in track temperature between the final two rounds for their loss of pace.

“I don’t think that the others have changed anything from Q2 to Q3,” he told Sky. “Where we’ve lost is on ourselves and that is mostly the tyres.

“The out-lap was extremely difficult, there was a bit more cloud in Q3, we lost one or two degrees of track temp and for us it was night and day difference. Already from the out-laps I felt like I was having lots of difficulties.

“It’s a shame that it happens in Q3 because I strongly believe that we had the pace to be fighting in front, but unfortunately not today, again.”

However Vasseur said the team cannot use the change in conditions as an excuse. “I think Q2 was a bit faster for everybody,” he said. “We all struggled to improve in Q3, perhaps a bit of wind or whatever, and it’s also a distraction for the drivers.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“But it’s the same for everybody, we can’t complain about the wind, this would be bullshit. Now I think we have to do a better job on the last lap, because we had the potential to be at least on the first row.”

Vasseur said he had “mixed feelings” about the session “because I think the potential was there all over the weekend.

“We had good pace in all the free practice [sessions]. Until the last corner we were fighting for the pole and it is like it is, it’s all part of the game.

“Now let’s be focused on tomorrow because I think tomorrow will be a different exercise, it will be difficult one with a lot of degradation and we’ll see what happens.

“But for sure there is a bit of frustration because we had very good potential. Until the last corner of Q3 I think we were in better shape.”

Sports.title: Antonelli beats Red Bull pair to pole position in Austin | 2026 United States GP qualifying report
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli will start the United States Grand Prix from pole position as he bids to clinch the world championship this weekend.

The Mercedes driver beat his closest championship rival George Russell by over four tenths of a second. The two Mercedes drivers will be separated by four of their rivals when they line up on the grid.

Red Bull looked like strong contenders for pole position as Max Verstappen and Isack Hadjar cruised into Q3 having only used a single set of soft tyres each. However Verstappen described his car’s handling as “tricky” after lapping 0.175s off Antonelli on his first run in Q3 and couldn’t get any closer on his second.

He was not alone in that, however: driver after driver failed to improve their time on their final run in Q3. Both Mercedes, Red Bulls and Ferraris also failed to. The latter’s drivers could only manage fourth and fifth on the grid despite leading all three practice sessions.

Lando Norris appeared to be one of the few drivers to improve, temporarily relegating Russell to seventh place. However his final lap time was deleted for a track limits infringement which dropped the reigning world champion to eighth place behind his team mate.

Racing Bulls did not run Liam Lawson in Q3, ensuring Arvid Lindblad out-qualified his team mate. With neither driver likely to out-qualify any of the other eight cars in Q3, this served to minimise the impact of Lindblad’s five-place grid penalty.

Both Alpine drivers were eliminated in the second round of qualifying. Pierre Gasly narrowly failed to make the cut having gone ninth with his final run before the two Racing Bulls drivers improved their times. Liam Lawson put him out by just two hundredths of a second.

The Audi pair also went no further. Gabriel Bortoleto, who has a total penalty of 80 grid places due to multiple power unit component changes, tried to help Nico Hulkenberg with a tow but it wasn’t enough for his team mate to make it through.
