Before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza started in October 2023, Kenan attended the Atfaluna Society for Deaf Children, which provided specialist teaching and opportunities to communicate with other hearing-impaired children.

But Atfaluna’s building in Gaza City was partially levelled during the war and quickly turned into an overcrowded shelter for displaced people, an example of the widespread destruction of infrastructure in Gaza. This includes the educational institutions disabled children rely upon.

Israeli attacks also forced Kenan’s family to flee to Gaza City’s Jalaa Street. Atfaluna has since set up temporary learning spaces, and Kenan has access to one near where his family now lives. But his father, Tamer al-Sabaa, said the interruptions to his learning during the war have left his son far behind in his studies.

He did not attend school at all during the first year of the war, and now attends classes only for a few hours a week, which Tamer says is not enough given the time he has lost at school during the war.

But Tamer fears that if Israel resumes large-scale attacks – an October 2025 “ceasefire” reduced the number of attacks but did not stop them – he will be forced to stop Kenan from attending.



“These few hours do not cover or repair the massive educational gap and academic decline my son experienced during the war,” Tamer said. “He is in dire need of restoring his equipped educational environment and the specialised care that was stripped away from him.”

“The school operates only three days a week, and for limited hours not exceeding two hours a day,” he told Al Jazeera.

“Being deaf makes Kenan’s movements fraught with danger, as he cannot hear the sounds of explosions, warning signals, or communicate with those around him.”

As a result, Tamer and his wife had to guide Kenan through unfamiliar neighbourhoods to help him learn about his surroundings.

Kenan can now reach school independently, but his safety is always a concern for his parents.

Little help available

The difficulties facing Kenan highlight the effect of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, on disabled children in the enclave.

Fadel Kuraz, a sign language interpreter and disability rights advocate with Atfaluna, said the war has increased hearing-related injuries and severely weakened the services available to children who need support.

“What we are experiencing today in the Gaza Strip represents an unprecedented health and humanitarian setback, and a real catastrophe unlike anything we have seen before,” Kuraz told Al Jazeera.

“To grasp the scale of the tragedy, the baseline number of persons with hearing disabilities registered before October 2023 was around 20,000 people. Today, according to field assessments, approximately 35,000 new individuals … have been added, having suffered total or partial hearing loss due to … explosions.”

Kuraz describes shortages of hearing aids, batteries, ear moulds, and spare parts, alongside major obstacles to specialist hearing tests and treatments. Children also face difficulties accessing visual learning materials because of electricity and communications outages, he said.

“The suffering does not stop at material needs. A deaf child suffers high levels of fear, stress and complex trauma without the ability to verbally express what is on their mind,” Kuraz told Al Jazeera.

Hearing-impaired children in Gaza are more often than not living in overcrowded tents or shelters which lack privacy or a proper space to do homework and study.

“I emphasise that responding to the needs of persons with hearing disabilities is no longer a secondary choice or a luxury; it is an urgent humanitarian necessity,” Kuraz adds. “It requires immediate intervention to break the siege, allow the entry of hearing aids, batteries, and spare parts, and establish safe, temporary alternative educational spaces to replace destroyed centres.”

Generation at risk

Children with visual impairments face issues similar to those faced by hearing-impaired children in Gaza, with the few educational facilities once available to them now closed or difficult to access. The materials and items they need to study, such as Braille, are also difficult to procure due to Israel’s siege on Gaza.



Al-Noor school was originally located in Tal al-Hawa, southwest of Gaza City, but was badly damaged in the genocidal war.

Duaa Omar Basheer worked as an educational counsellor at the al-Noor school for blind students in northern Gaza before the war. She said it was the only public school in Gaza designated for middle and high school students with visual impairments, but was forced to close during the war. Some primary education is available to children through educational centres run by the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.

Previously, the school served about 80 pupils from across Gaza, many of whom arrived on dedicated buses, but damaged roads and a lack of suitable transport created further barriers.

Without regular instruction, Basheer fears students could lose their Braille and independent-learning skills, which they have taken years to learn.

“We are facing an entire generation of visually-impaired individuals at risk of illiteracy and academic loss,” Basheer said.

Broken glasses

In the Shati refugee camp in Gaza City, Jana Shreim’s mother, Wafaa Shreim, says her 12-year-old daughter, who is legally blind, relies on prescription glasses with high magnification and very strong lenses. But she could still only perceive light, shapes and nearby objects.

Her glasses broke amid the harrowing mass exodus from the Shati camp during Israel’s offensive on the neighbourhood in November 2023. The family tried to fix them with wire, but the lenses were damaged beyond use, and replacement glasses were too expensive.

Since the glasses broke – and with no possibility of replacing them due to the blockade – her vision has deteriorated to the point that she can barely see.

Now, when Jana goes to unfamiliar places, she stumbles and falls. Her mother says she is bullied by other children, and that she experiences pain in her eyes when she tries to focus.

“My daughter now has to identify people by their voices,” Wafaa told Al Jazeera. “Her sister and I now act as her ‘eyes’ at every step and everywhere she goes.”

Before the war, Jana attended the al-Noor centre, travelling there on a dedicated bus service. Her school closed when it was badly damaged in Israeli bombing, leaving Jana without any access to education.

“I am currently trying to teach her at home myself using a Braille writing machine we have, so she doesn’t lose her limited educational skills,” Jana’s mother said. She also cares for another daughter with a visual impairment, making it even more difficult to provide the specialist support they both need.

“I searched extensively and knocked on the doors of many institutions and organisations concerned with visual impairment, but the bitter truth is that … we have been left entirely alone,” she said.

“My only message and wish to all responsible parties is to look at our visually impaired children with mercy: provide them with glasses and medical supplies, and open safe educational and recreational spaces that restore their basic right to life and learning.”

World.title: Serbia votes as student-led bloc challenges longtime leader Vucic
World.content:
NewsFeed Serbia votes as student-led bloc challenges longtime leader Vucic

Serbians are turning out in huge numbers to vote in a parliamentary election which could see Aleksander Vucic’s longstanding reign brought to an end. The vote follows months of student-led anti-government protests over corruption and accountability.

World.title: Portuguese police clear Lisbon housing protest camp, arrest 25
World.content:
Officers baton-charge demonstrators in overnight operation as activists demand government action on soaring rents and home shortages.

Police in Portugal have cleared a camp in central Lisbon set up to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis, baton-charging demonstrators and making 25 arrests.

Dozens of officers, some with police dogs, moved in on the camp in Rossio Square shortly after 2am (02:00 GMT) on Sunday.

They had warned protesters that their tents would be dismantled if they were not removed, threatening disobedience charges for those who resisted.

Protesters had pitched more than 100 tents after Saturday’s protest march by thousands along one of Lisbon’s main avenues.

A smaller camp of about 50 tents was also dismantled in Porto’s Praca D Joao I public square, where police made six arrests.

Police said the operation was “proportionate” and that the 25 people arrested in Lisbon were later released and are due in court on Monday.

While police reported seven minor injuries among officers and protesters in the two operations, the activist group Casa para Viver (Homes to Live) said 60 people were hurt and called for a fresh protest outside parliament on Tuesday.

“Choosing the early hours of the morning to unleash dogs and baton-charge peaceful protesters is a political decision. It shows this government would rather repress those denouncing the housing crisis than address it,” the group said.

Home affordability crises

Portugal is grappling with one of Europe’s most acute home affordability crises, as prices have more than doubled since 2017 while rents for new leases have nearly doubled, with young people among the hardest hit.



Protesters say soaring rents and higher living costs are squeezing households and turning housing into a growing source of discontent.

The Bank of Portugal estimates a shortfall of 300,000 homes nationwide, equivalent to Lisbon’s entire housing stock.

The protesters are demanding that the government scrap a bill to make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases, which passed a first parliamentary reading, although the far-right Chega party abstained.

The protests in Portugal echo recent demonstrations in Spain over home shortages and surging rents.

There have also been protests in cities including Paris, where small student demonstrations over school conditions broadened into wider protests against government economic policies.

World.title: Elena Rybakina retains Ningbo title, wins first trophy as world number one
World.content:
The victory helped the Kazakh take a big step towards securing the year-end number one ranking.

Elena Rybakina blazed past unseeded Canadian Leylah Fernandez 6-2 6-2 in the Ningbo Open final to retain her title and lift her first trophy as the world number one ahead of the WTA Finals next month.

The victory on Sunday also helped the Kazakh take a big step towards securing the year-end number one ranking, further burnishing a spectacular season in which she won the Australian Open title before adding the US Open crown to reach the summit.

Top seed Rybakina made the breakthrough with her trademark power in the fifth game and then unleashed a searing crosscourt backhand winner to go 4-2 up, before the 27-year-old wrapped up the opening set in only 38 minutes.

World number 30 Fernandez made a bright start to the next set but Rybakina absorbed the pressure and raised her level to force an error and break for 2-1, with the three-time Grand Slam champion breezing to victory from there.

Rybakina’s latest triumph is a timely lift after setbacks in Beijing and Wuhan, as she turns her attention to the Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo this week before launching her title defence at the season finale in Indian Wells from November 8.

World.title: UK PM Burnham says he wants to discuss a return to EU freedom of movement
World.content:
Burnham says Britain should have an ‘honest discussion’ about how immigration to the UK has changed since Brexit.

Share UK PM Burnham says he wants to discuss a return to EU freedom of movement on social media

Prime Minister Andy Burnham says he wants to discuss Britain returning to the European Union’s freedom of movement rules for workers, a key issue in the 2016 Brexit referendum which led to the United Kingdom leaving the bloc.

Addressing the need to rethink ties with Brussels, ⁠Burnham told The Sunday Times newspaper that the influx of EU workers into Britain before Brexit had posed significant challenges.

“But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now],” he said in a report released on Sunday.

“Revolving door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, ‌since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things,” he said.

The issue of immigration was a key factor in the 2016 Brexit referendum campaign that ended with Britons narrowly voting to leave the EU.

A decade later, Burnham, who has even touted the possibility of Britain applying to rejoin the EU one day, said the country should have an “honest discussion” about how immigration to Britain has changed since Brexit.

Long-term net migration to the UK nearly halved ⁠in 2025, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS), falling to 171,000 in 2025 from 331,000 a year earlier. This drop had not been seen since before the post-Brexit immigration system was introduced, as tougher government measures have restricted arrivals.

In his October 19 interview with The Sunday Times, Burnham said the issue of freedom of movement could be considered as part of a broader reset of the UK’s relationship with the EU, including on data sharing and migration.



“Consider what we’ve lost, which was the ability to be part of Eurodac and all the data collaboration around migration. You’ve got to see it in the round, rather than just looking at freedom of movement on its own,” he told The Sunday Times.

Nigel Farage, leader of the anti-immigration Reform UK party, called Burnham’s comments on free movement a “total betrayal of Brexit Britain”.

In his speech to the Labour Party conference last month, Burnham said Brexit had done “more harm than good” and called for Britain to consider its “long-term relationship” with the EU.

The prime minister, who is trying to find ways to ⁠speed up the UK economy, is due to meet top EU officials for ⁠a summit on November 20.

World.title: Wembanyama scores 23 as Spurs beat Mavericks for first win of NBA season
World.content:
Joel Embiid posts triple-double as 76ers handle Bucks. Devin Booker posts 43 to help Suns down Warriors.

Share Wembanyama helps Spurs to their first win of the season against short-handed Mavericks on social media

Victor Wembanyama has scored 23 points as the visiting San Antonio Spurs have earned their first win of the season by defeating the short-handed Dallas Mavericks 122-106 in the second of back-to-back games for both teams.

Dylan Harper added 22 points on Saturday, De’Aaron Fox and Stephon Castle scored 19 each, Julian Champagnie scored 12 off the bench and Devin Vassell tallied 11 points for San Antonio. Wembanyama also posted seven rebounds and four blocks.

Rookie Sergio De Larrea’s 21 points led Dallas. Marcus Sasser, PJ Washington and Daniel Gafford scored 12 apiece, Zaccharie Risacher had 11 and Naji Marshall contributed 10.

San Antonio led 68-60 at the break behind Fox’s 15 points, 12 from Wembanyama and 11 by Castle. De Larrea paced the Mavericks with 13 points off the bench with Washington and Marshall adding 10 each.

The Spurs expanded their lead to 14 early in the third before Dallas roared back, scoring 22 of the ensuing 29 points and regaining the lead at 85-84. The game went to the fourth quarter with San Antonio up 92-89 as Castle and Wembanyama hit late threes.

Embiid posts triple-double as 76ers handle Bucks

Joel Embiid recorded his 10th career triple-double, and Jaylen Brown scored 27 points on his 30th birthday to lead the Philadelphia 76ers to a 127-116 home win over the Milwaukee Bucks.

Embiid finished with 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists for Philadelphia.

Tyrese Maxey pitched in with 26 points for the Sixers while VJ Edgecombe made five three-pointers as part of a 17-point, 13-rebound performance.



While the Sixers are 3-0 on the young season, the Bucks fell to 0-3 despite eight players scoring in double figures. Jaime Jaquez Jr led Milwaukee with 21 points while Kel’el Ware had 19 points and 13 rebounds off the bench for the visitors.

The teams were tied at 82-82 with four minutes left in the third quarter before the Sixers ended the period on a 15-5 push. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope and Maxey each made a three-pointer during that surge.

Philadelphia started to pull away early in the fourth.

Embiid’s jumper gave the hosts a 113-98 lead with six minutes left. The Sixers still held a comfortable advantage at 117-108 with 3:18 to go before the Bucks rattled off six in a row in just over a minute to make it a three-point game.

Philadelphia knocked down five three-pointers in the first quarter – three by Edgecombe – en route to a 34-25 lead after 12 minutes.

Booker, Suns continue Warriors’ rough start to season

Devin Booker had 43 points, seven assists and seven rebounds, and the host Phoenix Suns beat Golden State 131-122 to send the Warriors to their worst start of a season in almost two decades.

Miles Bridges scored 16 points, and Dillon Brooks added 15 points for the Suns, setting a franchise record for points in a home opener.

Rookie Yaxel Lendeborg had 26 points and nine rebounds, and De’Anthony Melton scored 20 of his 25 points in the second half for the skeleton-crew Warriors.

Golden State was without starters Stephen Curry, Brandin Podziemski and Draymond Green and reserve Al Horford.

Brandon Williams added 20 points while Lendeborg made six of the Warriors’ 17 three-pointers and Melton had four.

Melton scored 13 points in the third quarter when the Warriors used a 12-0 run to take a 73-71 lead before the Suns came back. Booker’s four-point play with 35 seconds left in the third quarter made it 99-89 for Phoenix.

Luke Kennard’s three-pointer pushed the Suns’ lead to 117-102 with 6:07 remaining in the game.

Kennard had 11 points and three three-pointers in his Suns debut after missing the season opener with a knee injury.

The Warriors made 17 of 39 three-pointers and turned 19 offensive rebounds into 26 points.

Lendeborg had six points on a pair of threes, and Graham Ike had six points and five rebounds in the first quarter when the Warriors took an early seven-point lead and had a 25-22 edge at the end of the quarter.

World.title: Algerian parliament’s upper house approves troop deployment to Niger
World.content:
Vote to send forces comes after a recent defence pact between two neighbouring countries.

The upper house of Algeria’s parliament has unanimously approved the deployment of troops to neighbouring Niger.

The Algerian constitution empowers the president to send military units abroad, provided that both chambers of parliament approve it by a two-thirds majority.

The Council of the Nation held an emergency session on Sunday to vote on troop deployment, while the People’s National Assembly, or the lower house, is expected to hold a separate session later in the evening, Algeria’s popular newspaper El Khabar reported. If the deployment is approved, it would be the first mission outside Algeria’s borders since the 1973 War between Israel and several Arab countries, known to Arabs as the October War and Israelis as the Yom Kippur War.

The military units to be deployed by Algeria are expected to be tasked with securing oil facilities in Niger.

The vote came after a visit by Niger’s Defence Minister General Salifou Modi to Algeria last week, where he held talks with Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune and Chief of Staff of the People’s National Army General Said Chanegriha.

During that visit, the two sides signed a military cooperation protocol, the details of which were not made public.

Earlier this month, Tebboune confirmed that Algeria sent fighter jets to Niger in late August to help thwart a “coup attempt” that shook the capital, Niamey.

The Algerian Ministry of Defence previously said it had sent four jets to Niger following the unrest. It said two patrols of four Sukhoi Su-30 aircraft had landed at Niamey airport, accompanied by an air-to-air refuelling plane.



The warplanes were deployed at the request of Nigerien authorities on “a mission to support the Nigerien army in confronting an attempt to destabilise the brotherly state of Niger”, the ministry said on August 30.

Relations between Algeria and Niger have witnessed a significant rapprochement over the past few months on political, diplomatic, military and economic levels, following a period of tension between the two countries.

World.title: Voters in Brazil head to polls as Lula goes up against Bolsonaro's son
World.content:
Polls have opened in Brazil as people choose their new president in a closely fought run-off election.

The choice is between the 80-year-old incumbent, left-winger Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term in office, and right-wing senator FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, 45.

Bolsonaro is the son of former right-wing president Jair Bolsonaro, who was sentenced to more than 20 years in jail for plotting a coup after losing the last election in 2022.

This is Bolsonaro's election to lose after he came top in the first round of voting on 4 October, which US President Donald Trump called a "very big" victory.

Never before has a candidate who trailed after the first round managed to overturn the deficit and win in the second round.

The younger Bolsonaro appeared at a polling station in Rio de Janeiro early on Sunday morning, telling reporters outside that "time has come for real change".

World.title: Israel to close West Bank crossings on election day as crackdown escalates
World.content:
All West Bank land crossings will be closed during Tuesday's election in Israel, the country's military says, and Palestinian workers will be barred from entering all settlements.

The restrictions come amid a crackdown in the occupied West Bank after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in the territory.

The Israel Defense Forces announced a "ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers throughout Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley, including industrial zones, as well as the closure of all land crossings" on Tuesday.

It said most workers would also be barred from settlements from Sunday, with the exception of industrial zones and a limited number of other areas.

Before the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, more than 100,000 Palestinian workers were permitted to enter Israel. Since then only a small fraction have had their permits restored.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a major operation on Friday in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.

The Israeli military have been demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron, with hundreds of families having been displaced.

World.title: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
World.content:
Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved.

The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity - but denied being responsible for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart Starshield.

Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk's latest claim but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said his post was "very strange".

Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations for more than a week.

The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.

Musk's latest comments, and the seeming restoration of the service, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to "put it back", having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service.

"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X on Saturday.

"Ukraine['s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."

He went on to say that SpaceX had "done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth" and reiterated his stipulation that Starshield was a different system and controlled by the US government, adding: "What they decide to do is up to them."

He added in a later post: "[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back."

Reacting to Musk's post, Beskrestnov said that drones operating via Starlink in Ukraine had a speed restriction of 70-90km/h (43-56mph) and did not work on Russian territory.

"Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he wrote on Telegram.

"It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."

There was no immediate comment from Ukraine's defence ministry.

Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed, both of which run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX.

Starlink allows military units to co-ordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.

Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.

Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a "stable connection", with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h. Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h.

"The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram.

World.title: Gunmen kill at least 10 villagers and loot shops in north-east Nigeria
World.content:
Unknown gunmen have raided a remote village in the north-eastern Nigerian state of Taraba, killing at least 10 people, looting shops and setting houses ablaze, police say.

There are fears the actual death toll is much higher, with eyewitnesses speaking of 20 lives lost and a non-governmental organisation suggesting a toll of as many as 50.

The gunmen reportedly swooped on the village of Binnari in the Karim Lamido area mounted on motorcycles just after midday Muslim prayers on Friday in a rampage that went on for up to four hours.

Police say they are searching for other casualties in the bush but the authorities were accused by Amnesty International of failing to protect rural communities.

Nigeria continues to face attacks by armed groups across several regions, including the northwest, northeast and central regions.

The country is also battling a jihadist insurgency in its north-east that has lasted nearly two decades, drawing persistent criticism of the government's handling of insecurity.

Following the latest incident, police said they recovered 10 bodies with gunshot wounds after officers responded to a distress call.

The attackers had fled by the time they arrived but they continued to patrol the area to restore calm, they told BBC News on Saturday.

"We were able to disperse the unknown gunmen though there was no casualty on their side and ours because the terrain is difficult and they're used to the terrain," Assistant Superintendent of Police Victor Mshelizah said.

He added that officers were continuing to search the bush nearby for people who might have been killed or wounded, and warned the death toll could still rise.

Community leader Malam Abubakar Saifullahi told news agency AFP that the attackers had arrived on about 50 motorcycles, two men apiece.

"They looted shops and took cash, foodstuffs and other provisions," he said. "They also took motorcycles abandoned by people fleeing the attack."

World.title: More than 1,300 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
World.content:
More than 1,300 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France on Saturday that were followed by some clashes later in the day, officials have said.

After largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux.

Officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history.

The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000.

World.title: Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
World.content:
Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a 33-year-old German man during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.

Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 local time (19:15 GMT) on Friday and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.

Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to the scene where the blaze was still burning early on Saturday, as police said difficult terrain hindered efforts to bring the fire under control.

Police said they apprehended the man riding a motorcycle near the scene, German media reported. A criminal investigation has been launched.

There is currently nothing to suggest the involvement of further suspects, police official Gerhart Holzinger told a press conference on Saturday afternoon.

Public prosecutor Rainer Vietze said a psychiatric report had concluded the 33-year-old man showed signs of possible mental illness and diminished responsibility might therefore be assumed.

Vietze said a possible political motive was also being considered, but stressed the investigation was in its early stages.

The residence, above the town of Berchtesgaden, was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.

Hitler and top Nazi officials used his nearby Berghof residence to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941 and the whole complex was considered one of his headquarters.

He also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.

Local media reported that site had been "largely destroyed" and the public was urged to avoid the area.

Bavaria's Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann told reporters that the site would "under no circumstances remain a ruin", broadcaster BR24 reported. "It is important that we continue our work of remembrance," he added.

World.title: Vanessa Trump says she is cancer-free six months after revealing diagnosis
World.content:
Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Donald Trump Jr, has announced that she is cancer-free following her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year.

Trump, 48, who has five children with US President Donald Trump's eldest son, said that her recent tests results "came back clear, so I'm finally cancer-free", in a short video on her 19-year-old daughter Kai's Instagram account.

Vanessa and Kai Trump then released a longer video on Saturday, in which they discussed breast cancer awareness, early detection and prevention.

Vanessa Trump separated from Trump Jr in 2018 and announced last year that she had begun dating US pro golfer Tiger Woods.

"October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a time to raise awareness about early detection, education, and support for those affected by breast cancer," Kai Trump wrote on Instagram.

"I sat down with my mum and Dr Nicole Saphier to talk about my mum's journey with breast cancer and learn more about prevention and early detection."

Kai's post received over 20,000 likes and hundreds of comments from people offering support and well wishes, including from US singer and media personality Mary Millben.

Vanessa Trump explained in the YouTube video that she experienced arm pain for several months before discovering a pea-sized lump in her breast, which testing confirmed was a cancerous tumour.

"It's a process you have to deal with," she said of the days spent waiting for her test results.

"You have to be mentally strong for yourself because you're going to need the strength to fight whatever challenge it is that's coming towards you."

Trump said she was first diagnosed with breast cancer in April. She publicly announced the diagnosis in May, saying in a social media post that she had undergone surgery and was working on a treatment plan with her medical team.

She eventually had a lumpectomy and radiation treatments, she said.

The average risk of a woman in the US developing breast cancer is about 1 in 8, or 13%, according to the American Cancer Society. The disease also accounts for 30% of all new female cancers every year, it says.

Surgery cures most breast cancers, but if some cancer cells remain, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and endocrine therapy can reduce the long-term risk.

Treatments have been advancing, including more targeted therapies for early breast cancer, new types of hormonal therapies, and more precise and effective radiotherapy.

World.title: El Salvador president says bodies found in Haiti are not those of hostages
World.content:
Four bodies handed over to special forces on a mission to Haiti to recover Salvadoran hostages are "not our men", El Salvador's president has said.

Nayib Bukele said a nongovernmental organisation delivered the human remains to one of Haiti's airports claiming they were four El Salvadoran air technicians, but that one of the corpses was a child's and another was wearing a different country's army uniform.

He had dispatched a military contingent, reportedly of hundreds of soldiers, on Thursday after the four men vanished after being ambushed by "heavily armed criminal groups".

The hostages had been part of the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF), which is tasked with tackling worsening gang violence in Haiti.

The men had been travelling back to their camp in an armoured vehicle when they were attacked in an area of the Caribbean island nation controlled by armed groups called Croix-des-Bouquets. No gang has so far claimed responsibility.

Bukele previously said the Salvadoran military operation in Haiti had the sole purpose of returning the four men alive. Approximately 450 soldiers had so far been deployed, according to Haitian newspaper Le Nouvelliste.

Bukele said the bodies the mission had received included one of a man of "considerably greater height than that of our air technicians", a person "who was wearing part of a uniform from an army that is not ours", and that among the remains were identification cards and uniforms from other countries.

He posted pictures showing the ID card of a GSF member and a corresponding national ID card from Chad in Africa.

Bukele's comments poured skepticism on an earlier report in the New York Times, citing people close to the Salvadoran mission, that the bodies found on the outskirts of the Haitian capital, Port-au-Prince, on Saturday were thought to belong to the missing men.

The newspaper reported that the bodies delivered to the military contingent had been badly burned, meaning a medical examination would be required to identify them.

It cited one unnamed source briefed on the situation as saying the ID posted by Bukele in fact belonged to a soldier who had lost it when he had been injured.

Haiti has been ravaged by gang violence for years, but the situation has worsened in the political vacuum that followed the assassination of its president in 2021.

The multinational force dispatched to quell the violence and push back the armed gangs has struggled to penetrate areas where they hold sway.

More than 5,700 people have been killed or injured by gangs or during operations against them between 1 January and 11 September this year, the UN said at the start of October.

Bukele said the four GSF members had primarily been there to "carry out medical evacuations and save lives, not to wage war".

When they were abducted, helicopters were deployed and multiple attempts were made to reach the location, but these efforts were hampered by fighting in the area, the Salvadoran armed forces said.

World.title: The city does not smell of roses, By Temitope Sodipo
World.content:
Lagos does not need to experience its own Great Stink before taking decisive action. The warning signs are visible and painfully olfactory. This challenge presents an opportunity to rethink how a fast-growing metropolis can manage its resources and infrastructure more effectively. A cleaner Lagos will require investment, planning, innovation and sustained public cooperation. Above all, it calls for a shared commitment to protecting the environment, preserving public health, and creating a city in which people can live and work with dignity.

What is that stench? Oh, it is the waste collection and disposal truck leaving a trail of small debris and foul smell in its wake. Incidentally, each part of Lagos seems to have its own distinctive smell, but the common denominator is that none exactly smells of roses.

Like many rapidly growing cities, Lagos faces the arduous task of keeping its environment clean while accommodating an expanding population, increasing consumption and rising volumes of waste. With an estimated 13,000 to 15,000 metric tonnes of waste generated daily, the demands on its collection and disposal systems are enormous. From waste accumulating at collection points through an aging and insufficient fleet of compactor trucks to landfill capacity, blocked drainage channels, flooding and inadequate sewage systems, these challenges highlight the significant infrastructure deficit and the intricate relationship between urban growth, infrastructure development, and environmental sustainability.

Lessons from the Great Stink of 1858, a fascinating episode in London’s history? That summer, unusually hot weather intensified the stench from the River Thames, which had become the receptacle for much of the city’s untreated sewage. London’s population had grown rapidly, placing increasing demands on sanitation infrastructure that had struggled to keep pace. The resulting stench was so unbearable that parliamentary proceedings were disrupted. The crisis prompted legislation to fund a comprehensive sewerage system, which transformed London’s sanitation infrastructure and helped protect public health. What had begun as an intolerable environmental nuisance became a catalyst for an ambitious programme of urban renewal.

Yet, more than a century-and-a-half later, London continues to grapple with sewage pollution and other environmental pressures on the Thames. Similarly, the cleanup of the Seine ahead of the 2024 Paris Olympics required substantial investment in wastewater and sanitation infrastructure, as part of a broader €1.4 billion programme, underscoring the scale of investment and planning that environmental renewal can demand. These examples demonstrate that environmental management is never truly complete, even for cities with established infrastructure. The infrastructure for maintaining and renewing urban systems must continue to evolve as population grows, consumption patterns change, and environmental demands become more complex.

…a clean environment is a shared responsibility. Public authorities and waste management operators have important roles to play in providing reliable services, while residents and businesses can contribute through responsible disposal, waste segregation, and avoidance of the use of drainage channels as dump sites. Public education and consistent enforcement can reinforce these efforts.

What, then, can Lagos learn from these experiences?

First, waste management should be understood as an essential component of urban planning and development. Efficient collection and disposal involve more than deploying trucks. They require suitable transfer and disposal facilities, effective drainage, appropriate sewage systems, reliable funding, regular maintenance, and coordination across the relevant agencies.

Second, a clean environment is a shared responsibility. Public authorities and waste management operators have important roles to play in providing reliable services, while residents and businesses can contribute through responsible disposal, waste segregation, and avoidance of the use of drainage channels as dump sites. Public education and consistent enforcement can reinforce these efforts. Ultimately, the objective is to build a city where waste is managed safely and efficiently, rather than merely moved from one location to another. A refuse truck that leaves a trail of dirt behind may have removed waste from one street only to share it across geographies. Effective waste management requires more than collection, a process that still has room for improvement. The quality of transportation and final disposal matters just as much.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Apparently, urbanisation has expanded the cattle egret’s dietary preferences. After all, bird sef must chop! But there is a difference between adaptation and progress. The cattle egret may have found an alternative food source, but its resourcefulness should not become an excuse for ours to falter. Birds can adapt to our waste; our cities should not have to.

Few metaphors for the evolution of waste management as a developmental challenge are as apt as the cattle egret — Lagos Waste Management Authority’s unofficial mascot. Once commonly seen trailing cattle in search of food (ticks borne by the herds), these adaptable birds now seem equally comfortable accompanying refuse trucks and foraging around heaps of garbage. Apparently, urbanisation has expanded the cattle egret’s dietary preferences. After all, bird sef must chop! But there is a difference between adaptation and progress. The cattle egret may have found an alternative food source, but its resourcefulness should not become an excuse for ours to falter. Birds can adapt to our waste; our cities should not have to.

Lagos does not need to experience its own Great Stink before taking decisive action. The warning signs are visible and painfully olfactory. This challenge presents an opportunity to rethink how a fast-growing metropolis can manage its resources and infrastructure more effectively. A cleaner Lagos will require investment, planning, innovation and sustained public cooperation. Above all, it calls for a shared commitment to protecting the environment, preserving public health, and creating a city in which people can live and work with dignity. And perhaps, one day, when a waste collection truck passes, the only thing left in its wake will be the sound of its engine, not the stench.

Temitope Sodipo is a lawyer in the financial services sector. An avid gardener, birdwatcher, and arts enthusiast. She writes from Lagos.

World.title: Nigerian businesses need more than bank loans to thrive – Finance Minister
World.content:
The Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, says Nigerian businesses need more than conventional loans to grow, calling for patient capital, experienced investors and stronger institutional support to help promising enterprises expand.

Mr Oyedele said access to credit alone would not resolve the structural challenges facing entrepreneurs, many of whom struggle to secure the financing, skills and networks required to scale their businesses.

He spoke on Saturday in Abuja at the fourth edition of the Nigeria Sovereign Investment Authority (NSIA) Prize for Innovation, where seven startups received awards worth a combined $277,000.

Speaking through his Special Adviser on Finance and Investment, Marie Ukpere, the minister said small and medium-sized enterprises are vital to livelihoods and employment but often lack the resources to grow beyond their current size.

“We also recognise that high-potential businesses often require more than conventional credit. They need patient capital, experienced investment partners, and networks that can help them enter new markets and achieve scale,” he said.

Mr Oyedele said Nigeria’s ambition to build a $1 trillion economy would depend partly on its ability to help small businesses become medium-sized enterprises and, eventually, larger companies capable of competing in international markets.

Beyond conventional loans

The minister highlighted several government-backed institutions and programmes aimed at improving access to finance and supporting business development.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He cited the Development Bank of Nigeria and the National Credit Guarantee Company as part of efforts to ease financing constraints. The credit guarantee company is designed to reduce lending risks for financial institutions and encourage more lending to small businesses and manufacturers.

He also referred to the Nigerian Consumer Credit Corporation, which is intended to expand access to consumer credit and support household purchasing power, as well as the $618 million Investment in Digital and Creative Enterprises programme, which provides financing and business support to young entrepreneurs.

Mr Oyedele said the NSIA was also anchoring venture capital funds to attract institutional investment into Nigerian businesses.

He added that the authority was developing an impact innovation fund with the Japan International Cooperation Agency, with British International Investment expressing interest in participating.

The proposed fund is expected to support commercially viable businesses addressing economic and development challenges.

“The real measure of your success will not be the prize you receive today. It will be the businesses you go on to build afterwards,” the minister told the finalists.

Earlier, the Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer of the NSIA, Aminu Umar-Sadiq, said the 12 finalists were selected from more than 6,000 applications after five stages of screening and business development activities.

He said the competition formed part of the authority’s strategy to support entrepreneurs alongside its investments in infrastructure and other sectors.

This year’s competition focused on healthcare, manufacturing and food systems, which Mr Umar-Sadiq identified as sectors with the potential to create jobs, build skills and improve productivity.

He said all 12 finalists would participate in a six-week learning programme at Lagos Business School, while strategic partners would offer further opportunities for financing and business development.

According to him, the NSIA works with companies receiving its investment to strengthen corporate governance, improve management and expand demand for their products.

“When the equity injection goes into these companies, we work very closely with the management teams to enhance their value proposition, strengthen their governance and broaden the demand for their products,” he said.

Mr Umar-Sadiq cited previous winners, including Money Africa and Sycamore, as examples of businesses whose progress should be assessed over time.

He said the impact of startup investments should be measured over about five years rather than judged by immediate results.

Healthcare investment opportunities

Also speaking, the National Coordinator of the Presidential Unlocking Healthcare Value Chain Initiative, Abdu Mukhtar, described healthcare as a significant investment opportunity.

He estimated Nigeria’s addressable healthcare market at $20 billion and said the sector already has about 250,000 small and medium-sized enterprises, citing figures from the International Finance Corporation.

“We estimate that across the healthcare value chain, the addressable market is about $20bn. There are already about 250,000 SMEs in healthcare, according to the IFC,” he said.

Mr Mukhtar identified pharmaceutical manufacturing, medical devices, clinical research, telemedicine and healthcare logistics as areas where entrepreneurs could develop businesses.

Affiong Williams, founder and chief executive officer of ReelFruit and lead judge of the competition, said her company had raised more than $7 million over 14 years.

She attributed its ability to attract investment to preparation, credibility, and resilience, urging entrepreneurs to understand customer needs, build strong networks, and stay focused despite economic uncertainty.

Dave DeLucia, founder and director of Cascador, said preparing businesses to attract investment was as important as providing capital.

“Capital readiness is just as important or more than the capital itself,” he said, adding that entrepreneurs outside Lagos often needed greater institutional support.

Seven startups receive awards

At the competition, Come Again Foods emerged as the overall winner, receiving a combined prize of $105,000.

Protein Kapital came second with $70,000, while InstantRad placed third, receiving $50,000.

Other award recipients were Eight Medical, Uwana Energy, Tryctor and Smartei Agri Tech.

The NSIA said the $277,000 award package comprised $220,000 from the authority, $45,000 from Cascador and $12,000 from Wema Bank.

Beyond the cash awards, the finalists are expected to benefit from business development support and opportunities to connect with potential investors.

The competition is part of the NSIA’s efforts to support innovative businesses and help them develop into sustainable enterprises in Nigeria.

World.title: Must we destroy the evidence of our past to build our future?, By Lande Ọmọ Ọba
World.content:
And I asked myself: Must we destroy the evidence of our past in order to celebrate our freedom from it? Surely, preserving a colonial building does not mean celebrating colonialism! It simply means acknowledging that this was part of our history. Whether we like that history or not, it happened. I am told that even the fountain that replaced the courthouse is no longer functional. We lost an important historical building for a water fountain that is not functional. The list goes on and on.

On Tuesday, I had the privilege of listening to former President Olusegun Obasanjo speak at Harvard University Institute of Politics and Centre for African Studies. He had come to discuss peacekeeping in Africa and beyond, but there was something he said about our identity and history that has stayed with me. There were quite a number of young Nigerians in the room, many from the diaspora.

A young man, about 26 years old, asked a question about the Nigerian Civil War. He wanted to know whose account of the war was correct, considering that different people had different versions of what happened. As he spoke, I sensed that he was leaning towards finding fault with one ethnic group over another and allied to the current heated polity. President Obasanjo was not having it!

He gave examples of heroic acts by individuals from different ethnic groups and equally troubling acts by people from those same groups. In fact, he told a story of how he was saved from an assassination plot by a Hausa, Hassan Katsina. Then he uttered the words that I will hold dear for a long time. “There are only two types of Nigerians: good Nigerians and bad Nigerians. Not good tribes and bad tribes.” I thought that was profound.

But I also kept thinking about that young man. He is 26. He was not born when the civil war happened. So, whose version of history is he listening to? His grandfather’s? His parents’? Someone who experienced the war? Or perhaps something he read on social media? And what if the version he has heard is incomplete or coloured by someone’s personal experience or prejudice? How would he know? Which is why many like me worry about our attitude to history in Nigeria.

We talk a lot. We argue endlessly about our past, our leaders, the civil war, ethnicity, corruption, and everything in between. But how much do we actually document and, more importantly, how much do we learn so that we do not keep making mistakes? History is not just about remembering what happened. It is about understanding why it happened, what went wrong, what worked, and how we can do better. We cannot keep making the same mistakes and expecting different results. As President Obasanjo spoke about peacekeeping across Africa, I found myself thinking about Nigeria. We have played important roles in keeping peace in other countries, but today we are struggling with insecurity and divisions within our own borders. Surely, understanding our history must be part of finding lasting solutions.

And I found myself asking, why are we not doing more of this in Nigeria? Our history did not start from our independence in 1960. I was recently told a story about the old courthouse at Tinubu Square, near Kakawa Street on Lagos Island. Apparently, the site once housed the Court of Assizes, an important part of our judicial history during colonial rule. The building was demolished and replaced with a fountain commemorating Nigeria’s independence.

Not too long ago, I visited Concord, Massachusetts and had the opportunity to spend some time at the historic Colonial Inn, a building dating back to 1716! Nearby, British forces and American colonial militiamen fought during the Revolutionary War in 1775. The area has been carefully preserved, with buildings, monuments and records that tell the story of what happened. I stood there taking it all in. Here was a country preserving a history that is over 250 years old. Generations have come and gone, but the story remains accessible. Of course, people may disagree about how historical events should be interpreted. But the evidence is there to be examined.

And I found myself asking, why are we not doing more of this in Nigeria? Our history did not start from our independence in 1960. I was recently told a story about the old courthouse at Tinubu Square, near Kakawa Street on Lagos Island. Apparently, the site once housed the Court of Assizes, an important part of our judicial history during colonial rule. The building was demolished and replaced with a fountain commemorating Nigeria’s independence. A friend was telling me about how Professor Wole Soyinka has also commented critically on the loss of that historic building. The argument, as the story was told to me, was that we needed to put the memories of colonial rule behind us, and we replaced this site with a water fountain!

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

And I asked myself: Must we destroy the evidence of our past in order to celebrate our freedom from it? Surely, preserving a colonial building does not mean celebrating colonialism! It simply means acknowledging that this was part of our history. Whether we like that history or not, it happened. I am told that even the fountain that replaced the courthouse is no longer functional. We lost an important historical building for a water fountain that is not functional. The list goes on and on.

In the West, they have lectures on the life of Christopher Marlowe and William Shakespeare born in 1564! At one of the lectures, I felt an inner voice asking how many times I have attended or been invited to a lecture on the life of any outstanding African born even 100 years ago, but here I was listening with rapt attention to this lecture. Sometimes we are too eager to move on, to forget, to start afresh, without asking ourselves what we should have learnt from what came before.

What about the ordinary Nigerians who lived through those difficult years? The mothers, teachers, civil servants, journalists, and families whose lives were changed forever? Who is recording their stories? Who is listening to them? And who is making sure that the next generation has access to these accounts? We need to preserve our history, especially the difficult and uncomfortable parts.

We forget that progress is often about improving on yesterday, not pretending yesterday never happened. We are not only losing our living history, but we are also gradually losing the generation that witnessed some of the most important periods in Nigeria’s history. Those who experienced independence, the civil war and the early years of military rule are getting older. Many have already passed away. Every time one of them dies, we risk losing stories that may never have been properly documented. These people are living libraries. And I am not talking only about former presidents, governors, or military leaders.

What about the ordinary Nigerians who lived through those difficult years? The mothers, teachers, civil servants, journalists, and families whose lives were changed forever? Who is recording their stories? Who is listening to them? And who is making sure that the next generation has access to these accounts? We need to preserve our history, especially the difficult and uncomfortable parts. Not in order to keep old wounds open or pass blame from one generation to another, but to understand how we got here and what we must do differently.

I keep thinking about that young man at Harvard and President Obasanjo’s response. The young boy whispered to many around him: “He didn’t answer my question,” and someone else said “Our African parents avoid uncomfortable truths with long tales and proverbs.” I smiled. Will they act differently when they become elders? We owe future generations the truth about our history, not simply the version that suits our beliefs, our families, or our ethnic affiliations. Because if we genuinely want a better Nigeria, we must be willing to learn from the Nigeria that came before us. We cannot erase our past and then expect to learn from it.

By the way, I paid $15 to the tour guide to tell me about the revolutionary war and my brunch at the Colonial Inn cost $65. There is money to be made for history and tourism.

‘Lande Omo Oba, a lawyer, writes from Lagos.

World.title: Enugu traders reaffirm support for Gov Mbah’s second term
World.content:
Market traders and leaders across Enugu State have assured Governor Peter Ndubuisi Mbah of their support for a second term in office, declaring that his administration’s development strides, market-friendly policies and interventions in the trading sector have strengthened their confidence in his leadership.

The traders, under the umbrella of the Enugu State Market Amalgamated Traders Association (ESMATA), led by its President, Chief Chinwuba Igwesi, gave the assurance on Friday, 23 October during a high-level market stakeholders’ meeting with the governor.

The meeting, which brought together chairmen and secretaries of more than 50 markets across the state, provided an opportunity for the traders to express their appreciation for the administration’s development initiatives, highlight improvements in the business environment and discuss measures to further expand commercial activities across Enugu State.

Speaking on behalf of the association, Igwesi said traders across the 17 local government areas were prepared to support Governor Mbah’s re-election, citing what he described as visible development, improved business conditions and the administration’s responsiveness to the concerns of the market community.

He particularly commended the governor for ending the illegal Monday sit-at-home disruption that had previously forced traders to lose substantial income by shutting their businesses on Mondays. According to him, the restoration of normal commercial activities throughout the week has enabled traders to open their shops daily and improve their earnings.

The ESMATA president said the return of regular market activities had brought relief to traders, whose businesses had suffered from repeated disruptions, uncertainty and lost trading opportunities.

Igwesi also expressed gratitude to Mbah for approving the provision of transformers to markets without adequate electricity, the asphalting of road networks within several markets and the installation of solar-powered streetlights to improve visibility, security and commercial activities.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He noted that these interventions were helping to address long-standing infrastructure challenges that had affected traders and customers, while making the markets more accessible and conducive to business.

The market leaders further appreciated the governor for the construction of toilet facilities in markets, the release of utility vehicles to market leadership and the appointment of some market leaders into his administration. They also commended him for approving pilgrimage opportunities for some market leaders during the year, describing the gestures as indications that the government recognises and values the contributions of traders to the state’s economy.

Igwesi said the traders were particularly proud that Mbah understood their challenges because of his background in business, adding that they considered his performance in office a source of pride for the market community.

According to him, the governor’s understanding of the realities of trading had been reflected in policies and decisions aimed at improving the business environment, strengthening commercial activities and supporting the livelihoods of traders and their families.

The ESMATA president also addressed concerns surrounding taxation, dismissing rumours of a general increase in taxes. He explained that the administration’s approach had involved the unification of taxes into a single account, rather than the alleged increase being circulated.

He said traders were willing to pay their taxes because they could see development projects and public infrastructure being delivered across the state. He maintained that the visible use of public revenue for development had strengthened traders’ confidence in the government and its management of resources.

Igwesi further observed that business activities in Enugu were thriving, particularly in the building materials sector, which he said had experienced improved commercial prospects under the current administration.

He attributed part of the growth to the governor’s directive requiring contractors handling projects in the state to purchase construction materials from local suppliers in Enugu instead of sourcing them from outside the state where such materials were available locally.

According to him, the policy had helped retain more business transactions within Enugu, increased patronage for local traders and contributed to the growth of businesses dealing in building materials and related supplies.

The ESMATA president also praised the administration’s investment in healthcare infrastructure, recounting his experience during a visit to the international hospital project. He said the facility was so impressive that he momentarily felt as though he had travelled to Dubai.

He described the project as evidence of the scale of development taking place in the state and said such investments were helping to reshape perceptions of Enugu while improving the prospects for economic growth.

In a strong declaration of support, Igwesi said Mbah’s record of performance had given him an advantage over opposition candidates ahead of the next governorship election.

He assured the governor that the market community would stand firmly behind his re-election bid, urging him to remain focused on delivering development and improving the welfare of residents.

“When the time comes, your work will speak for you,” he said, while reiterating the traders’ position with the declaration: “No opposition in Enugu State.”

The market leaders, speaking in unison, also assured the governor that he could remain confident in the support of traders, insisting that the development taking place across the state had strengthened their resolve to back his administration for another term.

They maintained that the market community was encouraged by the governor’s approach to governance and the recognition given to traders as important partners in Enugu’s economic development.

Responding, Governor Mbah thanked the market leaders for the visit and for acknowledging his administration’s efforts, assuring them that the state would witness even greater development if they renewed his mandate by voting him back into office.

The governor said his administration remained committed to expanding the state’s economic opportunities, improving infrastructure and positioning Enugu as a leading destination for business, investment and commercial activities.

He outlined several initiatives intended to strengthen the trading sector, including plans to develop a cargo terminal at the Akanu Ibiam International Airport, Enugu, to improve the movement of goods and connect businesses in the state to international markets.

Mbah explained that the cargo terminal would help open Enugu to the world, facilitate the movement of goods and create opportunities for traders and businesses to participate more directly in international commerce.

He also disclosed plans for direct cargo operations between Enugu and China, which he said would soon commence, enabling Enugu traders to import goods directly from China at more affordable rates.

The governor said the initiative was designed to reduce the difficulties traders encounter when sourcing goods, improve access to international supply chains and strengthen the competitiveness of businesses operating in Enugu.

He further highlighted the ongoing construction of the International Market at Idodo, describing it as part of the administration’s broader strategy to expand commercial infrastructure and create more opportunities for traders, investors and other economic players.

According to him, the government is deliberately expanding Enugu’s business space through infrastructure, connectivity and strategic investments that will enable the state to attract more commercial activities and create opportunities for its people.

Mbah also spoke about his efforts to reconnect Enugu to the centre of national activities, noting that the state had been losing some of its historic prominence as the capital of the former Southern Region and a leading political and administrative centre in the South-East.

He said the construction of the International Conference Centre (ICC), Enugu, was part of the strategy to restore the state’s standing by providing a modern venue for major national events, conferences and gatherings.

The governor explained that hosting such events would bring participants, visitors and businesspeople into Enugu, creating opportunities for hotels, restaurants, transport operators, traders and other service providers to benefit from increased economic activities.

He stressed that the government’s investment in security was equally important to this ambition, noting that a safe environment was necessary to attract thousands of visitors and ensure that businesses could operate without fear.

Mbah said the administration was working to provide a secure environment supported by an effective security system, adding that safety, infrastructure and economic planning must work together to make Enugu an attractive destination for business and investment.

On the state’s economic future, the governor reaffirmed his ambition to grow Enugu’s economy from an estimated $4 billion to a $30 billion economy, stressing that the target was linked to his administration’s determination to expand productivity, attract investment, strengthen local businesses and create more opportunities for residents.

He described Enugu as a state with significant economic potential and expressed confidence that ongoing and planned investments would help accelerate its growth.

The governor also reassured the traders that their interests would remain a priority in his administration, declaring that he would not support policies designed to undermine the trading community.

Mbah said his personal experience in business had given him an understanding of the challenges traders face, including the demands of running businesses, sourcing goods, meeting financial obligations and sustaining livelihoods.

He assured the market leaders that he would continue to consider the implications of government policies for traders and ensure that the administration’s economic agenda supported rather than hindered their activities.

The governor’s remarks reinforced the administration’s position that traders and other business operators are central to Enugu’s development strategy and must benefit from policies intended to grow the state’s economy.

The meeting was attended by key government officials, including the Senior Special Assistant to the Governor on Market Liaison, Dr Chinedu Mbah; the Senior Special Assistant to the Governor on Security, Mr Vincent Onyeaboor; and the Special Adviser to the Governor on Political Matters, Chief Frank Anioma. The three officials accompanied the governor in receiving the market leaders.

The engagement underscored the importance of sustained dialogue between the state government and the market community, with traders expressing appreciation for completed interventions while the governor outlined further plans aimed at improving infrastructure, expanding access to international trade and strengthening Enugu’s commercial position.

With the ESMATA leadership and representatives of more than 50 markets expressing confidence in the administration, the meeting highlighted the growing significance of the trading sector in the state’s economic and political conversations ahead of the next governorship election.

For the traders, the central message was that market infrastructure, reliable security, access to goods, improved business opportunities and visible development would remain important measures of government performance. For Governor Mbah, the meeting provided an opportunity to reaffirm his commitment to building a more connected, secure and commercially vibrant Enugu State.

World.title: Choosing humanity over harm: A National Assembly’s duty to protect life, By Margaret Uddin Ojeahere
World.content:
This moment, however, presents an opportunity to demand the leadership Nigerians deserve. Nigeria does not need more punishment; it needs leaders that understand the weight of human suffering. The first step is clear: Attempted suicide must be decriminalised. People in crisis deserve care, not constraints. Criminalisation only worsens stigma, mental health problems, and hinders access to appropriate care. Equally urgent is the full implementation of the National Mental Health Act.

“Keep life alive.”

Those were the words my late teacher, Professor Albert Anjorin, repeated to us in medical school decades ago. They are simple, humane, and rooted in the belief that every life is worth protecting. It is heartbreaking that in 2026, I am hearing the opposite sentiment echoed from the hallowed chambers of Nigeria’s National Assembly.

Less than four days after the commemoration of the 2026 World Mental Health Day, a week filled with stories of lived experiences, awareness campaigns, and calls for compassion for persons struggling with mental health challenges and their caregivers, Nigerians were confronted with a statement that shook the conscience of the nation. Words attributed to the Senate President, Godswill Akpabio, went viral: “If you attempt suicide, make sure you die. Anyone who attempts and fails will go to jail.”

Words, once spoken, cannot be recalled, and these remarks landed like a blow on the progress Nigeria has made from repealing the Lunacy Act of 1958 to enacting the National Mental Health Act in 2022. For years, advocates have tried to help Nigerians understand a simple truth: anyone with a brain can develop a mental health condition. Mental health conditions do not respect tribe, class, religion, or political office. Research shows that one in four to five Nigerians live with a mental health condition, and with worsening governance, insecurity, unemployment, and collapsing amenities, the numbers may be even higher. The story below is not an outlier but it reflects the broader reality captured in these statistics.

“At twenty-eight, Daniel often felt older than his age, as trauma ages people in ways birthdays never do. Fifteen years had passed since the night insurgents descended on his village, leaving behind ashes and sad memories. Daniel remembered the sound of his father’s voice, firm, resisting the attackers. He also remembered how quickly courage could be swallowed by gunfire. His mother’s fate was worse. Daniel had seen what no child should ever witness. He survived only because his father had shoved him beneath a heap of rusted roofing sheets moments before the attackers reached their home. He lay there listening to the horror unfolding above him, praying for a miracle that never came. Thereafter, Daniel has lived with survivors’ guilt, depression and post‑traumatic stress disorder, words he learned much later. He tried to rebuild his life, but trauma clung to him like a second skin. Jobs slipped through his fingers. Relationships dissolved under the weight of memories he could not silence. Even the cost of his medications became a burden too heavy to carry. His aging uncle and cousin did what they could. They offered shelter, food, and reassurance. They sat with him through episodes, prayed with him when he felt lost, and accompanied him to therapy. His faith community embraced him, reminding him that survival was not weakness but a testimony. Still, there were times when Daniel felt like a burden. Nights when he wondered if the last vestiges of life were worth holding at all. But each time he dipped, someone pulled him back – a cousin’s hand on his shoulder, a therapist’s gentle words, a pastor’s reminder that healing is slow but possible. These small acts of care kept him going. Then one afternoon, while sitting outside the clinic waiting for his appointment, Daniel heard a statement on his phone, a voice from a trusted person who swore to protect him saying that anyone who attempted suicide should ‘make sure they die,’ and that those who survived should be jailed. For a moment, Daniel felt himself slipping again. But then he remembered his uncle’s voice, his cousin’s laughter, his therapist’s steady encouragement, his community’s prayers. He remembered that survival was not a crime. It was courage. He whispered to himself, ‘I am still here,’ and in that moment, he chose again to hold on.”

For years, advocacy efforts focused on educating the less informed, assuming that misunderstanding drove stigma. But the landscape changes entirely when a senior lawmaker suggests jailing people who survive suicide attempts. What message does that send to Nigerian youths who comprise over 60 per cent of our population? To the adolescents battling suicidal thoughts? To the adult drowning in depression, overwhelmed by economic hardship, or shattered by trauma and insecurity?

Suicide is the third leading cause of death among young people aged 15–29. Nigeria records an estimated 15,000 suicide deaths annually, and for every life lost, 20 to 25 more people attempt suicide. Each suicide also leaves about 135 people deeply affected, contributing to over two million suicide loss survivors. These figures are considered conservative, especially in countries like Nigeria where suicide remains misunderstood, stigmatised, and criminalised, leading to significant under‑reporting. Nigeria remains one of the few countries where surviving a suicide attempt can still lead to prosecution. Under Section 327 of the Criminal Code and Section 231 of the Penal Code, individuals may face up to 12 months’ imprisonment, despite the Federal Government’s reaffirmation of its commitment to decriminalising attempted suicide.

For years, advocacy efforts focused on educating the less informed, assuming that misunderstanding drove stigma. But the landscape changes entirely when a senior lawmaker suggests jailing people who survive suicide attempts. What message does that send to Nigerian youths who comprise over 60 per cent of our population? To the adolescents battling suicidal thoughts? To the adult drowning in depression, overwhelmed by economic hardship, or shattered by trauma and insecurity? Sadly, vulnerability is being treated as a criminal offence. Can this then be described as a governance deficit or profound moral failure? Interestingly, a kind of reaction formation plays out here. With mental health problems rising and at least a quarter of Nigerians affected, it is not surprising that some of the lawmakers who laughed during plenary may later seek mental health care quietly like Nicodemus in the night, when they or their relatives become vulnerable and need urgent support to prevent dire consequences. The hypocrisy cuts deep.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

This moment, however, presents an opportunity to demand the leadership Nigerians deserve. Nigeria does not need more punishment; it needs leaders that understand the weight of human suffering. The first step is clear: Attempted suicide must be decriminalised. People in crisis deserve care, not constraints. Criminalisation only worsens stigma, mental health problems, and hinders access to appropriate care. Equally urgent is the full implementation of the National Mental Health Act. Three years after its passage, it remains largely dormant, leaving millions without the protection, services, and funding it promises. Nigerians should not wait indefinitely for a law designed to safeguard their wellbeing. Our youth, who represent Nigeria’s future, need safe spaces, mentorship, opportunities, and accessible mental health support. Real progress also requires investment in mental health infrastructure. Community treatment centres, crisis helplines, trained professionals, and integration of mental health services into primary healthcare should be national priorities, not punchlines.

To paraphrase Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong’s view: When a person gets to the point of throwing in the towel and tries to end it all, we should protect, support, and never punish. The future of this nation depends on how seriously we take the mental wellbeing of its people. It is past time for our lawmakers to rise to that responsibility. Governance should never laugh at pain, and policies must not criminalise suffering, they should strengthen systems that uphold healthcare, dignity, and protection from despair.

Mental health does not exist in isolation. It is shaped by the conditions people live in: security, employment, education, and access to basic amenities. Addressing these social stressors would significantly reduce the rising cases of mental health conditions, and lawmakers must treat it as a core governance requirement. National awareness campaigns led by government can help reduce stigma and encourage help-seeking. And none of this should occur in siloes. Collaboration is essential. Nigeria has psychiatrists, other experts and civil‑society organisations already doing the work. Lawmakers should collaborate with them, not undermine their efforts.
