World.title: Rehab, Release, Repeat: Nana, the Seal Who Refuses to Return to the Wild
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019142/Rehab, Release, Repeat: Nana, the Seal Who Refuses to Return to the Wild
World.content:
In wildlife conservation, there are three steps to helping an injured or orphaned animal: rescue, rehabilitate, and release. “Returning” isn’t part of the plan, but try telling that to China’s celebrity seal Nana.

This 2-year-old wild spotted seal, a Class I protected species in China, was a must-see attraction this summer for visitors to Dachangshan Island, part of Dalian’s Changshan Archipelago in the northeastern Liaoning province.

Nana has been released twice far out into the Yellow Sea, with the hope he’d join a migrating colony. Both times he’s made his way back alone, once covering more than 200 kilometers in just six days.

When he first showed up on the island in June, he was wary of humans and swam away when approached. But over time, he grew braver. Tourists tempted him near with tasty fish, though this sometimes resulted in him receiving a prod or a kick, and often a startling camera flash.

Concerned for Nana’s welfare, the local government put up warning signs telling people not to feed him and to keep a safe distance, and vowed “not to use him to promote tourism.” Yet within months, a “Nana Line” shuttle service had opened, running directly from the island’s Yuanyang Port to its “best seal-watching spot,” while the local tourism bureau began working with a private business to make and sell seal-related merchandise.

For many locals, Nana’s presence has been bittersweet: he’s a cute addition to the neighborhood, but the risks to his safety outweigh the benefits, they say.

Despite the falling temperature, authorities have ruled out moving him again, much to the delight of those who feel the seal has “made his choice.” But as the tourist season ends and his steady, fan-fueled food supply dries up, others worry that Nana could face a harsh winter alone.

Hello, new neighbor

Nana was just a pup in the summer of 2024, when fishermen first spotted him resting on a buoy in waters off Beihai, in the southern Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Noticing he was thin and had wounds on his body, likely caused by boat propellers, they alerted the authorities, who transported him to the Beihai Aquatic Rescue and Rehabilitation Center.

The spot where Nana was discovered lies just off a migration route for spotted seals between the western Pacific Ocean and Dalian’s Liaodong Bay. Experts suspect he drifted from his colony and was stranded alone.

In November 2025, after being nursed back to health, Nana was transferred to a wild species rehabilitation center in Dalian operated by the Liaoning Ocean and Fisheries Science and Research Institute. There, he quickly went from 50 to 70 kilograms and grew a new coat of glossy fur. “You could see him looking better every day,” says Chai Yuqiao, a researcher at the base.

By this spring, Nana was deemed well enough to return to the wild. On April 16, the institute released him and two other rescued seals roughly 10 kilometers from shore in the Yellow Sea, thinking they would naturally head for the migration route and find a new colony.

Nana’s two companions did exactly that, but data from his satellite tag shows he never left the Yellow Sea. Two months later, he popped up at Dachangshan Island.

Locals first spotted the seal relaxing in a rocky tide pool on June 19.

“Back then he was wary and rarely came close,” recalls Feng Zhi, who runs a guesthouse on the island. “He’d just hang around, and if someone walked over, he’d swim away.”

But that changed the more he interacted with tourists. “Wherever the crowd was thickest, that’s where he’d be,” says Li Ai, who also works in the hospitality industry. “But he can be picky about people,” she adds, explaining that Nana appeared especially fond of a wetsuit-wearing livestreamer known as “Man in Black,” who has 24,000 followers on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. Nana often chased him and snuggled up to him.

Zhou Long, another guesthouse manager, says Nana once squeezed in between him and several friends as they stood in the shallows. The seal was warm, slippery, and plump, “like a balloon that’s about to pop,” he says.

People soon began feeding Nana fish and petting him when he got close. A local boat captain says he often tried stopping tourists from doing this, but few listened. He worried Nana might accidentally be fed a fish containing a fishhook, “the consequences of which don’t bear thinking about.”

Some people were even captured on surveillance cameras throwing Nana barbecued meat, bread, and potato chips, foods that could seriously upset his digestive system, while others kicked him, and thoughtless children threw stones at him.

“I couldn’t bear to watch and couldn’t do anything about it. I could only turn around and walk away,” says Li.

Many locals breathed a sigh of relief on Sept. 7 when the authorities finally arrived to take Nana away.

Gone, but not forgotten

To protect and “re-wild” Nana, the Changhai County government, which administers Dachangshan Island, decided to again transport the seal out to the Yellow Sea, this time to a spot about 140 kilometers away by boat.

Nana was back on the island just six days later. His tracking tag had fallen off a month earlier, but Tian Jiashen, director of marine rare animal conservation research at the Liaoning institute, estimates the seal’s return journey must have covered at least 200 kilometers.

Zhou had an inkling he’d not seen the last of Nana. Social media users had been eagerly sharing news of sightings, and the seal was getting closer all the time. On the evening of Sept. 13, Zhou went to the shore, opened a livestream, and lay in wait, with nearly 200 followers logging on to watch.

As night fell, Zhou heard a splash, like “a huge creature leaping into the water.” When he ran over, Nana was beside the blue pontoon bridge that he’d frequented all summer.

Within hours, Lin Gao, an employee at a beachside water sports center, had reinstalled the giant inflatable yellow duck Nana had liked to sleep on. “We couldn’t let him come back and find it gone,” he says, adding that work had felt “hollow” without Nana around.

Tian admits he never expected the seal to return but now believes Nana’s interactions with tourists might have reawakened his memories of being rescued and fed by humans.

Staff at the Liaoning institute recall that Nana was initially more curious than cautious. Marine researcher Chen Yanyu says he was once scrubbing the rearing pool when Nana surprisingly pushed a long-handled brush toward his hand. He badly wanted to pat the seal’s head, but that would be against the rules of “rehab and release.”

In wildlife conservation, keeping a safe distance is paramount. Rescued seals are fed by pouring live fish into the pool, while researchers deliberately approach the animals with nets to condition them to avoid people. By the time of his release, Nana had begun watching the staff from afar.

On that first release day, Chen watched Nana slide down the boat’s ramp into the sea with tears in his eyes.

However, when the seal became a celebrity, the institute came under attack from netizens who felt it had failed in its responsibilities to rehabilitate Nana.

Tian, who has worked there since 2010, believes the criticism was unfair. He explained that the institute is manned year-round by researchers who volunteer their time for free, and that in the past two decades it has helped rescue 244 spotted seals, releasing 223.

“The sea is his home, and he should go home,” he adds, talking about Nana. “Keeping him here, in a human environment — that would be cruelty.”

The risks human behaviors pose to wildlife are obvious. Ah Nong, a spotted seal rescued late last year after spending 15 months in waters off Wenchang, in the southern island province of Hainan, was found to have diarrhea, elevated liver function, and ultraviolet skin burns from being fed, touched, and photographed by tourists.

When Nana returned a second time, Chai and some colleagues wanted to go see him, “to find out whether he still remembered us.” Others, like researcher Shi Hongyue, held another wish: that one day they would come across Nana naturally during a survey of a wild colony.

Sealing his fate?

Nana became even more famous after returning to Dachangshan Island last month. By 7 a.m., at least 10 livestreamers would already be set up on shore, waiting for the seal to wake up. These channels quickly became a key marketing tool for guesthouses and other local businesses.

In August, Chinese media quoted an unnamed local official as saying that authorities “would not use (Nana) for cultural tourism promotions.” However, that attitude appeared to shift after the seal’s return in September.

The Changhai Culture and Tourism Bureau opened the “Nana Line” on Sept. 25, and beachside stalls hawking Nana-themed merch began popping up this month.

More warning signs and loudspeakers have been placed along the beach, reminding tourists that feeding protected species is forbidden, while enforcement officers and volunteers now regularly patrol the area. The local government has announced it will not attempt to move Nana again and is planning to build him a shelter on the pontoon bridge, away from the crowds.

Residents say the feeding and touching has declined, but it still happens.

This will naturally trail off as the tourist and fishing seasons wind down ahead of the coldest months, leading some to worry that Nana could starve. Despite the rules, in October, Sun Zongjun, the owner of the water sports center, pledged on a livestream that “we’ll definitely keep feeding him when it gets cold.” The county government has yet to confirm whether live fish stocks will be provided for the seal over winter.

Tian says it’s hard to predict whether Nana will ever leave and fully return to nature; it depends on diverse factors like water temperature, his physiological state, and whether he meets any companions and joins a new colony.

Scientific studies using tracking data show that spotted seals tend to rest or breed in the same place, year after year. Tian believes this behavior, and his memories of human interaction, could be what led Nana back to Dachangshan Island.

While most locals were happy to welcome Nana “home,” his presence has also brought pressure. “Our island lives off tourism. If anything happens to him, the criticism of millions of people could crash down on us in an instant,” says Lin, who regularly volunteers to patrol the pontoon bridge in the early hours.

On most nights, Nana can be found sleeping soundly on his giant yellow duck as it rocks gently in the waves. Soon, he will be joined in these waters by other spotted seals. No one knows what will come next.

“It’s fine if Nana stays,” says Liu Yi, a guesthouse owner on the island. “But I still hope he leaves.”

(Due to privacy concerns, Lin Gao, Feng Zhi, Li Ai, Zhou Long, and Liu Yi are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Qin Bing and Feng Haoni.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Beijing News. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: PaperBuddy; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Nana comes ashore at Dachangshan Island, Liaoning, Sept. 27, 2026. From Xiaohongshu)

World.title: Carlos Yulo dethroned in world vault final, finishes 7th
World.content:
STRENGTH. Carlos Edriel Yulo of the Philippines in action during the vault final of the 2026 World Artistic Gymnastics Championships in Rotterdam.

Carlos Yulo goes home empty-handed this time from the Artistic Gymnastics World Championships after missing out on the podium in his pet events

MANILA, Philippines – It appears fatigue may have caught up with the Philippines’ gymnastics golden boy Carlos Yulo.

For the second straight final, Carlos Yulo finished off the podium, placing seventh and falling short in his bid to defend his vault crown at the 54th Artistic Gymnastics World Championships in Rotterdam, Netherlands, on Sunday, October 25.

A day earlier, Yulo finished eighth and last in the floor exercise final.

Armenia’s Artur Davtyan claimed vault gold with 14.850 points, dethroning Yulo, who ruled the apparatus in 2021 and 2025.

Yulo scored 13.833 points, with 8.033 in execution and 5.600 in difficulty, while incurring a 0.30 penalty.

However, competing in two international events in just one month proved too much for Yulo.

His World Championships campaign came after Yulo captured gold in both men’s floor exercise and vault at the 2026 Asian Games in Japan.

Joining Davtyan on the podium were Great Britain’s Jake Jarman, who took silver with 14.650 points. Norway’s Sebastian Sponevik secured bronze with 14.366 in the eight-man final.

On Saturday, October 24, Yulo finished eighth in the floor exercise final with 13.233 points, recording 7.633 in execution and 5.800 in difficulty, along with a 0.10 stick bonus and a 0.30 penalty.

Floor exercise and vault are among Yulo’s pet events, having won gold in both apparatus at the 2024 Paris Olympics. – Rappler.com

World.title: 4 ways US foreign policy could change if Democrats win in November
World.content:
A man holds a 'Vote Blue' sign while sitting in a golf cart during a Democratic rally in The Villages, Florida, US, October 17, 2026.

Here are some ways a Democratic Congress could hem in Trump's foreign policy

WASHINGTON, USA – Nonpartisan analysts say Democrats stand a good chance of winning the US House of Representatives and possibly the Senate in the November 3 midterm elections, which would give them a slice of power in Washington after two years of Republican control.

Democrats argue that Republicans have allowed President Donald Trump‘s administration to declare war and control spending, even though the US Constitution reserves those powers for lawmakers.

Here are some ways a Democratic Congress could hem in Trump’s foreign policy.

Curb the Iran war

Trump did not secure approval from Congress before he launched the war with Iran on February 28, and Democrats have voted repeatedly to end the fighting unless he does so. One of these resolutions passed with support from a handful of Republicans, but Trump’s administration ignored it.

With control of the House or the Senate, Democrats could cut defense spending to pressure Trump to obtain permission from Congress to continue the war. They could also require administration officials to testify publicly about their plans.

Fresh support for Ukraine

Trump has largely halted direct US financial and military aid to Ukraine, despite broad support from Democratic and Republican lawmakers as it fights a Russian invasion.

Most recently, he has angered members of Congress, including many Republicans, by lifting sanctions on Russian diesel and waiving sanctions on Russian energy only weeks after signing them into law.

With a victory in both chambers in November, Democrats would be able to decide what gets voted on and when.

That could allow them to approve new aid to Ukraine, which likely would pass with the two-thirds majorities needed to overcome a Trump veto.

They could also target other Trump activities. For example, Representative Gregory Meeks of New York, who could head the House Foreign Affairs Committee if Democrats win control, has introduced bipartisan legislation to block Trump’s plan to bring Russian diesel back into the global market.

End military aid to Israel

Support for Israel has plummeted among Democrats over its conduct in the Gaza war, which has killed tens of thousands of Palestinian civilians. The ongoing violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s close alliance with Republicans have also been factors.

Democrats could limit or end military aid to Israel, which amounted to $3.8 billion in the most recent fiscal year. That is more than was provided to any other country.

Nearly half of House Democrats voted this summer to ‌cut off aid to Israel. Some of those who voted against that effort, such as Meeks, have backed limits on providing weapons like heavy bombs to Israel.

Limit military spending and restore foreign aid

Democrats are far more likely than Trump’s Republicans to limit military spending. Trump asked for an unprecedented 67% increase in the military budget this year, to $1.5 trillion, but Democrats blocked it in the Senate, citing his refusal to consult Congress about the Iran war and his steep cuts to social programs.

Trump has also withheld or canceled billions of dollars in foreign aid approved by Congress. Many Democrats have been angered by the cuts and say they will try to restore funding.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Teodoro warns PMA of ‘weaponization of information’ as warfare moves beyond battlefield
World.content:
DEFENSE CHIEF. Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. joins Philippine Military Academy officials, cadets, alumni, and guests during the Academy’s 128th Foundation Anniversary celebration at Fort del Pilar on October 24, 2026.

The Philippine defense chief says technological advances, geopolitical developments, disruptions to supply chains, and other changes can emerge quickly and carry consequences for the security of states and individuals

BAGUIO CITY, Philippines – Wars are no longer fought only with guns, ships, and aircraft. Information itself can be weaponized, and future military leaders must know how to deal with it.

Defense Secretary Gilberto “Gibo” Teodoro Jr. raised that warning during the Philippine Military Academy’s 128th Foundation Anniversary on Saturday, October 24, pointing to the “pervasive weaponization of information” as one of the security challenges that military institutions can no longer afford to treat as secondary.

Teodoro said technological advances, geopolitical developments, disruptions to supply chains, and other changes can emerge quickly and carry consequences for the security of states and individuals.

Some of these changes, he said, are not even the result of carefully planned government action but may come from technological breakthroughs or decisions by major global players that force everyone else to adjust.

The military, he said, must be able not only to respond but also to build leaders capable of managing organizations through that uncertainty.

For the Philippines, Teodoro said, that means strengthening the institutions needed to protect “our most sacred sovereignty, territorial integrity, and dignity as a Filipino people.”

Teodoro is among the most vocal in the Philippine government over China’s actions against the Philippines in the West Philippine Sea, enough for China to bar him from entering the country as well as from engaging in “any transaction, cooperation or other activities” with organizations or individuals in China.

‘Tall order’

Teodoro said the changing security environment also affects what PMA is expected to produce.

“We have to produce in this academy war fighters, make no bones about it. Every graduate of this institution is a war fighter,” he said.

He was quick to explain that he was not referring only to soldiers engaged in combat. “War fighting is not confined to combat operations and kinetic operations. War fighting spans the whole gamut of activities that will preserve the national objectives of any state,” he said.

That includes intelligence, analysis, logistics, personnel support, and the people who keep operations going behind the front line.

“Every person in uniform is a war fighter. Every member of the civilian human resource team of the Department of National Defense and the Armed Forces of the Philippines is a war fighter,” he said.

For PMA, this means doing two difficult jobs within the cadets’ four years at Fort del Pilar.

The academy must give them an education that can meet Philippine standards and stand alongside peer institutions in countries the Philippines works with. At the same time, it must produce junior officers ready to serve in the Armed Forces and, beginning three years from now, the Philippine Coast Guard.

Those graduates, Teodoro said, must leave with the proper military ethics, duties, responsibilities, and basic tactical skills required of their respective services.

“That is a tall order,” he said.

‘Today is not fast enough’

Teodoro also had a message for defense planners: Think bigger. Move faster.

“The Philippines cannot afford to be conservative in its planning,” he said.

If the country plans cautiously while similarly situated states are more ambitious, he said, the Philippines risks falling behind. That is particularly dangerous when sovereignty and national security are involved.

“Ambitious plans needed to have been laid down on the ground years ago,” Teodoro said. “But we cannot recoup the past. We can only make the present faster.”

Then came one of his sharpest lines: “And today is not fast enough. Tomorrow is certainly unacceptable.”

Teodoro said he had extensive discussions with PMA Superintendent Lieutenant General Michael Logico on the academy’s growth plans, infrastructure, curriculum, Corps of Professors, and the future design of the Cadet Corps, building on goals left by former superintendent Vice Admiral Caesar Bernard Valencia.

Education is not the same as training

Teodoro also questioned a habit he said he has seen in AFP education and training systems.

“Education is for knowledge. Training is for skills,” he said.

The two, he argued, should not simply be fused together. “Without knowledge, you cannot form skills. You cannot train skills.”

Military officers need a continuing and current body of knowledge across different fields, he said, because conflict has become increasingly multidisciplinary, unpredictable, and difficult to structure neatly.

That knowledge can then be translated into skills.

Teodoro also took issue with educational opportunities being awarded without sufficient regard for merit, particularly in advanced study and research.

“The opportunity for acquiring knowledge should be democratic,” he said.

Once that opportunity has been made available fairly, however, he said “individual merit and excellence” should determine educational qualification.

PMA cannot stay inside Fort Del Pilar

Teodoro also challenged the idea that PMA education and training should remain confined to its Baguio home.

“Fort Del Pilar houses the Philippine Military Academy. But the Philippine Military Academy should not be solely in Fort Del Pilar,” he said.

The Philippines has too many different operating environments, he said, for future officers to depend on a single training venue.

He linked this to the government’s push to secure military reservations for AFP use and to address infrastructure gaps that have affected operations, particularly in the maritime domain, as well as logistics, internal security, external defense, and disaster response.

Teodoro said the Armed Forces must be ready to enforce Philippine laws across the country’s vast maritime domain and deal with state actors that may not always follow international law.

That, he said, is why the defense establishment cannot afford timid planning.

The task for PMA is no longer simply to teach cadets how to fight the wars previous generations knew. It is to give them enough knowledge, skill, and judgment to understand what the next threat looks like, especially when it may arrive not as a bullet, but as information. – Rappler.com

World.title: Disenchanted Netanyahu supporters are prize of Israel election campaign
World.content:
CAMPAIGN. A person uses a smartphone next to a campaign van for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's Likud party at Hatikva market during Netanyahu's visit, ahead of Israel's national election, in Tel Aviv, Israel, October 22, 2026.

Some 13% of Israeli voters have yet to decide how they will vote, according to data collected by the Viterbi Family Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute

DIMONA, Israel – In the remote Negev Desert town of Dimona, long a bastion of Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, disenchanted voters are going door-to-door campaigning for his top rival, hoping to bring down the veteran prime minister in Israel’s election on Tuesday, October 27.

The ballot is Israel’s first since Hamas’ October 7, 2023, surprise attack that shook the country and plunged the region into turmoil, as Israel went to war on the militant group in Gaza and its allies in Lebanon and Iran.

The October 7 security breach saw Likud’s popularity plummet. Opinion polls for months have predicted Netanyahu’s coalition of right-wing, far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties losing its majority. But his top rival, centrist Gadi Eisenkot, has no clear path to power either, and the race has become tighter as the election nears.

Dimona, where an Iranian missile wounded dozens in March, has become a political battleground.

“We must have change. Bibi has to go,” said Yossi Assayag, 74, who says he has supported Likud most his life. “Bibi has brought disaster to Israel.“

Likud loyalists

Assayag is part of a cohort of town residents trying to convince their community to vote for Eisenkot’s party Yashar, which is neck-and-neck with Likud in the polls.

It’s a tough task in Dimona, where half the voters in the previous 2022 election cast a ballot for Likud.

“I will never betray Likud,” said Ruti Ohana, a pensioner, who says she has voted Likud ever since immigrating to Israel from North Africa more than 60 years ago. She said Netanyahu was a cut above his rivals, and the blame he receives from detractors for October 7 was unfair.

Right-wing Likud long ago formed a core voter base among Jews of Middle Eastern and North African descent, known as Mizrahis, who felt neglected by the European-influenced centre-left Labor Party that dominated Israel for generations.

Labor has since dwindled to a rump as Israeli politics have shifted rightwards, and there are now around half a dozen other parties courting Likud voters, from the centre to the far right. But the link to the party among its past supporters remains strong.

“Most people here vote for Likud just because that’s how they were raised,” said Oria Asaf, 25, a past Likud voter now backing Yashar. “The change will come when people start to think about their children’s future rather than their parents’ past.”

Battle for wavering Likudnics

While Netanyahu has a hard core of supporters that can’t be won over, the prize is undecided voters who “understand that we are in a state of crisis” and are open to persuasion, said Michal Elmalem Abu, elected as a member of the city council from Likud and now leading Eisenkot’s Dimona campaign.

Some 13% of Israeli voters have yet to decide how they will vote, according to data collected by the Viterbi Family Center for Public Opinion and Policy Research at the Israel Democracy Institute.

Of those who voted for Likud in 2022, just 55% now say they will vote for the party again on Tuesday. Fifteen percent will support parties aligned against Netanyahu, including 8% for Yashar. Another 14% will vote for alternative right-wing parties, and 9% are undecided.

It is in places just like Dimona where Eisenkot stands a chance to bite a chunk out of Likud’s base, said Amotz Asa-El, a political scientist at the Hartman Institute.

A child of Moroccan immigrants who rose through the ranks to become military chief of staff, Eisenkot, 66, has a personal story of humble origins from the Mizrahi community that “appeals to a big swath of the Israeli electorate, particularly Likud’s traditional electorate,” said Asa-El.

In an electoral field crowded with ex-soldiers, his peerless security credentials are an asset. The loss of his son, killed in combat in Gaza in December 2023, resonates with voters.

At a town hall during a visit to Dimona in July, residents said they were excited about the prospect of a leader of Mizrahi descent. Others approached him with hugs and tearful condolences for the loss of his son.

But a week later Netanyahu held his own event, demonstrating his powerful appeal in the hardscrabble Negev, where Likud governments have long boasted of bringing development funds.

“Look around you, look at your community, look at what was here then and what is here now, and ask yourselves which governments invested in this monumental effort. And I do this out of immense love,” he said.

Lior Katzav, a Likud former mayor of Kiryat Malachi, another small-town stronghold, said party surveys show voters who had abandoned Likud are returning as the election nears.

But even some who are sympathetic to Netanyahu say it may be time for a change. Israel’s youngest prime minister when he was first elected 30 years ago, he has since become its longest-serving, now 77, having governed for 18 years over six terms.

“It’s time for him to go,” said Dimona software engineer David Iskali. “He’s done a lot for Israel but it can’t go on. I won’t give my vote to someone almost 80-years-old.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Brazil heads to polls in runoff between leftist Lula and Bolsonaro Jr.
World.content:
ELECTION CAMPAIGN. Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate seeking re-election, waves a flag during a closing campaign rally ahead of the presidential runoff, in Sao Paulo, Brazil, October 24, 2026.

Polls show the candidates are practically tied going into the runoff, as Lula has closed the gap in the final days

SAO PAULO, Brazil – Brazilians head to the polls on Sunday, October 25, in a tight runoff vote that could shift Latin America’s largest nation sharply rightward, bringing it closer to the United States as part of a broader conservative shift across the region.

The runoff pits leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former President Jair Bolsonaro. Flavio scored a major upset at the start of the month by defying pollsters to lead voting in the first round.

A victory for Bolsonaro, 45, would extend a wave of right-wing victories for Latin American candidates friendly to US President Donald Trump, while a fourth mandate for Lula would be a disappointment in Washington, which has clashed with his government over trade and security.

The election race has been dominated by corruption scandals, economic anxiety, and accusations of US meddling, which Washington denies. It has also been colored by fallout from Jair Bolsonaro’s 2025 conviction for plotting a 2022 coup, with Flavio pledging to free his father if he is elected.

Trump has called the case a “witch hunt” and imposed a 50% tariff on Brazil in 2025, in a decision explicitly linked to Jair Bolsonaro’s trial. While many of those were later watered down, Trump unleashed new levies against Brazil this year, citing unfair trade practices.

Lula has cast the Trump administration’s proximity to the Bolsonaro clan as part of an attempt to sway the election, while labeling tariffs and other punitive measures as bullying.

On economic issues, despite falling inequality, and unemployment, Lula has struggled to win over an electorate grappling with high living costs and heavy household debt. Endemic gang violence also weighs on voters’ minds.

Bolsonaro has sought to capitalize on cost-of-living concerns and has also promised a heavy-handed approach to fighting crime, pledging maximum-security jails and chemical castration for serious sexual offenses.

Polls show the candidates are practically tied going into the runoff, as Lula has closed the gap in the final days.

Historical precedent favors Bolsonaro, however, as no candidate has ever won the presidency after coming second in the first-round vote.

Bolsonaro picked up 47% of ballots cast in the first round, while Lula trailed with 45%.

The senator’s first-round win sent Brazil’s markets and currency soaring on expectations of pro-business reforms.

His first-round success was mirrored in congressional elections for his Liberal Party and other right-wing politicians, which could pave a legislative path for him, or complicate governance for Lula. – Rappler.com

World.title: What schools will do amid intense heat during El Niño
World.content:
HYDRATION. A student at Rafael Palma Elementary School in Manila drinks from her tumbler on October 8, 2026.

How prepared is the Department of Education for the potential effects of El Niño?

MANILA, Philippines – The education sector will not be spared when El Niño worsens in the coming months. Across the country, temperatures are expected to be warmer than usual, which would pose another threat to students’ learning.

Education Secretary Sonny Angara previously said government protocols would ensure that El Niño’s effects are mitigated in public schools.

How exactly is the Department of Education (DepEd) preparing for the impact of the weather phenomenon? Pending formal guidelines, here’s what we know so far:

How to conduct classes

In an interview with Rappler on Friday, October 23, Education Undersecretary Malcolm Garma said the DepEd is concerned that lost school days may increase due to high heat index levels. The heat index, or the temperature that the human body perceives, is measured using the air temperature and the relative humidity in a place at a given time.

Garma noted that the DepEd’s existing class suspension guidelines, issued back in June, already spell out learning continuity plans for schools.

The DepEd said that under Level 1-Hayo, face-to-face classes continue during manageable conditions. Schools can set scheduled water breaks, shift outdoor activities to early morning or shaded areas, and allow students to wear comfortable clothing or Physical Education attire.

At Level 2-Hinay, schools may adopt modified class days with structured home-based or hybrid learning.

Level 3-Hinga may be implemented when temperatures can cause heat cramps or heat exhaustion or there is loss of water supply. Learning packets, short activities, and broadcast resources may be used to reduce academic demands.

Once the heat index reaches 42°C and above, academic activities are suspended at Level 4-Hinto, focusing on safety checks and psychosocial support referrals, according to the class suspension guidelines.

Garma said self-learning modules, activity sheets, and other materials needed for alternative learning will be prepositioned before the peak months of intense heat.

What if the heat is unbearable?

In case actual conditions turn out to be worse than projected, Garma said school heads can adjust class schedules or recommend granular suspensions of face-to-face classes. But he added that the situation must be properly assessed.

“Hindi naman ‘yung school head ay basta-basta na lang siyang magpapauwi o magsu-suspend. So kailangan mai-vet ito ng [schools] division office…or [they should] even coordinate with the local government unit. Para sa gano’n, talagang hindi naman maabuso din ‘yung pagsususpende ng klase,” the DepEd official said.

(The school head cannot just decide to send students home or suspend classes. This must be vetted by the schools division office or they should even coordinate with the local government unit. This is to prevent abuse of class suspensions.)

“While we are looking after…the welfare of our learners, we also have to ensure that learning continues. At alam naman natin na pinakamainam pa din na learning delivery natin ay kung school-based ito or face-to-face (And we know that the best learning delivery is school-based or face-to-face),” he added.

Measures for water supply, health

Garma said the DepEd has ordered schools to make hydration facilities and equipment, such as safe drinking stations and water dispensers, accessible to learners and personnel.

The DepEd also told schools to repair water leaks immediately and coordinate closely with local water concessionaires for rationing contingencies.

Social Welfare Secretary Rex Gatchalian earlier raised the possibility of deploying community water depots to public schools. These depots are rainwater catchment equipment with built-in filtration systems to provide potable water during shortages. Garma said the DepEd welcomes such proposals.

Regarding health, Garma said school clinics will be ready to address medical concerns like heat stroke or dehydration. Additional support from local government units (LGUs) and the Department of Health will also be tapped for emergency response.

With El Niño also threatening agriculture and food supply, schools division offices and schools were directed to develop contingency menus for the school-based feeding program, partner with LGUs and cooperatives for local food sourcing, and maintain buffer stocks of shelf-stable commodities.

How about school buildings?

Garma said public schools can use their funding for maintenance and other operating expenses to buy additional ventilators like electric fans.

But the DepEd’s long-term solution is structural intervention.

“For old classrooms, we cannot change their designs; we can only do mitigation. But for those classrooms under construction and for future ones, we’ll make sure that there will be structural intervention such as high ceilings, insulated ceilings, and wide airflow,” he said in Filipino.

Garma also said the DepEd is exploring the possibility of institutionalizing the use of solar power in schools to reduce electricity costs and possibly provide air-conditioning.

The DepEd said its upcoming formal guidelines for El Niño-related measures will mandate schools to conduct integrated school-level risk assessments covering water supply reliability, classroom thermal safety, electricity resilience, and fire hazard prevention.

The set of guidelines is also expected to prohibit schools from charging or requiring parents to buy cooling equipment, connectivity, or specialized attire as a condition for alternative learning modalities. – Rappler.com

World.title: Malversation, graft charges filed vs 2 ex-DPWH execs over GenSan right-of-way scam
World.content:
The Office of the Ombudsman in Quezon City on March 6, 2026.

The Office of the Ombudsman files charges against former DPWH Region 12 regional director Subair Saro Diron, former assistant regional director Laureano Suan Jr., and several other DPWH personnel and private individuals

MANILA, Philippines – The Office of the Ombudsman has filed malversation and graft cases against two former Department of Public Works and Highways officials, four DPWH personnel, and seven private individuals over their alleged involvement in a road right-of-way scam in General Santos City.

The Office of the Ombudsman said in a press statement on Sunday, October 25, that it “found prima facie evidence with reasonable certainty of conviction” against former DPWH Region 12 regional director Subair Saro Diron, former assistant regional director Laureano B. Suan Jr., and DPWH personnel Tomas Marquez Rodriguez, David Lucena Padlan, Paisal Amerol Padate, and Ansare Mariga Busran.

The Ombudsman also included seven private individuals in the cases filed before the anti-graft court Sandiganbayan: Wilma Mamburam, Nelson Ti, Evelyn Paloso, Rudy Hadji Ong, Marisa Seguirre, William Uy, Paul Michael Bagio.

“The Ombudsman filed 18 informations for Malversation of Public Funds or Property through Falsification of Public Documents under Article 217 in relation to Article 171 of the Revised Penal Code, and another 18 informations for violation of Section 3(e) of Republic Act No. 3019, or the Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act,” the Office of the Ombudsman said.

In 2018 and 2019, the National Bureau of Investigation submitted three investigation reports to the Ombudsman in relation to the DPWH Region 12 payment for right-of-way for 18 parcels of land allegedly affected by the construction of the Digos-Makar National Road in Lagao, General Santos City.

The witness, Roberto Catapang Jr., had admitted in his 2017 affidavit that he was involved in a syndicate that was allegedly “in collusion with respondent public officers, collected money from the government purportedly as payments for the acquisitions, by fabricating and submitting fake documents.”

Investigators found that the claimants, which were paid a total of P491,931,120.20, had presented falsified documents. The DPWH Region XII technical working group had approved the disbursement of the amount to the claimants.

“Investigators also uncovered the alleged unlawful use of a 2009 appraisal value of P3,500 per square meter to determine compensation for properties taken by the government in the early 1990s, resulting in inflated right-of-way claims,” the Office of the Ombudsman said.

The press statement also said that in a separate administrative decision, the Ombudsman ordered the dismissal from service of former DPWH Region 12 legal officer Ansare Mariga Busran. – Rappler.com

World.title: Before the Philippines even had a name, it had gold
World.content:
“When you look at this gold jewelry, you realize that once upon a time we had a golden age. It gives you a sense of what was pre-colonial culture,” historian Ambeth Ocampo tells Rappler

Gold is a patient metal. It does not rust or decay. It can be melted, worn, used, and reused from one generation to another, surviving long after the hands that first fashioned it have turned to dust.

And more than a thousand years ago, long before these islands were called the Philippines, our ancestors were already working gold into exquisite ornaments, delicate chains, and elaborate vessels. Some of these treasures have survived to the present day; in them, we see a glimpse of a civilization nearly forgotten.

Their rediscovery was a golden accident.

On a sunny April day in 1981, Edilberto “Mang Berto” Morales was operating heavy machinery for a government irrigation project in Surigao del Sur. Something glistened in the mud.

What he mistook for a helmet turned out to be a partly crushed gold bowl. Suspecting more, he shooed away his coworker and searched alone, combing some 300 feet of earth until late afternoon.

By day’s end, he had recovered around 22 pounds of ancient gold, including an extraordinary necklace he called kuwintas ni nanay (mother’s necklace.) He hid the long chain around his waist, beneath his shirt, away from curious eyes.

Now in the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP) collection, it consists of 12 individual kamagi necklaces joined end to end, their intricate links resembling one woven cord.

Photo from the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas

But the treasure began to scatter almost as soon as it emerged. Treasure hunters recovered more gold, dispersing objects among collectors and separating pieces of the same ornament.

Then-central bank governor Jaime Laya and collectors Leandro and Cecilia Locsin helped preserve significant portions, which entered the collections of the BSP and Ayala Museum.

Bahandi sa Atong Kagahapon

Florina Capistrano-Baker, the scholar behind the newly launched book Bahandi, calls the two collections as “twins separated at birth.”

“They preserve different parts of a shared history and even different parts of what was once one object,” she said on Thursday, October 22, during the book’s launch at the BSP.

In 2024, selected pieces were reunited at Ayala Museum, where the exhibition is scheduled to run until 2027.

And what a magnificent history they reveal. Ancient goldsmiths mastered techniques involving minute golden beads, delicate filigree, and interlocking chains so precise that the finished jewelry could resemble cloth.

“Even today, they cannot [recreate] some of it,” historian Ambeth Ocampo told Rappler in an exclusive interview, saying that ancient Filipinos possessed such a sophisticated understanding of gold that they even had distinct terms for its purity, including 24-carat and 20-carat gold.

Gold also proclaimed status. The wealthy could wear numerous chains around their necks, with some ornaments so heavy that their wearers were said to stoop beneath their weight, BSP Deputy Governor Bernadette Romulo-Puyat recounted in a separate interview with Rappler.

Yet these were more than displays of extravagance.

PAST. Florina Capistrano-Baker tells the crowd about the treasures that help us understand what a pre-colonial Philippines was like. Photo by Lance Spencer Yu/Rappler

“These are not just splendid ornaments. They’re evidence of social stratification, craft specialization, technical knowledge, and affluent individuals who had the means to commission these luxury goods,” Capistrano-Baker explained.

The treasure also points toward ancient Butuan, whose communities traded across the seas long before Spanish colonization. Their surviving goldwork bears influences shared with Java and other parts of South and Southeast Asia, suggesting a world of exchange far richer than conventional colonial histories might suggest.

For Ocampo, the gold offers a rich rebuttal for Filipinos raised on histories that often begin with the arrival of foreigners.

“When you look at this gold jewelry, you realize that once upon a time we had a golden age,” he told Rappler. “So it gives you a sense of pride, gives you a sense of what was pre-colonial culture.”

At the launch of Bahandi, BSP Governor Eli Remolona likened the generations who made, discovered, and preserved the treasure to links in a kamagi.

“May future generations find their place in the chain and ensure it never breaks,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: China Taps Myanmar’s Rare Earth Surge, Coffee Sell-Off, and More
World.content:
China’s rare earth imports swelled by Myanmar supply

China’s rare earth imports surged to 5,021 tons in September, up 23 percent from August, according to data from the Shanghai Metals Market.

Shipments of rare earth oxides from Myanmar accounted for 70 percent of the total, while arrivals from Laos fell to 1,369 tons. Together, Myanmar and Laos accounted for 97 percent of total imports. Cumulative imports for January–September reached 46,466 tons, up 14 percent year‑on‑year.

Rare earth mines along Myanmar’s northeastern border with China supply roughly half the world’s heavy rare earths, including strategically scarce dysprosium and terbium used in magnets crucial to China’s high-tech supply chain.

The surge comes as the US reengages with Myanmar’s regime, fueling speculation that global competition for rare earth resources is driving Washington’s policy recalibration. However, almost all of Myanmar’s rare earth mines are located in territory beyond regime control.

Myanmar specialty coffee faces Chinese fire sale

A Chinese fire sale beckons for Myanmar’s once-booming specialty coffee market. Once backed by USAID and American buyers, the coffee industry collapsed after the 2021 coup as Shan farmers responsible for some of the world’s finest beans were deprived of access to Western markets, transparent trade and certification. With the lucrative export path blocked, the regime and its Myanmar Coffee Association (MCA) are now aggressively pivoting to China.

MCA chairman Myo Aye told Xinhua that cooperation with Yunnan has deepened since the military takeover, with new MoUs locking in China as the top destination for Myanmar’s 3,000–4,000 tonnes of annual exports—tumbling from pre-coup levels of more than 5,000 tonnes. He said the association is looking to attract Chinese investment in value-added processing facilities, roasting plants and supply-chain logistics.

Myanmar’s coffee basket of Shan State has been ravaged by some of the fiercest fighting triggered by the 2021 coup.

Agriculture supplants industry at Myanmar-China forum

The Seventh Myanmar–China Think Tank Forum kicked off in Mangshi, Yunnan Province on Wednesday, with agricultural cooperation placed firmly at the center of discussions. Launched in 2017, the annual forum takes a different theme each year, but its underlying focus has consistently been the now stalled China–Myanmar Economic Corridor, a project designed to give Beijing direct access to the Indian Ocean.

This year’s session saw Myanmar regime officials highlight opportunities in rice and coffee. Yunnan is a major buyer of both. They urged deeper cooperation to expand exports, boost trade and investment, develop value‑added products, and facilitate technology exchange.

The forum comes as regime leader Min Aung Hlaing promotes agriculture as the key sector to revive an economy devastated by his coup and international sanctions. He has emphasized rice, cotton, oilseed crops, pulses, and rubber as priority industries to drive growth.

Earlier this month, Myanmar’s Pawsan variety won global recognition at the World Rice Conference 2026. At the 23rd China–ASEAN Expo in Nanning last month, three Myanmar rice exporters signed five MoUs with Chinese companies. According to the Myanmar Rice Federation, Myanmar earned US$ 338 million from rice exports in the first half of FY2026–27, which began in April.

Travel alert over Myanmar scams sparks Thai pushback

The Chinese Embassy in Bangkok issued a safety advisory on Oct. 16 warning its citizens of trafficking risks linked to scam compounds along the Thai–Myanmar border, prompting a scrambled response from Thailand’s foreign and tourism ministers.

The advisory cautioned Chinese nationals to be on alert for kidnapping and trafficking schemes disguised as high‑paying job offers, fraudulent investment projects, and bogus filming contracts targeting livestreamers and entertainers. It urged travelers to verify overseas employment opportunities, avoid suspicious transport arrangements, and steer clear of high‑risk areas on the Thai-Myanmar frontier where criminal networks remain active despite official crackdowns.

The warning followed recent cases that rattled public opinion in China, including the abduction of a shopping livestreamer who was lured by a bogus contract to Thailand before being trafficked to Myanmar last month. The high‑profile kidnapping of soap actor Wang Xing in Myawaddy in 2025 had already triggered a trilateral crackdown by China, Thailand, and Myanmar.

Following the latest advisory, a Chinese actress cancelled a fan meeting in Bangkok, underscoring the potential impact on Thailand’s tourism sector.

Thai Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow responded by urging the embassy to ensure its warnings are proportionate to the situation and avoid sparking unnecessary alarm. He stressed that Thailand takes visitor safety seriously and will investigate incidents, but cautioned that exaggerated advisories risk undermining confidence in Thailand as a safe destination. Chinese nationals are Thailand’s largest tourism market.

Naypyitaw eyes tourism lifeline in Kunming

Even as reports of trafficking and scam compounds along the Thai–Myanmar border dominate headlines in China, Myanmar’s regime is pressing ahead with plans to lure Chinese visitors back to Myanmar to revive a tourism industry shattered by the 2021 coup.

The regime’s Hotels and Tourism Ministry has announced it will open a tourism promotion office in Kunming, Yunnan Province. At the China–Myanmar cultural tourism exchange meeting held in Kunming from October 13–17, Tourism Ministry Secretary Maung Maung Kyaw described the proposed office as a potential “major corridor” for public‑private cooperation between the regime and Chinese tour companies. A business‑to‑business memorandum of understanding was also signed between Chinese and Myanmar tour operators.

Chinese travelers remain Myanmar’s largest foreign tourism market, but numbers have collapsed since the coup. Just over 250,000 Chinese arrivals were recorded last year—a fraction of the pre‑coup boom—despite having access to visas on arrival. In 2019, Myanmar saw 749,719 Chinese arrivals out of a total 4.4 million tourists.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Rare Earth Exports Surge Amid Illusion of Regime Control
World.content:
China’s rare earth imports rose sharply in September to 5,021 tons, up 23 percent from August, according to data from the Shanghai Metals Market.

Shipments from Myanmar accounted for 70 percent of the total, while arrivals from Laos fell to 1,369 tons. Cumulative imports for January–September were up 14 percent year‑on‑year.

Meanwhile, recent U.S. reengagement with Naypyitaw has fueled speculation that rare earth competition is driving Washington’s policy recalibration.

Regime supporters are now boasting that the embattled junta has a “rare earth card” to play in its bid for international recognition, pointing to parallel interest from India.

Yet, although Myanmar is home to around 600 rare earth mines primarily feeding China’s supply chain, almost all of them lie beyond the regime’s territorial control.

Why are rare earths important?

Rare earth elements (REEs) are indispensable for high‑tech industries, serving as raw materials for magnets in electric vehicles, wind turbines, smartphones, and defense systems.

China dominates global mining and refining, producing nearly 70 percent of rare earth oxides and controlling more than 85 percent of refining capacity. Yet its domestic deposits are dominated by light REEs, leaving it reliant on Myanmar’s northern mining belt. Myanmar produces roughly half the world’s heavy rare earths (HREEs), including strategically scarce dysprosium and terbium used in powerful magnets crucial to China’s AI ambitions.

Kachin State’s riches

Kachin State, which borders China and India, hosts nearly 80 percent of over 600 rare earth mines identified by satellite imagery across northern Myanmar, with the highest concentration clustered in Chipwi and Momauk. These two townships alone contain over 370 active mining sites featuring more than 2,700 active leaching pits, according to data from the Stimson Center and Institute for Strategy and Policy-Myanmar.

Before late 2024, Kachin’s rare earth mining hubs were controlled by the New Democratic Army–Kachin (NDA-K), a junta-aligned militia turned Border Guard Force (BGF) led by warlord Zakhung Ting Ying. Under NDA-K control, rare earth extraction expanded with virtually no environmental oversight, generating tens of millions of dollars in informal taxes and dividends shared between militia leaders and top generals in Naypyitaw.

Their control collapsed in October 2024 when the Kachin Independence Army (KIA) launched a major territorial offensive. The KIA routed NDA-K forces and seized the mines in Chipwi and Pangwa, with victory placing Myanmar’s primary HREE extraction infrastructure under the direct administrative control of an armed group actively fighting the military regime.

Shan State: the new player

While Kachin State remains Myanmar’s rare-earth hub, mining in Shan State has expanded 48 percent on average over the past five years, outpacing Kachin’s 15 percent. Nearly 90 rare earth mines have been detected in territory controlled by the Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA), United Wa State Army (UWSA), and National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA).

While the UWSA and NDAA have maintained ceasefires with the Myanmar military for nearly four decades and are heavily reliant on China, the TNLA fought the regime after the 2021 coup, seizing territories beyond its self-administered zone. Today, the group operates 12 rare earth mines in Mantong, transporting the extracted minerals to China through Namhkam, opposite Ruili.

The supply chain in Mantong Township involves Chinese and Wa businesses, as well as technical and logistical support from the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army and the UWSA, according to Stimson Center.

Myanmar’s rare earth mining boom is fueled by growing global demand, coupled with China’s tightening of its own environmental regulations in the 2010s. With domestic output restricted, China turned increasingly to Myanmar, where the concentration of mines near the border led to a thriving overland trade.

Between 2017 and 2024, Myanmar supplied at least 60 percent of China’s rare earth imports, peaking at US$1.4 billion in 2023.

Environmental Destruction

Most of Myanmar’s rare earths are extracted in situ through leaching, a process in which acid solutions are poured directly into shallow pits or boreholes to dissolve rare earths from clay deposits. Unlike China, which has tightened environmental rules, Myanmar’s border mines operate with little regulation and no post-mining restoration. Environmentalists have warned of soil destruction and water pollution in Kachin’s Chipwi Township, where untreated wastewater and chemicals from mines flow directly into the N’Mai Kha River, which feeds Myanmar’s main lifeline, the Irrawaddy River.

Geopolitical Overlay

In July 2025, Reuters reported that advisers to President Donald Trump had met with Myanmar intermediaries to explore potential access to the country’s rare earth reserves. While no formal agreements were announced, the outreach underscored how Myanmar’s heavy rare earths have become central to Washington’s strategy to counter Beijing’s dominance in high‑performance magnet manufacturing.

Earlier this month, American officials held talks with Myanmar regime representatives in Tokyo, the second such meeting since mid-September. Analysts point to two factors driving the US thaw: efforts to combat online scam operations run by junta-aligned militias that have defrauded Americans of billions of dollars, and the scramble to secure rare earth resources.

India has also joined the race for Myanmar rare earths as global supply chain competition heats up. In July, Ambassador Abhay Thakur outlined growing bilateral collaboration during a mining forum hosted by the Indian Embassy in Mandalay, where officials from both sides discussed joint ventures and investment opportunities. The talks reflected New Delhi’s growing interest in Myanmar’s mineral deposits as part of its broader “Act East” strategy and its push to divert supply chains away from China.

Myanmar military sympathizers argue that rare earths offer a crucial bargaining chip for the isolated and embattled regime. Yet as rare earth competition reshapes foreign policy, global superpowers face a glaring irony in courting the military regime: the junta controls virtually none of the mines.

World.title: A Fitting Conclusion to an Intellectual Life: James C. Scott on the Irrawaddy
World.content:
James C. Scott (2025). In Praise of Floods: The Untamed River and the Life Brings. Yale University Press. 220 pp.

In Praise of Floods, puts the Irrawaddy River itself—not generals, kings, peasants or revolutionaries—at the center of Myanmar’s history, and in doing so establishes principles for how river basins are best understood.

James C. Scott (Shwe Yoe) was one of the most important social scientists of the last 50 years. He began his international career in Burma in 1958 but was unable to return after Ne Win’s 1962 coup until 2012. His affection for Myanmar, however, did not diminish, and he then went back regularly until 2021. He was even known to give lectures in Burmese in the 2010s. He died at the age of 87 in 2024, and In Praise of Floods is his final book.

What Scott is most famous for is descriptions of how farmers resisted exploitation by feudal lords and politicians who sent armies and police to tax them. His research led to provocative books like The Moral Economy of the Peasant, Weapons of the Weak and The Art of Not Being Governed. Their creative tension was always between the cunning of the “weak” peasantries and the simplifications powerful governing elites make to squeeze surpluses from them.

In Praise of Floods is a departure in focusing instead on rivers and floods. Scott believes that they are “alive” in the sense that they are born, develop and shrink across millennia. In the Irrawaddy’s case, it created the fertile plains of central Burma at the end of the last Ice Age 12,500 years ago.

Scott’s point is that rivers emerge at particular times, support different types of life, shift channels and courses, and eventually disappear. He calls this process the river’s “pulse.” For the Irrawaddy, the low-water point is usually in February, and as the rains resume, about eight times as much water flows out of the highlands above Mandalay by September, bursting out of the meandering channels formed in previous years.

For thousands of years, perhaps from 10,000 BCE until about 5000 BCE, this meant that migratory people avoided the floods by annually moving their camps to higher ground. Life came from the rich topsoil the floodwaters laid down across the flat plains stretching from Mandalay, which is only 80 m above sea level, to the Andaman Sea some 1,000 km to the south. Early humans harvested the bounty of the river by fishing, netting birds, hunting game, collecting mussels, and gathering fruit and roots. The flood pulses determined what the people ate, and where they lived and settled.

By about 3000 BCE people began creating new ways to use the temperamental river and sought to bend the Irrawaddy’s surges to their own needs. They started by scattering seeds along the shoreline as the flood waters receded. After tending the crop of grain for a few months they could harvest more food than ever before, but this type of food needed to be processed and stored in granaries, to be eaten while waiting for the next harvest to mature.

This is also when they began managing water flows with weirs, fish traps, drainage canals and dikes, and eventually developed the engineering capacity to flatten fields with animal-drawn plows and other tools needed to harvest paddy rice. Human societies came to see the living river as a tamable resource, whose annual surges could be engineered, so people confidently settled into permanent villages near the rivers. There, the arts, markets, religion, literature, architecture and other human pursuits flourished. By about 2,200 years ago, the Pyu states began to emerge, building permanent cities, markets and worship centers.

And when the river behaved as planned, it was a great thing and populations flourished. But there were new dangers too for people living in fixed villages and cities, because the river pulses did not always rise and fall as humans intended—after all, Scott writes, the river was also alive, and perhaps even had a mind of its own. So when the monsoons arrived late or not at all, there would be a drought. Or when they arrived early and in force, there were floods.

Humans and the rest

A particularly creative touch in Scott’s book is his concluding chapters about non-human life, which includes fish, animals and plants, as well as the ubiquitous Burmese spirits, the Nats. A charismatic character, the Irrawaddy river dolphin organizes the other creatures of the river to comment on the algae, molluscs, worms, larvae, zooplankton and microbes, most of which are ignored by homo sapiens, who is only interested in the river as it applies to human endeavors.

As Scott admits, these chapters fit awkwardly with the overall tone of the book. But surely in his final book he can be given some leeway. He is correct, moreover, that social science needs to acknowledge the spiritual life that is important to the ecology of places like the Irrawaddy valley and delta.

Flooding is a catastrophe for humans, but the “infrastructure” of non-human life, including plants, fish, mammals, birds, and of course the river itself are perhaps more ambivalent, or at least have a different perspective on the river pulses. So, for that matter perhaps do the Nats.

Scott’s emphasis on these spirits reflects stories that his research associates Maung Maung Oo and Naing Tun Lin collected while travelling along the Irrawaddy seeking to understand what locals knew. They travelled from the headwaters of Kachin State through the dry zone of Magwe and Sagaing. The spirits must be placated because they are believed to cause both those disastrous floods and the good fortunes of farmers, fishers and hunters. And then there are the dangers of the surrounding forests, which are also effected by the Nats.

Scott soon segues into more modern descriptions of the Irrawaddy watershed, in which the hydrodynamics of the water surges are highlighted in the context of modern social problems like deforestation, mining, and rebellion. All such activities disturb the ecological balance, and the capacity of humans to manage the Irrawaddy.

Full circle

Scott’s lifetime of creative scholarship is impressive. He started in Burma, studied in Vietnam, went to Malaysia, and ended up studying the economics, politics and psychology of the oppressed, and how highlanders respond to attempts to control them. In Praise of Floods brings this career full circle; he is back in Burma and writing about geography. As he writes in his preface, he planned two more years of field research, following the stories of farmers, river dolphins, spirits and flooding himself, but was prevented by the 2021 coup. His own public activism supporting the Spring Revolution made a return even less likely.

But even without these field data, the book pushes social scientists yet again to consider the perspectives of beings they typically ignore. Scott spent a lifetime searching for what he once called “hidden transcripts“—the voices of people overlooked by rulers and states. In this final book he tries something still more audacious: hidden transcripts of dolphins, spirits, forests, floods and the river itself. It is an appropriately unruly ending to the provocative intellectual life of James C. Scott.

Tony Waters is a professor of sociology at Leuphana University, Germany. His most recent book is The Socio-Political Systems of Highland Burma and the Art of Governance.

World.title: Myanmar Regime Pushes on Four Fronts in Southern Chin State
World.content:
Thousands of regime troops are advancing on four fronts across southern Chin State as they push to seize the gateway to Rakhine State, according to resistance sources.

On Wednesday, the military claimed its forces had secured Hlaingdoke and nearby villages in Kanpetlet Township along the Rakhine border after clearance operations along the Laung She-Hlaingdoke-Kyindwe road.

The regime’s counteroffensive to retake Chin resistance strongholds spans from Magwe Region’s Tilin and Saw townships, across the border into Mindat, Kanpetlet and Kyindwe townships.

Intense clashes have erupted in Magwe’s border villages of Shweaungthar and Kyee as regime forces advance to cut off supply lines to Mindat, according to resistance sources.

“The regime has deployed roughly 3,000 troops across all the fronts,” Yaw Meng, spokesperson for the Chin People’s Army (CPA), told The Irrawaddy.

Regime forces began massing for a southward push five months ago after securing the northern Chin towns of Tonzang, Falam, and Thantlang. The southern Chin campaign launched in May, when around 1,500 troops advanced on Kanpetlet and Mindat from Magwe’s Saw and Kyaukhtu townships respectively, according to the CPA.

“During five months of clashes, resistance forces repelled regime troops and defended the Chin State and its people,” Yaw Meng wrote in an October 20 Facebook post.

He declined to comment on the current battlefield situation in southern Chin, where the regime’s ground offensive is accompanied by indiscriminate airstrikes.

On Sunday, a bomb struck the Paletwa jetty, killing nine civilians including a six-month-old child and injuring four others. A regime airstrike on the same site killed another person the following day, according to the Chin People’s Union, the CPA’s political wing.

World.title: Myanmar Ranks Worst in World for Internet Freedom
World.content:
Myanmar has scored just 9 out of 100 on the Internet Freedom Index for the third consecutive year in 2026, making it the world’s worst environment for internet users as the military regime continues its aggressive crackdown on media freedom and online expression, U.S.-based rights group Freedom House said.

Under the group’s rankings, Myanmar has long been categorized as “Not Free” for internet freedom, but its score dropped significantly from 36 in 2019 to 17 in 2021 after the military staged a coup, and finally to 9 from 2024 onward.

It said the military maintains control over all major service providers to enforce mass censorship, localized shutdowns and digital surveillance.

Following the coup, the Myanmar military regime stepped up suppression of internet freedom and digital rights by enforcing shutdowns, blocking social media and news platforms, and criminalizing virtual private network (VPN) use to crack down on political dissent.

As a result, Myanmar netizens have lost access to information and had their freedom of expression curtailed.

During December-January elections, authorities intensified the blocking of news platforms and the use of anti-censorship tools while arresting individuals for online expression under restrictive new laws.

“This is a very concerning situation,” Thit Nyan, a digital rights analyst from the Myanmar Internet Project, told The Irrawaddy. “This is a life-and-death matter for the public.”

He added that the people of Myanmar, whose lives are seriously affected by conflict, rely heavily on mobile and internet connections for information about airstrikes and to facilitate basic services such as health, education and money transfers.

Myanmar internet users require digital literacy for their own safety, he said.

More than 2,000 netizens have been detained as of September since the 2021 coup for sharing posts or comments criticizing the regime and supporting anti-regime movements, mostly on Facebook, according to Data for Myanmar, a monitoring group.

The regime relies mostly on the Penal Code’s Section 505A outlawing “incitement”, the counter-terrorism law, and the telecommunications law to arrest online critics, including artists and celebrities.

Data for Myanmar said, however, that in 2026 the regime has expanded its scope of action to target individuals who merely express their political views online, rather than just those who are deemed to pose a security threat.

At the same time, experts point out the regime has shut down or restricted mobile and internet networks to control information flow, in an effort to prevent military information from leaking and to conceal its human rights violations.

A total of 140 out of 358 monitored townships are facing communication shutdowns, according to Athan, a group that focuses on freedom of expression. Most of the affected townships are experiencing fighting between regime and anti-regime groups.

Meanwhile, users require VPNs, whose use the regime has criminalized, to access the most-used social platforms such as Facebook.

“I have to swallow my own feelings and control myself not to share them online,” a Yangon netizen told The Irrawaddy. He said he was using his real name for his social account and was aware of many people in major cities who had been arrested for sharing their views in favor of the anti-regime resistance.

“This is a violation of our rights to express ourselves freely and to live safely,” he said.

World.title: China’s Myanmar Policy—Consistent but Fundamentally Flawed
World.content:
Observers are often baffled by China’s outright support for Myanmar’s criminal military regime in the face of global opprobrium. But Beijing has been remarkably consistent in terms of where it believes its interests lie. During a visit to Naypyitaw in August 2024 that followed the Myanmar military’s unprecedented battlefield defeats in northern Shan, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi outlined what he called Beijing’s “three bottom lines”. Myanmar must not descend into civil strife, drift away from the ASEAN family, or be infiltrated or interfered with by external forces.

The position, in other words, was support for resolving Myanmar crisis within the ASEAN framework, with a warning that escalating civil war, state collapse, or intervention by other countries—especially of course Western countries—would directly harm Chinese interests. Stability comes before everything else.

Military first

China’s Myanmar policy has consistently centered on the Myanmar military. Since the late 1990s, Beijing has treated Myanmar military as the decisive force in stabilizing the country.

After the popular pro-democracy uprising in 1988 toppled the then-regime and the China‑backed Communist Party of Burma collapsed the following year, Myanmar’s military broke with the Western powers. With that, the assistance they had given it under the pretext of a counter‑narcotics campaign came to an end. Facing sanctions, the military turned instead to China and became Beijing’s trusted partner in assuring border security.

Beijing concluded that only the military could hold the country together. Despite its brutality, China viewed it as the sole practical guarantor of the status quo, aligning with Chinese interests and counterbalancing Western hostility.

Strategic energy interests

In 2003–2004, then President Hu Jintao highlighted the risks posed by great‑power competition over the Malacca Strait to China’s energy security. To reduce dependence on that chokepoint, Beijing proposed building oil and gas pipelines across Myanmar into Yunnan. Than Shwe’s regime obliged, and relations improved as a result.

Through these pipelines, China now imports about 22 million tons of crude oil annually—worth roughly US$16 billion—bypassing the Malacca Strait. Beijing’s recognition of Than Shwe as a trusted ally further entrenched its military‑centric policy.

The position today

China continues to prioritize the Myanmar military, treating ethnic armed groups along the border as secondary entities it must keep in check and largely ignoring forces farther afield such as the National Unity Government (NUG), People’s Defense Forces (PDF) and Spring Revolution alliances.

It was only natural, then, that when the military was on the verge of collapse after losing the northern Shan capital of Lashio in 2024, Beijing propped it up rather than let it fall.

To be sure, China’s policy on Myanmar has delivered some success, leading to the junta’s bogus elections and cosmetic transformation into a civilian government, and now ASEAN governments’ re-engagement with Myanmar. Their dealings with the putschist regime are motivated not only by trade, migration, drug trade and online scam concerns, but also by China’s political and economic influence.

It is an entirely pragmatic, interest‑driven diplomacy, prioritizing national interest over moral principles, and of course that is not unique to China. The U.S. is increasingly open about the transactional nature of its own international policies, and ASEAN has been taking note.

Drawbacks

Yet the core problems remain unresolved. The war has not abated. Myanmar is not stable. Min Aung Hlaing’s elections led to worsening airstrikes and intensified military campaigns, mass killings and war crimes.

Unlike the Thein Sein government, the rebranded regime has offered no political reforms of any kind. It rejects inclusive peace, aiming instead to divide resistance forces.

In practice, the regime remains keen on military solutions alone—retaking lost territory with Chinese backing. Since China intervened, hostilities ceased in northern Shan but the regime escalated fighting in the rest of the country, forcibly recruiting 100,000 young people under Conscription Law since 2024 for use as cannon fodder. The resulting brain drain has left the country poorer in human resources than ever.

Two years of heavy Chinese support have only allowed the regime to recapture 21 townships out of more than 100 lost. Over 80 remain under resistance control. And now its gains are slowing dramatically, with rural areas and key routes beyond its control.

China’s goal of stability in Myanmar, in other words, is further out of reach than ever. By trusting the military to deliver it, Beijing has handcuffed itself to failure. Is it too late to change course?

Thet Htar Maung is a political analyst.

World.title: Son of Aung San Suu Kyi Says He Has First Call With Her in 5 Years
World.content:
YANGON—The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi said he spoke Thursday to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.

“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook.

Aung San Suu Kyi is detained at a “designated residence” in the capital, Naypyitaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.

AFP could not immediately reach Aris—who lives in the United Kingdom—and it was not clear how he spoke to his mother, who won the 1991 Nobel Peace Prize for efforts to bring democracy to Myanmar.

However, images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show him standing outside the Myanmar Embassy in London.

“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” Aris wrote.

“But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”

Myanmar’s military held Aung San Suu Kyi in almost total seclusion for five years following the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy.

But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life” of the octogenarian.

On Monday, authorities in Myanmar said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles III, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch.

Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.

Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyitaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.

After ruling Myanmar as military chief for five years, Min Aung Hlaing—who ousted Aung San Suu Kyi in the 2021 coup—was earlier this year installed as civilian president.

Analysts describe the election putting him in elected office as a charade, and say he may be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in a bid to court international legitimacy.

World.title: Japan’s Sasakawa Renews Myanmar Peace Pledge as Regime Battles Arakan Army
World.content:
Yohei Sasakawa, honorary chairman of Japan’s Nippon Foundation, met putschist president Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyitaw on Monday, pledging once again to assist Myanmar’s “internal peace process.”

Sasakawa made a similar promise during his last visit in August. This time, regime media said only that he offered to help strengthen Myanmar’s “human resources,” without elaborating on what that would entail. No details were released on what progress had been made since his earlier pledge to support peace efforts.

Sasakawa’s latest visit comes amid fierce fighting in Rakhine, where the regime is struggling to defend the state capital, Sittwe, from the ethnic Arakan Army (AA)’s attacks. Sasakawa previously mediated a ceasefire between the Myanmar military and the AA in 2021, though fighting resumed in late 2023 after Operation 1027. The regime has since lost 14 of 17 townships in Rakhine.
