World.title: Donald Trump labels Obama 'incompetent' in post rally retaliation
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has retaliated after his Democratic predecessor, Barack Obama delivered scathing criticisms of the incumbent during rallies in Ohio and Michigan.

Mr Trump labelled the former leader "incompetent" during his own rally in Michigan, which came one day after Mr Obama campaigned alongside Democratic Party candidate Abdul El-Sayed in the same state.

"Obama was a grossly incompetent President! He paid off Iran with $Billions, and gave them a road to a Nuclear Weapon." Mr Trump wrote in a post on social media.

The US president also slammed Mr Obama for supporting US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

The back and forth unfolded after both parties campaigned across Michigan and Ohio one day apart. (AFP: Roberto Schmidt)

The hit at Mr El-Sayed comes after Mr Trump and Republican candidate Mike Rogers have repeatedly tried to tie Mr El-Sayed to the Muslim Brotherhood, falsely branding the Democrat a "jihadist."

In the same post on social media, Mr Trump called Mr El-Sayed a "Fake Doctor, who runs what is considered to be the WORST CLINIC IN AMERICA."

"Michigan doesn't want an arrogant, Open Borders, Fake Doctor, Jihadist, whose reputation will only get worse as more information is revealed."

Mr Trump has been telling voters to view the midterm elections as if he were on the ballot, and on Saturday Mr Obama did just that.

Obama unleashes

Ten days out from the November 3 elections that will determine control of the closely divided Congress, Barack Obama took to the campaign trail to accuse the Republican president of corruption.

Mr Obama used Democrat campaign rallies as a stage for criticism of the current President. (Reuters: Evan Vucci)

Mr Obama spared no mercy when it came to criticism surrounding Mr Trump's strategy for Iran, and skewered the gilded aesthetic he has applied to White House renovations.

Taking aim at new renovation projects across the US capital, including the National Mall's Reflecting Pool and the construction of a White House Ballroom.

The decorations added to the Oval Office during Mr Trumps second tenure were also not safe from critique.

"He's got the White House looking like Saddam Hussein opened a Cheesecake Factory," Mr Obama said.

Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in the Oval Office. (Truth Social: Donald Trump)

The former president has retained considerable popularity among the Democratic base, which he is keen to leverage to support his party's candidates.

In both states, Mr Obama blamed the Trump administration for the rising cost of living, one of the top voter concerns.

"The current president chose to make a series of bad decisions," Mr Obama said in Cleveland, Ohio, where he rallied in support of former Democratic senator Sherrod Brown.

"Most importantly, he decided to start an unnecessary war that nobody asked for."

The war on Iran has sent oil prices soaring as Tehran effectively blocked the Strait of Hormuz after being attacked.

"After two years of chaos and cruelty and corruption and incompetence, the likes of which we have not seen in the modern era, you get a chance to say, enough is enough," Mr Obama said.

Why Michigan was a crucial Democrat primary Abdul El-Sayed's victory in the Democrats' Michigan primary race could shape the party's messaging to voters and how it responds to Donald Trump ahead of November's crucial midterms.

Later, in Michigan he campaigned for Abdul El-Sayed, from the party's left wing, who is in a close race with Republican Mike Rogers for the US Senate.

"Imagine the power duo of Abdul and Elissa," Mr Obama said, referring to the incumbent Democratic Senator Elissa Slotkin, who is not up for election this year.

" You got a Muslim man, you got a Jewish woman fighting for you in the United States Senate. That's something, Michigan, you can be proud of. "

Obama says 'don't procrastinate'

The former president also urged voters to cast their ballots as soon as possible since early voting is already open in both states.

"Don't procrastinate, don't equivocate," Mr Obama said.

Polls in Ohio give Democrats a slight lead in both races, but results are expected to be close.

Nationally, polls also suggest that Democrats could regain control of the House of Representatives but face a much more competitive contest for the Senate.

AP/AFP

World.title: Iran says resumption of war with US would not change its mind
World.content:
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says a potential resumption of war with Israel and the United States would not change his country's positions.

The remarks on Sunday came amid mounting US and Israeli threats of renewed attacks on Iran.

US President Donald Trump said on Friday that Washington "may do another little Epic Fury," referring to the US-Israeli campaign on Iran that began on February 28.

Mr Araghchi said a fresh attack would not yield a different outcome.

"Recently, there has been talk of a new war, but I am already thinking about the post-war period. Whether there is war or not, our policies remain the same," Mr Araghchi said during a televised event in Tehran.

" They have already done so twice and have seen the results. If they want to try again, they know they will achieve no different outcome from those of the past. "

A plume of smoke rises after a US strike in Tehran in March. (AP: Vahid Salemi)

An April 8 ceasefire between Iran and the US put an end to the most intense fighting, apart from sporadic exchanges of fire in and around the strategic Strait of Hormuz, a key route for global energy supplies.

These military flare-ups have lulled in recent weeks.

Iran has claimed control over the strait since the outbreak of the war and has regularly targeted vessels that attempt crossing without its authorisation, moves strongly opposed by Washington and countries in the region.

In response, the US has been maintaining a naval counter-blockade on Iranian ports.

In June, Iran agreed with the US to a memorandum of understanding laying out a pathway to a permanent settlement of the conflict, only for the deal to later unravel as each side accused the other of violating it.

Tehran has since called for a return to the accord to end the conflict.

"The current war has changed everything," Mr Araghchi said.

"We must accept that new realities are taking hold. Shipping routes through the Strait of Hormuz will no longer be the same, and the management of the strait will no longer be the same.

"To achieve peace and stability, our region must move towards the complete absence of foreign forces."

Ten ballistic missiles intercepted over Riyadh

The Houthis have warned they could again target Saudi Arabia, with Riyadh's airport "a military target". (Reuters: Mohammed al-Mahdi)

Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia intercepted drones and missiles over its capital Riyadh and southern areas on Sunday, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said, as fighting with the Iran-aligned Houthis persisted.

The conflict has become an increasingly destabilising front in the US-Israeli offensive against Iran, turning US ally Saudi Arabia into a pressure point in the wider war.

On Sunday, Saudi civil defence authorities issued emergency alerts for Riyadh, Abha and Khamis Mushait, before announcing minutes later that the danger had passed.

The coalition said two drones and a ballistic missile were launched towards Riyadh, and a cruise missile towards the southern city of Khamis Mushait.

Travellers were told that the King Khalid International Airport was again operating normally. (AP Photo)

It later said it intercepted 10 ballistic missiles fired towards southern Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis warned they could again target Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, which resumed operations at two terminals on Sunday after a deadly attack earlier this month.

The Houthis said they attacked the airport and Saudi oil facilities on Saturday. Saudi authorities did not comment directly on the Houthi statements.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the airport remained a "military target" and warned all airlines, airport staffers and travellers against using it.

Wires/ABC

World.title: Kangaroos escape with World Cup win after Fiji threatens upset
World.content:
The Kangaroos have locked in their semifinal spot at the Rugby League World Cup, beating Fiji 36-22 after receiving an almighty scare in Brisbane.

Tom Trbojevic's second-half hat-trick helped Australia over the line after the Bati twice took the lead either side of half-time at Lang Park.

Fijian five-eighth Kurt Donoghoe was rightly named player of the match after laying on three tries and dictating terms for much of the game.

"I think we need more from everyone," Kangaroos coach Kevin Walters said after the game.

"We know we can play better but let's give Fiji a lot of credit. At times it seemed like we were getting on top and they pulled themselves back into the game."

Taane Milne's try gave Fiji an early lead. (Getty Images: Bradley Kanaris)

Despite coming into the game as 50-1 outsiders, making three early errors and conceding the first try of the night, Fiji hit back through Semi Valemei and Taane Milne to lead 10-6 after half an hour.

For the second straight game, Kevin Walters's side looked vulnerable in defence and struggled with their last-tackle options, but still led at half-time after some James Tedesco brilliance led to a try for Sam Walker on debut.

But again the Fijians hit back, with Valemei's second retaking the lead for the underdogs just after the break and Solomone Saukuru appearing to extend soon after, only for the bunker to rule a line-ball obstruction.

The Kangaroos immediately went up the other end and Tom Trbojevic dove in for his first of three straight tries to snuff out the Fijian challenge.

Valemei completed his hat-trick late on before Jacob Preston added Australia's sixth shortly before full-time to lock in their semifinal berth, playing a double-header with the similarly undefeated Jillaroos at the Sydney Football Stadium next Sunday.

Fiji will have a chance to push for a surprise final-four spot if it can pull off an upset win over New Zealand next week, which suddenly does not seem so far-fetched.

Look back at all the action in our live blog below.

World.title: Hand-delivered death threat, being spat at among abuse ACT politicians cop
World.content:
A hand-delivered death threat, being spat at and misogynistic abuse are just some of the incidents ACT politicians say they've experienced.

Several members of the ACT Legislative Assembly have spoken out about the abuse they've been subjected to, following the attack on federal independent MP Helen Haines outside her Victorian electorate office on Monday.

It's not yet clear what motivated Brendan Nugent, 43, to allegedly run her down in the incident that led to both her legs being amputated.

But the incident has renewed concerns about the safety of elected representatives across Australia, and highlighted the risks that come with their jobs.

Canberra Liberals MLA and former ACT opposition leader Elizabeth Lee said she has had to contact police twice over "very serious threats" she received.

"I had a death threat that named my daughter and my partner, and it was actually dropped at my front gate, so it came to my house," Ms Lee recalled.

"That was a pretty scary moment, and it does actually question, to me, as a parent especially, whether it's worth it.

"I have got this duty to ensure that I am prosecuting the issues that are really important to the community, but does that come at the cost of safety to my family?"

Elizabeth Lee says threats against her family have left her questioning whether to stay in politics.

The incident came on top of the many sexist and racist comments she has received online over the past decade of representing her community.

"Belittling criticism on a personal level. Criticisms on my weight and my body shape as well, what I'm wearing sometimes," she said.

The mother of two daughters, Ms Lee said she tried to find the balance between ignoring the comments and calling them out to show her girls that such behaviour was unacceptable.

"I try and ignore it on the whole, but at the same time I know that there are people who need to know that it's not okay," she said.

"So, every now and then I will take that and make an example out of it to call it out."

'Disturbing part of the job'

ACT Health Minister Marisa Paterson has also had some "pretty horrible" encounters with constituents.

"Yelling abuse at you, names at you," Ms Paterson said.

" I've been spat at; I've had things like that happen, standing outside the front of the shops and I've had people make violent threats to me face-to-face. "

Marisa Paterson says that while most of her interactions with constituents are positive, some recent encounters have been "pretty horrible". (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie )

Ms Paterson said she enjoyed meeting and greeting Canberrans at local shops and community events, and that "97 per cent of interactions" were "amazing".

But she said the abuse she received, both in person and online, was a "disturbing part of the job" that made her "feel very vulnerable".

"It's predominantly men. In fact, all of my examples are men," she said.

" And I don't know … why they feel they can say these things to me and speak to me like that. But that is what happens. It's really disturbing. "

Online, Ms Paterson said the abuse had "ramped up" over the past 18 months "very, very significantly", particularly with misogynistic, violent and hateful comments.

"The online world is a very unhappy place at the moment, I think," she said.

"Aside from having this job and needing to be there, other than that, I would have no part of it.

"It is a pretty awful environment with the online comments."

'Tough being a woman in politics'

For Greens MLA Laura Nuttall, it's her sexuality, gender and appearance that are often targeted on social media.

"You'll get some pretty nasty comments, which are often nothing to do with the debate [of the social media post], and everything to do with your appearance, your political leanings," Ms Nuttall said.

"I have had my sexuality speculated on and then sort of taken through the mud. I've copped a bit of queerphobic abuse, which is never fun.

"It is tough … being a woman in politics, particularly right now."

Laura Nuttall says that while most of her interactions with the public are positive, some encounters have been genuinely frightening. (ABC News)

Ms Nuttall said the comments she received could be demoralising and that she "would be lying" if she said the attack on Ms Haines hadn't scared her.

"I have occasionally … felt the impact of that in my personal life in terms of just a loss of confidence," she said.

"And at times, even though it's momentary, a little bit of loss of faith in humanity, that people could be so mean and so remorseless about it."

'Rage gets clicks'

Independent MLA Thomas Emerson said he had seen his female counterparts cop far more abuse, particularly online, than he and his male colleagues did.

"Some of the men get criticised as well, but I think criticism on the basis of policy or disagreeing is really critical, that's part of our democracy and that's what a good, vibrant democracy looks like," Mr Emerson said.

"We should be able to disagree and disagree respectfully, debate those ideas. But when that flips into just abuse that's got nothing to do with the issue at hand, it is concerning."

Thomas Emerson acknowledges that his female colleagues are having "very different experiences as politicians" to his own. (ABC News: Stuart Carnegie)

He said there was a lot more political leaders could do to lead by example.

"Every time we allow policy disagreement to devolve into denigrating the people we're disagreeing with, we're basically saying to the people we're supposed to be representing, and leading in some ways, that actually this is the right way to conduct yourself," he said.

"So there's some blame there for politicians.

"We know that rage gets clicks and it gets picked up in traditional media, on social media, and that can lead to some pretty perverse incentives for politicians themselves and for people out in that community."

Ms Lee agreed that "we all need to take responsibility as a society".

"Political leaders particularly have a role, but it's anyone who has a public voice including the media and the big companies that obviously are responsible for social media," she said.

"Anyone who has the opportunity and the privilege to be able to shape public discourse and debate has a responsibility."

Laura Nuttall says she wants to continue meeting with Canberra constituents at local shops. (ABC News)

As politicians across the country review their security measures, these ACT MLAs are determined to remain publicly available to constituents as part of a healthy democracy.

"It is absolutely the key part of my job that I love," Ms Paterson said.

"It is my job to be out and about talking to people, listening to people, listening to what their concerns are."

Ms Nuttall agreed that she did not want the pockets of aggression, venom and vitriol to detrimentally impact the way she did her job.

"The whole point of being a representative is to be as accessible as humanly possible," she said.

World.title: Fishermen racing crocs for crabs in Wadeye as new industry emerges
World.content:
Before dawn, the sea farmers are already on the water.

As the fishermen steer their boat along the mangrove-lined banks, they know they must move fast so they can load their catch onto a light plane bound for the Darwin Fish Market by the afternoon.

For Theo Dooling, these waters feel familiar. He has fond memories of catching crabs from mud holes with his family as a child.

Loading

"You can put in a stick and just take the crab out," he says.

Back then, the biggest challenge was avoiding a pinch on the finger.

Now, the sea farmers compete with crocodiles for their bounty. Mr Dooling says the reptiles have crushed five of his crab pots in their jaws, desperately trying to poach the fleshy crustaceans.

In Wadeye, a small mud crab venture has grown into a full commercial operation. (ABC News: James Elton)

As the pots are hauled in, it is easy to see why. Nearly all contain mud crabs, with the biggest weighing two kilograms.

A remote community

Sitting on the west coast of Australia's Top End, Wadeye is one of the NT's most unique Aboriginal communities.

Traditional culture thrives here through music and dance, and both adults and children speak the Aboriginal language Murrinh-patha fluently.

Wadeye's main ceremonial groups performed traditional dances during the 2025 Yidiyi Festival. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Its approximately 2,500 residents are cut off for half the year when the rugged Port Keats Road washes out.

But in recent years, the community has also been one of the NT's most troubled.

Wadeye is one of the largest Aboriginal communities in the Northern Territory. (ABC News: James Elton)

It has made headlines for large-scale street fights involving weapons such as spears and crossbows.

Standard three-bedroom houses have as many as 20 people living in them, and black-market liquor is widely available but cripplingly expensive.

Desmond Longmair says a group torched his car using a Coke bottle filled with petrol in a recent round of fighting. (ABC News: James Elton)

Yet, nearly everyone in town points to the lack of jobs as the biggest problem.

At the 2021 census, only about one in five adults had a job.

The lack of jobs is a major issue for the residents in Wadeye. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

It is against this backdrop that the Thamarrurr Sea Farmers have used Aboriginal coastal licences to grow their modest operation into a larger commercial venture that could change outcomes for the Wadeye community.

The acquisition of a full commercial licence means the fishermen can have up to 60 crab pots in the water, and they have expanded their team from three to nine workers within a year.

On average, they send 35 to 50 kilograms of mud crabs to Darwin each week.

Sea farmer Maurice Bitting with freshly caught crabs. (ABC News: James Elton)

"The people we brought on to the team, they are really very good," says Johnson Katuura, the sea farmers coordinator.

"They're people who have fished all their lives."

Joel Martin, one of the team's youngest members, said the sea farmers had already inspired local schoolkids.

Joel Martin is one of the youngest members of the Thamarrurr Sea Farmers. (ABC News: James Elton)

"We go out to school sometimes, talk to the students, let them know that they're going to have to graduate, then they can find a good job," Mr Martin says.

" We want more young boys to come in so they can have a good life, good job. "

Sustainability a top priority

The NT's largest crab licence holder, the Aboriginal Sea Company, says Wadeye is the only "community-run" commercial fishing operation in the NT.

The operation is getting mentoring and training from Humpty Doo Barramundi, one of Australia's biggest aquaculture players.

The Thamarrurr Sea Farmers have grown to a workforce of nine. (ABC News: James Elton)

Elsewhere in the NT, concerns about mud crab numbers led to a pause on commercial licences so stocks could recover.

It came at a bad time for the sea farmers, who were about to begin commercial operations.

But once they negotiated with authorities, the licences were temporarily converted back to Aboriginal coastal licences, then returned to commercial when the pause ended.

Tracey Leo, the deputy CEO of Thamarrurr Development Corporation, backed the way the sea farmers do business.

Tracey Leo is the deputy CEO of the Thamarrurr Development Corporation. (ABC News: James Elton)

"We fully support sustainable harvest strategies," Ms Leo says.

She says the crew keeps detailed records of where they fish and how many crabs they take, "so that we're not over-harvesting in one … location".

The corporation is also lobbying for the Territory's fishery management zones to be reviewed, arguing that rules designed for more heavily fished areas don't necessarily make sense in the relatively "un-fished" waters around Wadeye.

Mr Katuura says the industry's sustainability is the top priority.

Johnson Katuura hopes the commercial operation will be sustainable and long-lasting. (ABC News: James Elton)

"We want it to be long-living," he says.

" We are focused on making a stronger foundation [rather] than rushing to numbers. And I believe that will be the game changer. "

Slow and steady investment

Ms Leo previously worked with Humpty Doo Barramundi and helped establish a two-way training relationship between the operators.

She believes a fully-fledged seafood industry could emerge in Wadeye within a decade, employing about 100 people across mud crabs, a black-lip oyster farm, and some other fisheries.

The black-lip oysters are yet to reach commercial production. (ABC News: James Elton)

"When we first invested in the Sea Farmers, there was a lot of capital infrastructure required, with a big shed and the boats and crab pots and oyster cages, but that's not going to translate to 100 jobs in a short period of time," Ms Leo says.

"We need government to recognise … those employment outcomes [are] going to take a long time.

"[Humpty Doo] were [running] 14 or 15 years before they were even profitable. And they've been going 30 years or whatever it is now … extremely successful."

The impact of 100 jobs to Wadeye would be significant, boosting family incomes in a town where only about 300 adults are currently employed.

But it's also about the type of work. Ms Leo says most of the existing jobs in Wadeye are "very service-based", staffing places such as the local supermarket or the family centre.

"Client-focused jobs, they don't meet the aspirations of local people … there's a lot of kinship complexities, and you might not be able to serve someone if there's relationships in the kinship system," Ms Leo says.

" Working on Country is what everyone wants to do. "

Mr Katuura says it is important to grow the industry sustainably and carefully.

There are hopes the crabbing operation could go on to provide 100 jobs for the local community. (ABC News: James Elton)

"We talk to the people who run [Humpty Doo] all the time," Mr Katuura tells 7.30.

" They train us. They inspire us. And what they tell us is 'take baby steps'. "

While most of the mud crabs go to the market in Darwin, some are going direct to seafood restaurants. (ABC News: James Elton)

Mr Dooling says working with his hands on his traditional Country has given him peace and purpose.

He also wants customers to know where the mud crabs came from, and that they were caught with pride.

"It makes me feel happy when I go out where my sea Country is," he says.

"I'm not an inlander. I'm a seaman."

World.title: Another Perth beach closed as more whale remains found
World.content:
Whale remains have closed another Perth beach today, as authorities warned of possible shark activity in Sorrento after removing the tail of a carcass found just off the shore.

This is the second whale carcass to wash up on the city's beaches this week, and the third in the past month, raising concerns about a further increase in shark activity just as beaches are about to become more crowded ahead of summer.

Sorrento Beach was closed about five weeks ago when Perth father Greg O'Neill was attacked and killed by a large great white shark as he was swimming close to the shoreline.

Sorrento Beach was closed last month after the fatal shark attack. (ABC News: Andrew O'Connor)

He was the third person killed by a shark in Western Australia this year.

Greg O'Neill, left, was killed by a shark while swimming at Sorrento Beach. (Supplied)

The City of Joondalup removed the whale remains from Sorrento Beach a few hours after surf lifesavers reported seeing them, but said the beaches in the area remained closed as "residue from where the whale carcass was beached may attract sharks to the area".

AI-powered drones on cards for WA shark monitoring Western Australia's shark-tagging program will be expanded and the use of AI-powered drones investigated as new funding is announced.

The Department of Primary Industries and Regional Development (DPIRD), along with staff from other agencies, is monitoring the situation, according to the government's SharkSmart app.

On Thursday, a 3-metre, significantly decomposed partial whale carcass washed up at South Cottesloe beach, triggering the closure of all beaches in the area.

The remains were buried at the Red Hill Waste Management Facility.

Council staff remove the whale carcass from South Cottesloe. (ABC News: Lauren Smith)

On September 27, a 13-metre, 72-tonne humpback whale carcass washed up on South City Beach, requiring an excavator to remove it.

The state government is expanding its shark-tagging program and may use AI-powered drones as part of a suite of measures aimed at keeping beachgoers safe.

World.title: Darwin pregnant patients' medical information posted to Instagram in breach
World.content:
Royal Darwin Hospital has issued an apology for a privacy breach that led to confidential medical information belonging to about a dozen pregnant patients being shared to 28,000 followers on Instagram by a "medical observer" associated with the hospital.

In the letter sent to affected patients, RDH management said NT Health had been informed an overseas trained doctor attached to the hospital's obstetrics and gynaecology unit had posted to social media images and videos where "patient details were visible".

The information exposed included patient names, their presenting condition or any diagnoses they had. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"The information visible about you from our handover sheet included your name, your hospital record number, the ward and bed number, the name of the consultant, the presenting problem, medical history, investigations, and plan of management," the letter said.

"I recognise that learning of this incident may cause distress, embarrassment or concern about your privacy and your trust in our service.

" You should not have had to experience this and we are deeply sorry. "

The content, which has been seen by the ABC, was posted to the Instagram account of Dr Neda Mogharehabed and also included a video from a staff meeting, where health professionals can be heard discussing a woman's care.

Screenshots of the posts featured on the Instagram account @dr.neda.mogharehabed (Supplied)

In a statement to the ABC, Dr Mogharehabed said she "cannot confirm how these images were posted" or "whether they originated from the account I currently control", noting "there may be other accounts using my name".

Dr Mogharehabed added she "did not intend to disclose any patient information" and that she takes "patient privacy seriously".

"I am sorry for the concern this situation has caused. At this stage, however, I cannot verify the origin or circumstances of the images," she said.

In their statement, RDH management noted the doctor as a "medical observer" who was not permitted to undertake any patient management and that her attachment to NT Health had since been terminated.

Dr Neda Mogharehabed is no longer associated with NT Health. (Supplied)

'Shocking' and a 'violation'

One of the women whose information was exposed was ABC Radio Darwin producer, Shanelle Tobin, who is 17-weeks pregnant with her second child.

Ms Tobin said when she went for her appointment at RDH two weeks ago she was asked if she consented to a "medical observer" being present.

"I didn't give it a second thought, I was like 'yep, they're here to learn, to get exposure, whatever it is, I'm comfortable', and now I guess I'm reflecting on that [choice]," Ms Tobin said.

Shanelle Tobin is expecting her second child in April-May next year. (ABC News: Grace Atta)

The expectant mother said the information shared in these medical appointments was detailed and highly sensitive.

"You go through everything from previous pregnancies, whether or not you've had terminations, they talk through your mental health generally and how it was with your last pregnancy," she said.

"Every facet of physical health, so that goes into STIs [sexually transmitted diseases], any issues with your reproductive organs ... your fertility journey, whether that's with IVF or not, and your experience of domestic violence.

" So, yeah it is a very vulnerable space ... and you're just putting your trust in them that this is the cone of silence. "

When Shanelle Tobin saw the screenshots of the images posted showing private informaiton she was shocked. (ABC News: Grace Atta)

Ms Tobin said she discovered her personal information had been shared online when a member of the public reached out to her saying they had seen the post and her name featured.

"It was obviously shocking," she said.

"I then received a phone call from Royal Darwin Hospital from the head of obstetrics who outlined that this breach had happened."

Ms Tobin said when she realised the account had 28,000 followers the "feeling of violation really set in".

Shanelle Tobin says the exposure of her information made her feel "violated". (ABC News: Grace Atta)

'Major wake-up call' for RDH

In a statement, the vice president of the NT Branch of the Australian Medical Association Dr Dayna Duncan said "any breach of patient confidentiality is unacceptable in all situations".

"There are very clear laws and guidelines about patient privacy in Australia, including social media," Dr Duncan said.

"All patients should expect that everyone in their treating team keeps their personal information confidential, with no exceptions."

Dayna Duncan says all patients should expect confidentiality from their treating medical professionals. (ABC News: Marcus Kennedy)

Ms Tobin said she hoped the incident would be a "major wake-up call" for RDH about how it manages patient privacy and educates its staff, including international medical observers, about this principle.

The ABC asked Dr Mogharehabed if she had received any training from RDH about expectations around social media use and patient confidentiality.

Dr Mogharehabed said did not receive any specific training about "photography, video recording or posting content on social media" and that she was "not specifically informed during my observership that posting such content on social media was prohibited".

She added: "To my knowledge, the content I became aware of did not tag or mention Royal Darwin Hospital by name."

NT Health was contacted for comment.

Shanelle Tobin gave birth to her toddler at Royal Darwin Hospital almost three years ago. (ABC News: Grace Atta)

Despite her recent bad experience, Ms Tobin said she still planned to access care and give birth at RDH.

"My birth at RDH with my first baby was a really amazing experience, thanks to the people that work there.

"They are some of the hardest workers you could ever imagine and ... I will put my trust back into those people because I know this is one individual who's decided to act in a certain way."

World.title: Final MotoGP race at Phillip Island washed out
World.content:
The MotoGP race at Phillip Island has been cancelled as heavy rain and poor visibility washed out what was the final race at the island circuit.

All races at the track, including the Australian Superbikes race three and both the Moto2 and Moto3 races, were cancelled earlier on Sunday, with hopes that fans would see the MotoGP take a final turn around the iconic circuit fading as the day passed.

The race will move to a street circuit in Adelaide, South Australia in 2027, after three decades at the circuit on the Bass Coast.

The wet weather derailed plans for a final lap of the Ventnor circuit, with the announcement made at 3:30pm that the MotoGP race had been called off after motoring fans sat in the stands for hours in the rain.

Jack Miller farewells fans after the race was cancelled. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

The race had been delayed from its original 2pm start time, with hopes it would begin at 4:30pm.

A MotoGP riders farewell lap was being held at 3:45pm.

Racing fans braved the wet and windy conditions at the track before the race was cancelled. (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

In a statement, the Australian Grand Prix Corporation said poor visibility that prevented the medical helicopter from flying was behind the cancellation.

"We know this is an incredibly disappointing outcome for fans, teams and everyone who has contributed to the event," it said.

"Safety must always come first, and racing cannot take place without the medical helicopter able to operate."

The corporation said it would provide full refunds for Sunday ticketholders and partial refunds for multi-day ticketholders.

The official morning warm up was also cancelled, along with track side entertainment such as the monster trucks and a celebratory legends lap with world champions Mick Doohan, Casey Stoner and Wayne Gardner.

World.title: A third of households struggling to feed themselves
World.content:
PoliticsFederalInflation A third of households struggling to feed themselves Shane Wright October 26, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One in three households are going hungry as the cost-of-living crisis bites, new research by one of the nation’s most important charities has found, and many people are reducing meal portions to make ends meet. The research by Foodbank, to be released on Monday, shows 3.6 million households are suffering “food insecurity”. Renters, the disabled, young people and people on low incomes are among the most affected. A third of Australian households reported suffering from food insecurity over the past year. iStock The situation has become so dire that many Australians are being forced to cut their use of shampoo, toothpaste and soap. Inflation data to be released this week is expected to confirm ongoing price pressures for household essentials, prompting a further interest rate hike from the Reserve Bank when it meets at the start of next month.



The biggest increase in prices over the past year has been in petrol – up by almost 14 per cent. But there have been steep lifts in other essentials including beef (9.4 per cent), lamb (10.1 per cent) and milk (8 per cent). Related Article Charity Revolt grows over Labor’s $2m cut to lifeline for struggling Australians Foodbank surveyed almost 6000 Australians, testing their access to food against the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation’s definition of insecurity, which is when a person does not have regular access to sufficient nourishing food to provide for proper development and a healthy life. It found 33 per cent of households experienced food security over the past 12 months – a slight increase on the 32.8 per cent found in 2025 but still well short of the 35.9 per cent discovered in 2023. But there were wide differences depending on income, family structure and location.



Food insecurity was most common among young households, which covers people aged between 18 and 34, at 48 per cent. It was lowest among households with people over the age of 55 at 19 per cent. Forty-five per cent of households with children suffered food insecurity compared to 28 per cent among households without children. The highest insecurity rate was among Indigenous households at 57 per cent. Households in regional areas (36 per cent) had a higher insecurity rate than people living in metropolitan areas (32 per cent). Foodbank Australia chief executive, former independent MP Kylea Tink, said it appeared food insecurity had become entrenched across the country and that it was affecting more middle income households.



“We call ourselves the lucky country, but for one in three households, Australia is now the hungry country,” she said. “Sadly, hunger has become part of the Australian story.” Among middle income households with incomes between $33,800 and $90,999, 37 per cent reported food insecurity. “A wage used to be what kept food on the table, but for a growing number of working Australians, their pay packet no longer stretches that far,” Tink said. Foodbank found that the most common way food-insecure households dealt with cost-of-living pressures was to drive less or use less expensive forms of transport. While 41 per cent of households with secure food access had cut driving, 70 per cent of those in food security had done so.



Related Article Opinion

Retirement living The retirement dilemma no calculator in the world can solve Bec Wilson Money contributor This week’s inflation figures pre-dates the recent surge in global oil prices, which have pushed Brent crude beyond $US110 a barrel – its highest level since the earliest stages of the war against Iran. Since the end of August, unleaded prices at the pump have climbed by almost 40¢ a litre to beyond $2.40. Two-thirds of food-insecure households reported they had cut spending on personal care and grooming services such as haircuts and similar numbers looked for sales or discounts to buy grocery items and cut their use of heating or cooling. Food portions or ingredients in meals were reduced in half of food-insecure households while 21 per cent of secure households had done so. In another bid to make ends meet, 47 per cent of insecure households revealed they had reduced spending on cleaning or personal care goods such as soap, shampoo and toothpaste. Just 4 per cent of those facing food insecurity said they had not changed their spending habits, compared to a more than a fifth of those in food security.



Last week, Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser said that while interest rate increases were hitting people with a mortgage, they were in much better financial health than people on low incomes, including renters who were being hurt by high inflation. The Foodbank survey confirmed the hit to renters, of whom 51 per cent said they were in food insecurity. The charity wants the federal government to establish a national minimum standard for school breakfast programs. World.title: AFLW round 11: ‘Difficult decision’ as Dons sack inaugural coach; Kangas back on top
World.content:
Essendon will replace inaugural AFLW coach Natalie Wood next season after informing her that her contract would not be renewed for 2027 after the team’s 1-10 record this season.

Wood was informed on Tuesday about the decision, but players were only told after Sunday’s five-point loss to Hawthorn.

Bombers coach Natalie Wood leads her side on Sunday. AFL Photos

Wood is still planning to coach the final round game next Sunday against fellow strugglers Collingwood.

The Dons will be the third AFLW club seeking a coach, joining St Kilda and expansion club Tasmania Devils.

“The club is not offering me a contract as of next year,” Wood said post game on Sunday.

“It’s been a topic of conversation and a lot of questions with our poor performances this year

“It’s a disappointing end, as clearly I would have liked, like the last couple of years, to have better performances on the field.”

The Dons have struggled with injuries and form this season, but Wood was heartened by the club locking in several future leaders to new contracts but they will look for a new coach.

“We have fallen short of what we wanted on field. We believe a change is the right step,” Essendon chief executive Tim Roberts said.

“Natalie has handled this with real integrity, and her commitment to coaching out the season says a lot about her and how much she cares about the players.

“We thank Natalie for everything she has given the club over five seasons, and we wish her all the best for the next step in her football journey.”

Wood was the first female coach to reach 50 games while leading the team for five seasons since they entered the competition.

“[I] just continued on with the week as normal,” Wood said.

“We had two amazing players in Alex Morcom and Maddi Gay having their 50th and 75th game today, so really important celebrations, and we also had Amelia Radford announce her retirement.

Hayley McLaughlin of the Hawks kicks for goal against Essendon on Sunday. AFL Photos via Getty Images

“I would prefer no one ever knows, and I’d just disappear off into the sunset without any discussion or interview, but I was particularly aware this week of not wanting to get in the way of those three players.

“We really wanted to beat Hawthorn today. I thought we put up a really good fight, it was an ugly game of footy, tricky conditions. But always forefront of my mind is playing group first – so I thought it was best to hold off until today.

“Aysha (Ward, AFLW general manager) is heavily pregnant and is going on leave in two or three weeks, so I think the club is keen on getting a start in searching for their new coach.”

Wood said it was hard leading the AFLW side while Essendon as a club has faced so many leadership changes in recent seasons.

“Am I disappointed it’s fallen out this way? It depends how narrow of a view I have of it. Sometimes,” Wood said.

“I remember in my job interview, we were discussing about the wants of the role. [At the time], no female coach had lasted longer than two years, and I was not wanting to step into a senior coaching role without being well prepared and supported to have a career that’s longer than two years,” Wood said.

“To be the first female coach to coach 50 games, I’m really proud of that. To build a team from ground-up, as one of the last expansion teams and the season coming forward, it was a mad rush.

“At the same time, the club’s had a lot of instability. There’s been four CEOs, three presidents, three men’s senior captains and three senior coaches, so to build a culture within a program while the instability of the club – and it’s in a good spot now – it’s been hard at times while there’s been so much change in structure and leadership.

“When I look back to the start of the season and we had so many players sign long-term contracts, players who are really important to the program going forward - we’ve built a culture and place where players really want to be. I’ve done something right.”

The Hawks scored a vital win in their quest to make the top eight, winning by five points in rain-soaked conditions at the club’s new base in Dingley.

The Bombers were brave but couldn’t find the last goal they needed to get the win.

With AAP

World.title: Voters call for local AI safeguards as data centre concern rises
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalAI Voters call for local AI safeguards as data centre concern rises Shane Wright October 25, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Voters want Australian-specific laws to regulate AI rather than reliance on an international agreement, exclusive polling shows while also showing rising concern that a multibillion-dollar data centre building boom will hurt local communities and the environment. Amid claims that new data centres will drive up power prices by $50 billion over the next six years if developers fail to build new energy sources for them, a Resolve poll of 2200 people shows a generational gap between those who think the technology will deliver revolutionary long-lasting benefits to the world and those who fear its consequences. Data centre construction has become a lightning rod in some communities. Chris Hopkins AI proponents argue the technology will unleash a new wave of productivity growth akin to the advent of the personal computer or electricity. The building of data centres is driving global economic growth and contributing to a sharp increase in Australian private sector investment. But even supporters have expressed concern about AI’s impact, from wiping out jobs to its use of power and water and the way the AI boom is contributing to higher interest rates on government debt.



A House-Senate select committee, due to report to the government by end of next month, is examining AI and its impact on the national jobs market, productivity, copyright laws and workers’ rights. The Resolve poll found two-thirds of respondents now use AI. A quarter said they used it daily. In 2023, when Resolve first posed this question, just 31 per cent said they had used AI. Younger Australians, aged between 18 and 34, were the most likely to use AI, at 87 per cent. But even among those aged at least 55, almost half had used the technology. Among regular users, 23 per cent said the technology posed a danger to mankind and society, but among non-users this figure climbed to 60 per cent. Fifty-four per cent of regular users said AI carried some risks but the benefits of the technology outweighed those issues. Just 26 per cent of non-users had the same view. And while 17 per cent of regular users agreed that AI posed minimal risks and would deliver revolutionary benefits to society, just 2 per cent of non-users were as optimistic.



Related Article Updated

Investigations ‘Worse and worse’: Data centre backlash threatens billions in building boom The level of concern about the overall risks posed by technology is growing. In 2023, an overwhelming 72 per cent backed constraints on the technology, with 44 per cent supporting international regulation compared with 29 per cent who wanted Australian-designed laws. Overall regulation support has now lifted to 81 per cent. But there has been a change in views on who should regulate: 41 per cent now back Australian-led laws compared with 40 per cent for an international approach. Just 20 per cent of those questioned believe AI regulation should continue at its current pace. Thirty-one per cent said it should slow, 10 per cent said it should it be paused temporarily, and another 18 per cent agreed it should completely stop.



Resolve Political Monitor pollster Jim Reed said it appeared most workers believed AI would help them or not unduly affect their work, but at the same time a large share of people feared for the fate of the planet from the technology. “Less than one in five think it is a danger to their job or wages,” Reed said. “However, more than a third think it is a real danger to mankind. No wonder around six in 10 think AI development should at least be slowed or paused, if not given the boot altogether.” One of the most contested parts of AI has been data centre construction. Westpac economists have estimated new data centres worth $155 billion or more than 5 per cent of GDP are in the nation’s construction pipeline. But Resolve found while 32 per cent supported data centres in Australia, 33 per cent were opposed and 35 per cent were unsure.



There was a large age gap between supporters and opponents, with 42 per cent of those aged between 18 and 34 backing them compared with 22 per cent among over 55s. Half of regular AI users support them compared with just 16 per cent of non-users. The single largest concern about data centres, shared by 50 per cent of respondents, was their use of power, with 48 per cent expressing concern about their water use. Thirty-seven per cent were worried about a data centre being built near them, and the same proportion were concerned about their impact on the environment.



Modelling to be released on Monday by the Smart Energy Council shows the concerns over power and water may not be misplaced. The modelling found that adding an extra five gigawatts of demand for power from data centres without additional clean power and storage would “cannibalise” the existing grid and force up household and consumer prices. The federal government wants data centres to supply their own renewable energy sources, but there is a push by some states and territories to use existing and new fossil-fuel power sources. But the energy council argues building new fossil-fuel power stations will drive up overall costs, which it estimates at between $6.8 billion and $11.1 billion for domestic power bills and between $35 billion and $38.8 billion for the business sector. The hardest-hit state would be Queensland. The council argues the cost of new coal-fired power stations could add $1157 to the power bills of residents there over a six-year window. Victorian and NSW consumers would also face higher power bills.



“Data centres must bring their own new, clean electricity to the table,” council chief executive David McElrea said. “If tech giants are allowed to plug straight into the existing grid without building dedicated new renewable generation and firming storage, it is ordinary families and local businesses who will

pay the price through sky-high power bills.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Turbo hat-trick seals win but Kangaroos left with more questions than answers
World.content:
Australia triumphed, but Fiji – and especially their five-eighth Kurt Donoghoe – were the real winners.

The Kangaroos survived an almighty scare against Fiji on Sunday night when they prevailed 36-22 at Suncorp Stadium.

The Roos were largely out-enthused by the Bati who were still pushing for a miracle win late in the second half.

Most of the 41,108 fans who turned up on a humid night in the Queensland capital were expecting the Roos to run riot.

Tom Trbojevic’s hat-trick helped Australia sneak past Fiji. Getty Images

Bradman Best, Sam Walker, David Fifita and Blayke Brailey were all making their debut in the green and gold, while coach Kevin Walters had one of the best six-man benches ever assembled, but only used three reserves, and kept Cameron Munster, Harry Grant, Latrell Mitchell all fresh for next Saturday’s clash against the Cook Islands in Townsville.

Australia will want to use that game to blow out the last of the rust and get serious about their World Cup campaign.

They got the job done against New Zealand last week courtesy of some Jack Bostock aerial theatrics, a couple of intercept tries, and Reece Walsh X factor.

Against Fiji, James Tedesco ran the ball on the last just before half-time to give Australia a 12-10 lead they did not deserve, while Trbojevic bagged a hat-trick in the space of 15 minutes to all but seal the result.

Trbojevic, however, would have been frustrated knowing Fiji targeted his right side, with Donoghoe setting up Semi Valemei for his own treble.

The win over Fiji means they will now play their semi-final in a fortnight’s time, on November 8, in Sydney.

At one stage early in the second half, when Fiji were playing with spirit, and could sense a boilover against the top-ranked rugby league nation, there was plenty of confusion and activity on the Roos’ bench. In the end, ‘Turbo’s’ tries restored the peace.

Whether Walker or Tom Dearden should partner Munster in the halves is no clearer. Tedesco was also excellent, which makes for a fascinating No. 1 battle given Walsh’s outstanding performace against the Kiwis.

Sam Walker celebrates his first try for the Kangaroos. Getty Images

Fiji were winning the physical battle and making plenty of metres through the middle of the field at the start of the game, despite coughing up the ball on three seaprate occasions.

But Tedesco spotted some tiring defenders on the last tackle, sprinted past some defenders, found Walker who found Trbojevic who passed to Walker to score.

A lovely ball from Tedesco put Kotoni Staggs into space for the opening try after ten minutes.

A Trbojevic handling error inside his own half allowed the visitors to go on the attack, and they were over a minute later when Donoghoe floated a brilliant ball for Valemei for his first.

Fiji then took the lead when Brandon Wakeham’s grubber sat up perfectly for Taane Milne.

There were no injuries for Australia but Cam Murray did need a head injury assessment, which he passed, only to be given a rare spell with ten minutes remaining.

World.title: The Melbourne Cup is not the only vital race being staged at Flemington
World.content:
Blinkers On SportRacingVictorian racing The Melbourne Cup is not the only vital race being staged at Flemington Danny Russell October 25, 2026 — 7:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Ladies and gentlemen of the Flemington members’ stands, start your engines. A coveted place at one of the most prestigious tables in this country’s sporting landscape is up for grabs – a seat on the Victoria Racing Club board – and the contest is shaping somewhere between a demolition derby and a boat race. The Victoria Racing Club board is set for change following this year’s Melbourne Cup week at Flemington. Getty Images Nominations to join the board opened last week, and if trackside chatter is to be believed there will be some robust jostling, and behind-the-scenes campaigning, to get to the front of the queue. At least one seat will be filled by a new face. Club chair Neil Wilson announced his resignation last month and will be stepping away from the role at the annual general meeting in December.



Related Article Victorian racing Profits prompt Wilson’s departure from VRC as he downplays talk of board rift But adding spice to the mix is the fact that Wilson’s anointed successor, director Vin Cox, as well as club treasurer Glenn Carmody and fellow committee member Michael Saadie are all up for re-election. That’s four seats up for grabs. This throws up some startling possibilities. If more than one nomination is ratified, and there is behind-the-scenes talk of up to five interested parties, it will lead to an election that could change the composition of a long-stable VRC board. The director with the most to lose, or gain, is Cox.



Firstly, he needs to be re-elected before accepting the chair’s role from Wilson at the coming AGM - a controversial succession plan decided by a secret ballot last month. The Age quoted an inside source two weeks ago who claimed Cox was given the nod 6-5 – in a vote involving 11 directors – over vice-chairman Michael Ramsden. VRC chairman Neil Wilson, left, at the Cox Plate with Racing Minister Anthony Carbines and Moonee Valley chairman Adam Lennen. Wayne Taylor Secondly, if Cox is re-elected, he then needs to quickly reaffirm numbers at the boardroom table to quell speculation of a coup. In theory, a 6-5 vote in favour of Cox is easily reversed with at least one director being replaced.



But there are even wider ramifications than Cox’s potential rocky ascension to the throne, including the future direction of the VRC, which governs Flemington and runs Melbourne Cup week. Wilson has long been loyal to the VRC’s history and need for independence. He has continually shut down merger talks, as racing looks for new ways to make Melbourne’s three major clubs more efficient, and recently opposed changes to government legislation because he felt it would strip autonomy from his club. Only time will tell whether a Wilson-less VRC board will offer the same resistance. Nominations close on Oaks Day. Sheza Alibi gaps the field in the Doncaster Mile in April. Getty Images





It is a question that historically would have had an answer. In the trouble-free years before New South Wales’ self-serving creation of a $10 million pop-up race – the Golden Eagle – the country’s best four-year-olds ran in the country’s best weight-for-age race. Anamoe won at four in 2022, Winx in 2015, So You Think in 2010, Sunline in 1999 and Saintly in 1996. Not any more. History is being rewritten and Australia’s racing pattern (fixture) is in disarray. As the Cox Plate shows, we no longer have the best horses competing against each other in our grand final races. Instead, we have split the pack and become racing’s version of LIV Golf.



Sheza Alibi, trained by Peter Moody and Katherine Coleman, is a case in point. Her connections have bypassed the $6 million Cox Plate, and a clash with Cosmic Crusader, to chase greater riches. She will start odds-on favourite in Saturday’s $10 million 1500m Golden Eagle at Randwick – a race restricted to four-year-olds that was surprisingly awarded group 1 status by the Asian Racing Federation this year. Or, it should have been surprising had Racing Australia not been so impotent while the landscape was being reshaped – we say for the worse – by NSW in recent years. Cosmic Crusader wins the first Cox Plate run at Flemington. Getty Images Cosmic question No,2



The second question to emerge from Saturday’s Cox Plate meeting is also unanswerable, but equally worthy of debate. Related Article Cox Plate No October joy for Carlton stars on Cox Plate’s sojourn to Flemington Would Cosmic Crusader have beaten the same Cox Plate field on the tight-turning circuit of Moonee Valley instead of the long, wide straight of Flemington? No one will ever know, of course, but will next year be any different? Because if a rebuilt Moonee Valley is to reclaim its standing as the race’s spiritual home in 2027, as most believe it should, it needs to have its house on order to become a worthy host.



That’s no easy feat when a crowd of 30,000 punters are clicking through your turnstiles, and you don’t have a grandstand. In comparison, Flemington has three. The pressure is on the Valley hierarchy to get it right. Their promise of hosting members and dignitaries in elaborate Birdcage-like structures that line a new, longer straight is one thing, but catering for the rank-and-file punters, the backbone of the sport, is another. They will need somewhere to sit, like a mega temporary grandstand. Without it, Cosmic Crusader could be defending his crown back at Flemington. Heaven forbid.



Punters cheer home a winner at Flemington on Cox Plate day. Justin McManus Odds against punters. Again Flicking through the World Pool tote dividends continues to make for depressing reading. Those who placed a TAB tote bet on Flemington races on Saturday were once again sold short. Cox Plate winner Cosmic Crusader paid $9.50 TAB fixed odds and just $8.20 on the TAB’s World Pool tote; Moonee Valley Gold Cup winner Juja Kibo paid $8 fixed compared to $6.35 World Pool; and Crystal Mile winner Surfin Bird paid $2.80 fixed and $2.35 world pool.



That’s a significant difference, and all nine races at Flemington had a negative price discrepancy. The problem, as this column has raised before, is the takeout. Related Article Blinkers On

Victorian racing Racing’s big gambling problem, and why it’s hurting punters The World Pool tote, which merges with the Australian tote for big race days, continually operates above 120 per cent. This means for every $120 bet, it keeps $20, meaning a poorer return for punters.



When the Hong Kong-based World Pool merges with our tote for Australian races, it creates a bigger cash pool and a bigger turnover by attracting international punters, which then increases returns to the industry and rebates for professional syndicates, but leaves the grassroots punter worse off. Leek jumps for joy Despite its many detractors, the shaky future of jumps racing must be given new consideration following the profound impact it has had on Melbourne’s spring. The jumps jockeys have reigned supreme, and there has not been a hurdle in sight. Consider these achievements.



Caulfield Cup winner Kingswood is trained by former jumps jockey Gavin Bedggood and ridden by part-time jumps jockey John Allen. Trainer Andrea Leek poses with the trophy. Getty Images Cox Plate winner Cosmic Crusader is trained by former jumps jockey Andrea Leek, the first female trainer to win the race in 32 years. And that is before we even start on Ciaron Maher – the one-time farm boy from Warrnambool who cut his teeth by tackling the jumps. As career moves go, Maher’s decision to become a trainer has proven a masterstroke.



Not only is he neck-and-neck with Chris Waller as the country’s leading stable, he ran the trifecta in Saturday’s Moonee Valley Gold Cup with rising stayers Juja Kibo, Kings Valley and Mr Monaco. Maher could have an unprecedented nine starters in next week’s Melbourne Cup, including Point Of Law, Saint George, Middle Earth, Shockletz, Zahrann and Royal Supremacy. “A lot of jump jockeys are hands-on, where maybe the flat jockeys aren’t as hands on,” Leek said of her ability to train a horse. “The flat jockeys are sort of on and off (the horse), where we do the background work as well. “Everyone loves to get their horses fit, but we just do it that little bit differently. And I think having a jumping background, like Ciaron Maher is showing that and Gavin Bedggood, it really helps you know the differences in your horse.”



How does the racing industry place a price on that? Bad day for Ballarat Interesting to see the jockey fraternity vote with their feet on Friday, forcing the abandonment of the Ballarat meeting because of concerns over the surface. The riders first raised the issue with trackside stewards after a runner slipped near the 1000m mark during the second race. Quick repairs were ordered, but they did not do the trick.



The jockeys voted 14 to three to call the meeting off. Sports news, results and expert commentary.

World.title: Test cricket isn’t going anywhere. But it does need some help
World.content:
SportCricketTest cricket Opinion Test cricket isn’t going anywhere. But it does need some help Greg Chappell Former Australian Test captain October 25, 2026 — 7:33pm

October 25, 2026 — 7:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Early in my career, I learned that when things weren’t going my way, bemoaning my luck got me nowhere. I had to change my approach. The same lesson applies to Test cricket today, and the first change we need is how we read the evidence. This follows the second Test between South Africa and Australia at St George’s Park in Gqeberha, where rain did not save Australia from a humbling defeat. It was grim stuff for Pat Cummins and Australian in Gqeberha. AP Photo/Themba Hadebe Worryingly, the familiar chorus has started: sparse crowds, the critics say, prove the longest format is dying. I don’t think they prove that. But the game’s administrators should feel distinctly uncomfortable because the real threats to Test cricket are less visible than empty seats, and they can fix them.



What the empty seats tell us A thin weekday crowd is a scheduling result, not a verdict on the format. This series sits in a shoulder window: after the peak of the rugby and soccer seasons, before the domestic summer begins, and across school and university exams. Asking families, students and young professionals to give up several consecutive weekdays at that time of year is asking the impossible, and that is before we count the cost of tickets, transport and food for households under real financial pressure. Fans hardly flocked to the first Test between South Africa and Australia in Durban. AP Put the same contest in the middle of summer and the picture changes. Boxing Day, New Year’s Test and Ashes Tests still fill grounds. Demand for the best Test cricket, played when people can attend, has not disappeared. So the gate is a poor test of the format’s health. Better questions are:



Do the best players choose to play Tests?

Do broadcasters and streamers pay properly for them?

Can smaller nations afford to host and tour? On those questions, the news is more worrying. The real threat is collision T20 is not Test cricket’s executioner, but I won’t pretend it is a harmless neighbour. When the SA20 overlapped with South Africa’s tour of New Zealand in early 2025, the Proteas had to send a squad featuring seven uncapped players, led by a captain (Neil Brand) who had never played a Test match. With stars such as Virat Kohli, the Indian Premier League has gone from strength to strength. AP



That is the ultimate indignity when franchise leagues and international cricket overlap in the same weeks and one pays far better. I don’t blame players for choosing to secure their families’ futures. The failure belongs entirely to administrators who built (and tolerate) a calendar that forces that choice. Right now, Test cricket is thriving—but only if you belong to the “Big Three” of India, Australia and England, who pass a profitable revenue bucket back and forth in five-match marquee series. For the rest of the world, hosting a Test match is a fast way to go broke. Yet T20 also pays the bills Both things are true. The IPL, the BBL and the SA20 generate the broadcast and sponsorship revenue the sport relies on. Boards outside the wealthiest nations cannot fund Test hosting and touring from Test revenue alone. The answer is neither to fight T20 nor to hope it will be generous. Make co-existence a condition of doing business.



The one-way street Any serious settlement has to begin with the IPL because it is the world’s biggest league yet, paradoxically, the least reciprocal. It already occupies more than two months of the calendar, and it is reportedly set to expand further in 2028. For nearly two decades, it has drawn on the best players from every other country. Yet Indian players under BCCI contracts are barred from every other franchise league. I understand the case for that: workload and protecting the IPL brand. But a league cannot systematically strip the world’s asset pool while keeping its own off-limits and then expect everyone else to bend their Test calendars to fit its ever-expanding footprint. That cost falls on the other boards and on the players, who are left to choose between country and contract. Leagues need sanction from national boards and the ICC, and their players need release from their home boards. That gives the game leverage, and it should use it. I would write four conditions into every single league sanction:



A Test levy and guaranteed match fees: A fixed share of domestic league revenue must go into a global Test fund. This fund should serve two purposes: subsidising hosting costs for smaller nations so they can afford three-Test series instead of hollow two-Test jokes, and establishing a competitive global minimum Test match fee. If a young West Indian, Kiwi or South African cricketer knows that pulling on the creams guarantees a premium, reliable income, the temptation to abandon a Test tour for a short-term franchise contract evaporates.

A fixed share of domestic league revenue must go into a global Test fund. This fund should serve two purposes: subsidising hosting costs for smaller nations so they can afford three-Test series instead of hollow two-Test jokes, and establishing a competitive global minimum Test match fee. If a young West Indian, Kiwi or South African cricketer knows that pulling on the creams guarantees a premium, reliable income, the temptation to abandon a Test tour for a short-term franchise contract evaporates. Protected windows: The Future Tours Programme must ring-fence each host nation’s peak summer for Test cricket. The domestic leagues must schedule around international windows, not the other way around. Series should also be long enough to matter. A two-Test series is a cipher. Barely a story, forget an event.

The Future Tours Programme must ring-fence each host nation’s peak summer for Test cricket. The domestic leagues must schedule around international windows, not the other way around. Series should also be long enough to matter. A two-Test series is a cipher. Barely a story, forget an event. Full-strength squads: No sanctioned franchise window can overlap an ICC-scheduled Test series. Selectors must be free to pick their absolute best XI without forcing a player into an agonising contract dispute between country and club.

No sanctioned franchise window can overlap an ICC-scheduled Test series. Selectors must be free to pick their absolute best XI without forcing a player into an agonising contract dispute between country and club. Absolute reciprocity: Any league that draws on international players must accept the same rules as everyone else. The IPL has completed 19 seasons, drawing on global talent throughout its existence while barring Indian players under BCCI contract from participating in overseas leagues. Player release must work both ways. A league that wants the world’s best should be willing to share its own. English and Australian administrators, in particular, need to be tougher. We must stop being pusillanimous collaborators and sycophants when the future of Test cricket is at stake. Australia is one country where Test cricket isn’t a financial impost. Getty Images Scarce, not exclusive Some argue Test cricket should become a luxury product, like the majors in tennis and golf. I take one lesson from that: fewer, better-placed Tests, each treated as an event. I reject the price tag. The majors are annual showpieces. Tests are how most of us first fell in love with the game. In a country where cost-of-living pressure is real, pricing families out would be self-defeating. Make Tests premium in the calendar and accessible at the gate: cheap weekday tickets for schools and students, affordable family days and broadcasts that tell the contest’s story and the score.





That is a management failure, and leadership, not appeasement, must fix it. I learned long ago that bemoaning your luck changes nothing. The custodians of the game should stop wringing their hands over empty seats in Gqeberha and write rules that let the longest format thrive alongside the shortest. After all, it demands more of a player than any other form of the game: skill, patience and character – just ask Kohli or Starc. And that is worth protecting. World.title: A third of households struggling to feed themselves
World.content:
PoliticsFederalInflation A third of households struggling to feed themselves Shane Wright October 26, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One in three households are going hungry as the cost-of-living crisis bites, new research by one of the nation’s most important charities has found, and many people are reducing meal portions to make ends meet. The research by Foodbank, to be released on Monday, shows 3.6 million households are suffering “food insecurity”. Renters, the disabled, young people and people on low incomes are among the most affected. A third of Australian households reported suffering from food insecurity over the past year. iStock The situation has become so dire that many Australians are being forced to cut their use of shampoo, toothpaste and soap. Inflation data to be released this week is expected to confirm ongoing price pressures for household essentials, prompting a further interest rate hike from the Reserve Bank when it meets at the start of next month.



The biggest increase in prices over the past year has been in petrol – up by almost 14 per cent. But there have been steep lifts in other essentials including beef (9.4 per cent), lamb (10.1 per cent) and milk (8 per cent). Related Article Charity Revolt grows over Labor’s $2m cut to lifeline for struggling Australians Foodbank surveyed almost 6000 Australians, testing their access to food against the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organisation’s definition of insecurity, which is when a person does not have regular access to sufficient nourishing food to provide for proper development and a healthy life. It found 33 per cent of households experienced food security over the past 12 months – a slight increase on the 32.8 per cent found in 2025 but still well short of the 35.9 per cent discovered in 2023. But there were wide differences depending on income, family structure and location.



Food insecurity was most common among young households, which covers people aged between 18 and 34, at 48 per cent. It was lowest among households with people over the age of 55 at 19 per cent. Forty-five per cent of households with children suffered food insecurity compared to 28 per cent among households without children. The highest insecurity rate was among Indigenous households at 57 per cent. Households in regional areas (36 per cent) had a higher insecurity rate than people living in metropolitan areas (32 per cent). Foodbank Australia chief executive, former independent MP Kylea Tink, said it appeared food insecurity had become entrenched across the country and that it was affecting more middle income households.



“We call ourselves the lucky country, but for one in three households, Australia is now the hungry country,” she said. “Sadly, hunger has become part of the Australian story.” Among middle income households with incomes between $33,800 and $90,999, 37 per cent reported food insecurity. “A wage used to be what kept food on the table, but for a growing number of working Australians, their pay packet no longer stretches that far,” Tink said. Foodbank found that the most common way food-insecure households dealt with cost-of-living pressures was to drive less or use less expensive forms of transport. While 41 per cent of households with secure food access had cut driving, 70 per cent of those in food security had done so.



Related Article Opinion

Retirement living The retirement dilemma no calculator in the world can solve Bec Wilson Money contributor This week’s inflation figures pre-dates the recent surge in global oil prices, which have pushed Brent crude beyond $US110 a barrel – its highest level since the earliest stages of the war against Iran. Since the end of August, unleaded prices at the pump have climbed by almost 40¢ a litre to beyond $2.40. Two-thirds of food-insecure households reported they had cut spending on personal care and grooming services such as haircuts and similar numbers looked for sales or discounts to buy grocery items and cut their use of heating or cooling. Food portions or ingredients in meals were reduced in half of food-insecure households while 21 per cent of secure households had done so. In another bid to make ends meet, 47 per cent of insecure households revealed they had reduced spending on cleaning or personal care goods such as soap, shampoo and toothpaste. Just 4 per cent of those facing food insecurity said they had not changed their spending habits, compared to a more than a fifth of those in food security.



Last week, Reserve Bank deputy governor Andrew Hauser said that while interest rate increases were hitting people with a mortgage, they were in much better financial health than people on low incomes, including renters who were being hurt by high inflation. The Foodbank survey confirmed the hit to renters, of whom 51 per cent said they were in food insecurity. The charity wants the federal government to establish a national minimum standard for school breakfast programs.
